SEVENTH EDITION 2026
© Ministry of Health, Dodoma, Tanzania
FOREWORD
In line with the 2014 World Health Assembly resolution 67.22 and the 2008 African Union resolution 141 on Access to Essential Medicines, the Government of Tanzania, with great pride and deep commitment to the health and well-being of our people, presents the Revised Standard Treatment Guidelines and the National Essential Medicines List 2026. This edition represents a significant milestone in our ongoing effort to strengthen the delivery of equitable, high-quality, evidence-based health care services across all levels of the healthcare system. This commitment is well enshrined in Article 14 of the 1977 Constitution of the United Republic of Tanzania, which states that everyone has the right to life and to receive protection of their life from society, in accordance with the law. Access to safe, effective, and affordable medicines guided by clear, context-appropriate clinical standards is fundamental to achieving Universal Health Insurance (UHI) and improving health outcomes for all Tanzanians.
Aligned with the 2009 Public Health Act, Tanzania has made notable progress over the years in reducing maternal and child morbidity and mortality, combating communicable and non-communicable diseases, and addressing emerging and re- emerging public health threats. According to the 2007 National Health Policy Paragraph 5.41b(v) and 5.4.3c(i) and Tanzania Vision 2050, the Government of Tanzania, working with its partners, is mandated to provide stewardship in ensuring an affordable, adequate and safe supply of quality medicine and nutrition products to all health facilities and the community in need. In light of the above, and given evolving disease patterns, emerging scientific evidence, antimicrobial resistance, and persistent health system gaps, the regular review of the Standard Treatment Guidelines and National Essential Medicine List (STG/NEMLIT) is important. Periodic updates ensure alignment with the Essential Medicines List, promote the rational use of medicines, enhance the quality and standardisation of care, improve cost-effectiveness, and ensure that treatment recommendations remain responsive to national priorities and the changing health needs of the population.
This 2026 revision has been undertaken through an inclusive, consultative and transparent process engaging stakeholders from the Ministry of Health and its Institutions, the Prime Minister's Office, the Regional Administration and Local Government, Frontline healthcare workers from primary to tertiary health care facilities, both public and private, Professional associations, Academic institutions and implementing partners. Different levels of evidence, from local to regional epidemiological data, pharmacoeconomic analyses, and the 24th World Health Organisation (WHO) Model List of Essential Medicines, have guided the review process and the selection of National Essential Medicines, ensuring relevance to the Tanzanian context, disease burden, and available resources.
The revised Standard Treatment Guidelines provide clear, practical clinical pathways for the diagnosis, treatment and referral of priority conditions encountered in our health facilities. These Guidelines are designed to support health care providers at the primary and tertiary levels of the health care system in making informed clinical decisions that enhance patient outcomes. The accompanying National Essential Medicines List reflects our commitment to rational use of medicines, prioritising those interventions that are scientifically proven, cost-effective and aligned with national health priorities. Further, the document will guide the procurement and supply of medicines at the Medical Stores Department (MSD), the prescribing and dispensing of medicines in public health facilities, and the reimbursement of medicines by the National Health Insurance Fund (NHIF).
We realise that the successful implementation of STG/NEMLIT depends on the collective efforts of all health sector stakeholders. Mentorship, supervision, supply chain management, monitoring and evaluation will be vital to translating STG/NEMLIT into quality of care at the point of service. We call upon all health care professionals and policymakers to champion the adoption and rational use of these tools within their respective spheres of influence.
Finally, we extend our heartfelt appreciation to all individuals and institutions who contributed their expertise, time, insight, and financial support to the development of this seventh edition, 2026. Your dedication has helped shape a resource that will guide clinical practice over the next three years. Together, let us continue to strive for a healthier Tanzania where every person has access to the care they need, when and where they need it.
Lastly, in exercising the powers conferred on me by the President of the United Republic of Tanzania through Government Notice No. 686 19th December of 2025, I hereby declare that the Standard Treatment Guidelines and the National Essential Medicines List – 7th Edition 2026 are endorsed for public use.

Hon. Mohamed O. Mchengerwa (MP)
MINISTER OF HEALTH

ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS
This document was developed through a broad, inclusive, and consultative process involving diverse stakeholders across the health sector. Such a participatory approach promotes shared ownership of the Standard Treatment Guidelines and National Essential Medicines List for Tanzania (STG and NEMLIT) and enhances commitment to its effective implementation. The review process began in October 2024 with the identification of key stakeholders, who were provided with a structured tool to systematically gather their recommendations. These recommendations were based on their experience with the use, awareness, and implementation of the STG/NEMLIT, as well as their assessment of its effectiveness, relevance, and areas requiring improvement.
The Ministry of Health conducted a survey to gather recommendations for the review of the Standard Treatment Guidelines and National Essential Medicines List for Tanzania (STG and NEMLIT). A wide range of stakeholders participated in this process, including healthcare facilities from Dodoma, Geita, Iringa, Kigoma, Mbeya, Ruvuma, Mtwara, Tabora, Manyara, and Dar es Salaam, representing primary, secondary, and tertiary levels of care. These facilities actively contributed valuable recommendations to inform the review.
Additional stakeholders included institutions, programmes, and departments operating under the Ministry of Health, as well as academic institutions, professional associations, and development partners.
I extend my sincere appreciation to all healthcare workers and stakeholders who contributed their time, expertise, and valuable recommendations. Their inputs were carefully consolidated and used to strengthen and enrich this document.
In a further step, Lead reviewers for the individual chapters were nominated. We sincerely thank all professional associations that participated in the review through their peer reviewers, thereby making the process fully participatory and technically robust. I acknowledge the valuable contributions of the Medical Association of Tanzania (MAT), Association of Physicians of Tanzania (APHYTA), Association of Gynecologists and Obstetricians of Tanzania (AGOTA), Emergency Medicine Association of Tanzania (EMAT), Nephrology Society of Tanzania (NESOT), Pediatric Association of Tanzania (PAT), Pharmaceutical Society of Tanzania (PST), Tanzania Cardiac Society (TCS), Tanzania Dental Association (TDA), Tanzania Diabetes Association, Tanzania Ear Nose & Throat Society (TENTS), Tanzania Gastroenterology and Endoscopy Society (TGES), Tanzania Oncology Society (TOS), Tanzania Ophthalmology Society, Tanzania Orthopedic Association (TOA), Tanzania Society for Dermatovenereology (TASOD), Tanzania Radiology Society (TARASO), Tanzania Psychological Association (TPA), Tanzania Association of Urological Surgeons, Tanzania Neuroscience Association, Tanzania Society of Haematology (TASH), Society of Anesthesiologist of Tanzania (SATA), Tanzania Surgical Associations (TSA) and Pharmaceutical Society of Tanzania (PST) for their technical input and commitment throughout the review process.
We also extend our sincere appreciation to the institutions operating under the Ministry of Health, including the Tanzania Medicines and Medical Devices Authority (TMDA), the National Health Insurance Fund (NHIF), and the Medical Stores Department (MSD), for their active participation and valuable contributions throughout this review process.
We further acknowledge the programmes operating under the Ministry of Health, including the National Malaria Control Programme (NMCP), the National AIDS, STIs and Hepatitis Control Programme (NASHCOP), the Neglected Tropical Diseases Control Programme (NTDCP), the Immunization and Vaccine Development Programme (IVD), and the National Tuberculosis and Leprosy Programme (NTLP), for their technical input and continued collaboration.
Special appreciation is also extended to the Department of Preventive Services (DPS), the Department of Curative Services (DCS), the Department of Diagnostic Services (DDS), and the Government Chemist Laboratory Authority (GCLA) for their valuable technical contributions, expertise, and commitment throughout the review process.
I sincerely thank the National Medicines and Therapeutics Committee (NMTC), all Lead Reviewers from their respective professional associations, the stakeholders who participated in the survey and the Secretariat that coordinated the entire review process; their names are annexed. Finally, I gratefully acknowledge the financial support provided by the Global Fund, UNICEF, NextGen Ugavi Bora Afya Bora (UBAB), Africa Academy for Public Health (AAPH) Results for Development (R4D), and Medical Stores Department (MSD) whose support was instrumental in the successful completion of this review.

Dr. Grace E. Magembe
PERMANENT SECRETARY

Background Information

PART I
THE NATIONAL ESSENTIAL MEDICINES LIST (NEMLIT)
The National Essential Medicines List (NEMLIT) identifies the medicines considered essential for managing priority health conditions at all levels of the healthcare system. NEMLIT is grounded in the World Health Organization’s (WHO) concept of essential medicines—those that address the population’s most critical health needs, are consistently available within a functioning health system, and meet standards of quality while remaining affordable to both individuals and the community. This approach relies on a careful, evidence-based selection process that evaluates safety, efficacy, and comparative cost- effectiveness. Limiting the list to essential medicines helps strengthen supply chains, promote rational use, and reduce overall healthcare costs.
Updates on the of Antibiotics categorization.
The previous edition of the Standard Treatment Guidelines introduced the classification of antibiotics into Access, Watch, and Reserve (AWaRe) categories to promote optimal antibiotic use and address antimicrobial resistance (AMR).
The National AWaRe List 2025 was developed using Tanzania’s AMR, antimicrobial use (AMU), and antimicrobial consumption (AMC) surveillance data from 2020–2023, together with research evidence from 2014–2024. The list classifies 70 antibiotics, compared with 54 in the 2020 list, and is incorporated into the seventh edition of the STG/NEMLIT to guide rational antibiotic use, support antimicrobial stewardship, mitigate AMR, and improve patient outcomes.
Access antibiotics: First- or second-line treatment options for common infections with relatively lower resistance potential. They should be widely available and account for more than 60% of total antibiotic use.
Watch antibiotics: Antibiotics with a higher resistance potential that should be used cautiously and for specific indications. Their use should account for ≤28% of total antibiotic use.
Reserve antibiotics: Last-resort antibiotics for confirmed or strongly suspected multidrug-resistant infections. Their use should, whenever feasible, be guided by culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing and account for ≤12% of total antibiotic use. The AWaRe classification provides a framework for monitoring antibiotic use, improving access to essential antibiotics, promoting appropriate prescribing and preserving the effectiveness of critical antimicrobial agents.
Prescribing of Medicines with Regard to th e Level of Service Provision and Professional Expertise.
As observed in Sixth Edition of the STG/NEMLIT 2021, the NEMLIT has been assigned with levels of healthcare facilities and level of expertise, which guides the stocking and prescribing of medicines to facilitate ordering from Medical Stored Department (MSD) and reimbursement by the National Health Insurance Funds (NHIF).
These guidelines indicate three levels of the healthcare system, which includes Primary, Secondary and Tertiary level of care. The Primary level comprises Dispensaries denoted by letter (A), Health Centers denoted by letter (B) and Council/District Hospitals denoted by letter (C), while the Secondary level includes Regional Referral Hospitals denoted by letter (D) and the Tertiary level, which consists of Zonal, Special and National Hospitals denoted by letter (S).
Additionally, these guidelines recognize the prescriber’s level of expertise in relation to medicine prescribing, regardless of the level of the healthcare facility. This means that a prescriber may, based on their professional qualification, prescribe medicines appropriate to their level of expertise even when working in a facility classified at a level lower than his /her level of expertise, provided that approval has been granted by the Ministry following verification confirming the presence of the expert at that facility (the approval procedure is outlined in the Note:2 box below). For example, if a specialist is stationed at a dispensary, he or she may be authorized to prescribe Level S medicines in accordance with the guidelines.
Under these guidelines, prescribing authority is aligned with the level of professional expertise. Specialists, denoted by (A, B, C, D & S), are authorized to prescribe all medicines listed in the STG/NEMLIT. Medical Officers, indicated by (A, B, C & D), may prescribe medicines assigned to those levels, while Assistant Medical Officers, denoted by (A, B & C), are permitted to prescribe medicines within those categories. Clinical Officers, indicated by (A & B), are limited to prescribing medicines classified under Levels A and B, and Assistant Clinical Officers, denoted by (A), are authorized to prescribe only medicines categorized under Level A. Important Notes.
All medicines indicated for the treatment of various diseases in the Standard Treatment Guidelines (STG) are included in the NEMLIT.
This NEMLIT contains dosage forms and strengths including levels of medicines to be stocked and prescribed at different levels of healthcare systems from primary to tertiary.
The dosage forms and strengths included in this NEMLIT are representative and are not intended to be exhaustive. Unless otherwise specified, all other global approved dosage forms and strengths of the molecules included in this NEMLIT are recognized under these guidelines and may be used where clinically appropriate, in accordance with national regulatory requirements and accepted standards of clinical practice.
During the reimbursement of medicines in both public and private health facilities, the NHIF shall adhere to the molecules listed in the NEMLIT, regardless of formulation or strength taking note of (c) above.
All public sector health facilities shall adhere to the NEMLIT when procuring medicines from Medical Stores Department (MSD) and other sources. Taking note of (c) above.
Some medicines in the NEMLIT designated for higher facility levels may also be indicated for use at lower levels for the treatment of specific disease conditions. For example, Azithromycin is categorized at Level B but may be prescribed in Level A facilities for the treatment of STIs only.
The NEMLIT shall serve as the baseline for developing a separate list of selected priority medicines for measuring the availability of health commodities in health facilities. The priority list shall also include selected medical devices, diagnostic products, and dental commodities.
For fixed-dose combinations (FDCs) containing molecules with different prescribing levels, the FDC shall be assigned the prescribing level of the molecule with the highest level
In the event that a health facility has a prescriber whose professional qualification is above the level of the facility, the following procedure shall apply for approval to stock and prescribe medicines:
The District Medical Officer (DMO) shall scrutinize and compile a list of health facilities with prescribers whose qualifications are above the designated facility level.
The list shall include the name of the council, name and level of the health facility, names of prescribers, professional qualifications, and valid practicing license numbers (including the Medical Council of Tanganyika license number).
The request, together with the list, shall be submitted to the Ministry of Health through the Prime Minister’s Office – Regional Administration and Local Government (PMO-RALG) for approval.
Upon approval, the Ministry shall notify the respective health facilities through the appropriate administrative channel, authorizing them to stock and prescribe medicines according to the level of expertise available at the facility.
The Ministry shall also inform the Medical Stores Department (MSD) and the National Health Insurance Fund (NHIF) to facilitate medicine ordering and reimbursement of prescribed medicines.
If the approved prescriber is transferred or ceases to work at the authorized facility, the District Medical Officer shall notify the Ministry of Health through the appropriate administrative channel.
For further enquiries or recommendations during the implementation of these guidelines, please contact the Ministry of Health for clarification.

PART II
THE STANDARD TREATMENT GUIDELINE (STG)
Standard Treatment Guidelines (STGs) provide standardized guidance to health professionals on the diagnosis and management of various medical conditions. They serve as an essential tool for promoting rational use of medicines and ensuring consistent, evidence-based clinical practice across different levels of the health system. The guidelines also provide critical support to healthcare practitioners, particularly those with limited experience or those newly entering clinical practice. STGs are systematically developed recommendations intended to assist practitioners and prescribers in making appropriate decisions regarding the management of specific clinical conditions.
The guidelines include information on disease conditions, diagnostic criteria, Pharmacological Management which involve the medicines of choice and alternative treatment options, Non-Pharmacological Management, as well as key prescribing information such as dosage, duration of treatment, contraindications, side effects, warnings, medicine interactions, and referral criteria. To remain relevant and responsive to advances in medical science and evolving public health priorities, the STGs are reviewed and updated regularly. In Tanzania, the review process is conducted every three (3) years. The Seventh Edition (2026) of the Standard Treatment Guidelines has been comprehensively revised to incorporate new therapeutic interventions, updated diagnostic approaches, and guidance for the management of emerging and re-emerging diseases.
During the development process, strong emphasis was placed on the application of evidence-based medicine. Each chapter was reviewed and updated by a Lead Reviewer, a recognized expert in the respective disease area, nominated by professional associations, with assistance from a multidisciplinary team of technical experts. The STGs address the priority disease conditions in the country and are organized into twenty-seven chapters, as outlined below:

CHAPTER ONE
APPROACH TO PATIENTS WITH EMERGENCY CONDITIONS

The Concept of Emergency Care and Resuscitation
Emergency care and resuscitation involve rapid assessment and early intervention. The approach to Emergency care and resuscitation needs to be systematic; hence the use of the ABCs. The ABCs approach provides the framework for evaluation and treatment of severely ill patients.
Primary survey
Airway
Assess the airway to establish patency of the airway. This includes: Looking for signs of airway obstruction (signs of trauma, swelling, secretions, presence of foreign body).
Listening for abnormal sounds like a stridor and snoring.
If there are signs of airway obstruction, intervene by positioning, opening and clearing the airway. Perform a chin lift or jaw thrust maneuver to open the airway (If suspecting cervical spine injury, use the jaw thrust maneuver). Use suction to remove secretions. Airway adjuncts, such as oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal airway can be used.
Note
Remember to reassess the airway after performing interventions.
Some patient may require use of advance airway devices like endotracheal intubation or surgical airway.
Use video laryngoscopy over direct laryngoscopy helps to improve first-pass success.
emergency intubation
Breathing
Upon completing airway assessment and intervention, assess for the presence of breathing, signs of respiratory distress such as tachypnea, hypoxia, cyanosis, apnea and abnormal breath sounds. Provide oxygen when oxygen saturation is below 92% or when the patient is dyspneic. Oxygen can be administered using the nasal prong, simple face mask, non-rebreather mask or Ambu bag. Advanced interventions include mechanical ventilation.
Circulation
Check for pulse (central pulse) for not more than 10 seconds. If absent, start CPR (Refer cardiopulmonary resuscitation section 1.3). Assess for signs of poor peripheral perfusion (shock) such as cold extremities, prolonged capillary refill, dry mucous membrane and hypotension. If there are signs of shock, establish two (2) IV large bore cannula and give IV fluids (crystalloids) bolus (2lts in adults and 20mls/kg in pediatrics). Limit fluids to individuals whom you suspect of having heart failure, renal failure or malnourished children.
Disability
This involves a rapid assessment of neurological status. This includes assessment for the level of consciousness (use of AVPU or Glascow coma scale), signs of convulsions, random blood glucose level, examination of the pupils and presence of focal neurological deficit. Interventions that can be performed during the disability assessment include correction of hypoglycemia, airway protection, stopping the convulsions by administering anticonvulsant.
Exposure
This involves fully exposing the patient and rapid assessment of the body for signs of trauma, rashes or infection.
Secondary survey
After assessment and stabilization of ABCs during the primary survey, focus is turned into secondary survey. The secondary survey is a systematic assessment of the rest of the body to identify injuries and illnesses. Common approaches include a head-to-toe or organ –system-based assessment. It is important to note that the secondary survey is performed after the primary assessment and interventions.
When performing a secondary survey, if the patient condition changes, then you must stop immediately and redo the primary survey and necessary interventions.
Note:
All patients with compromised airway, breathing, circulation or disability must be attended in the resuscitation rooms. (Refer Triage overview section)

Triage Overview
Triage is the process of determining the priority of a patient to medical care based on the acuity (severity of condition) and capacity of the system to address the condition to optimize outcome.
Importance of Triage
Triage enables quick identification of patients who need immediate attention and hence improves patient outcomes by avoiding potential delays. It helps in organizing, monitoring, evaluating and determining the department resources that patients might need.
Triage system
The triage system is based on recommendation of Emergency Medicine expert’s basic principles of triage, which uses specific criteria to categorize patients into three main levels of acuity:
Emergency
All patients with immediate life or limb threats who are deemed salvageable, but likely to further decompensate without immediate intervention will be triaged in this level. This category can also be labeled as RED. Priority: those seriously injured/ill patients with potential to decompensate if not treated within 1 hour are triaged as priority cases. This category can also be labeled as YELLOW.
Queue: this level includes all the walking wounded or those with less serious injury/sickness who are unlikely to decompensa te. Patients in this category can safely wait for their turn. However, they should be monitored as their conditions may change and warrant immediate care. This category is also labeled as GREEN.

Cardiac Arrest and Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation
Cardiopulmonary resuscitation is an emergency lifesaving procedure performed when there is a sudden cessation of heartbeat. It involves the combination of chest compression and artificial ventilation to preserve blood flow to the organs including the brain function. Early initiation of CPR can double or triple the chances of survival after cardiac arrest.
Note: HIGH QUALITY CPR
Compressions:
Infant: heel of one hand (if alone) or thumb encircling technique (if you have assistance)
Child: 1 or 2 hand
Adult: Two hands
Compression rate: 100-120/min
Compression depth: approximately 1/3 antero-posterior diameter of the chest
Compression/ventilation ratio: 30:2 (adults and children), For Infants-30:2 (if alone) and 15:2 (if you have assistance), for neonates’ compression/ventilation ratio 3:1
Allow chest recoil
Minimize interruptions
Adequate ventilation
Clinical Presentation
Unresponsiveness (sudden loss of consciousness)
Absence of central pulse (carotid pulse/femoral pulse or brachial pulse in infants)
Loss of spontaneous respiration
Investigations
While continuing with CPR, point of care (POC) tests are conducted while looking for the reversible causes of cardiac arrest (Hypovolemia, hypoxia, hypo/hyperkalemia, acidosis, hypothermia, hypoglycemia, tension pneumothorax, toxins, thrombi, cardiac tamponade). These include:
Blood gases
Bicarbonates
Electrolytes- Potassium, sodium, Calcium, Chloride,
Creatinine, POC urea
RBG
Bedside ultrasound- looking for pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade or thrombi
Toxicology serum blood and urine screens (If available)
ECG (if there is return of spontaneous circulation)
Lactate
Troponin
Non- Pharmacological Management
HAZARDS- ensure safety and use of PPEs
HELLO- Check for responsiveness, Carotid pulse (not more than 10 seconds) and breathing
CPR starts with early recognition (unresponsiveness, loss of spontaneous breathing and absence of carotid pulse.
In infant’s CPR is initiated when the heart rate is below 60 beats/min
Call for HELP and immediately start chest compression. As more members arrives to help assign different roles including airway and breathing management, time recording, documentation, AED/monitor operation and medications administration
Open the airway by performing chin lift or jaw thrust (if suspecting C spine injury). Use airway adjuncts to open the airway.
Give 2 breaths using bag valve mask connected to oxygen source and observe for chest rise
Establish IV access for administration of fluids and medications; if failed, perform Intraosseous access
After FIVE cycles of compression/ventilation (2 minutes), check for pulse and use AED/Defibrillator to analyze rhythm if there is a need to deliver shock
If no need for shocking, continue with CPR for another 2 minutes (FIVE cycles)
Use capnography (ETCO₂ monitoring) during CPR to assess quality. Maintain ETCO₂ >10 mmHg as a marker of effective compressions
Double sequential defibrillation (DSD) may be considered for refractory VF/pVT

Approach to Stridor
Stridor is an abnormal, high-pitched sound produced by turbulent airflow through a partially obstructed airway. Stridor is a dangerous finding and may indicate imminent airway obstruction. It can be inspiratory, expiratory or biphasic.
Clinical Presentation:
Hypoxia
Respiratory distress
Altered mental status
Inability to speak
Inability to swallow
Differential diagnoses
Infectious causes- croup, epiglottitis, peri-tonsillar abscess, retropharyngeal abscess, non-infectious causes- Foreign body obstruction, burns, trauma, anaphylaxis, malignancy, laryngotracheomalacia, stenosis.
Note: Assess the airway (If unstable, consider surgical intervention/consult; if stable, consider imaging or direct visualization of larynx with fiberoptic scope or video laryngoscope
Investigations
Blood gases analysis, Lateral neck X-ray (for foreign body, masses or soft tissue swelling), CXR (foreign body, evidence of aspiration), CT- scan Neck, Blood Sugar, Lactate, Electrolyte analysis, and/or Serum creatinine and urea
Non-Pharmacological Management
Keep the patient calm by allowing the patient to assume their most comfortable position. Give oxygen if there are signs of increased work of breathing.
Pharmacological Management
It will depend on the underlying cause. The following medications can be used in the management of stridor;
A: epinephrine (adrenaline) (nebulization) 0.5mls/kg
AND/OR
B: dexamethasone (PO/IV/IM) 0.15- 0.6mg/kg stat (Max 10mg)
Note:
Since stridor can be as a result of various causes, management should be focused on the underlying causes
Administer IV fluids (if signs of shock) – refer section on the management of shock
All patients with stridor whose cause have not yet been established must be referred to higher health facilities

Cough
Cough is a common reflex action that clears the throat of mucus, allergens, dust or other foreign irritants. A cough can be caused by several conditions, both temporary and permanent. Frequent coughing indicates the presence of a disease.
Characteristics of cough/sputum
If cough is dry without sputum and fever, it is probable an allergic condition or mild upper respiratory illness (e.g., allergic rhinitis or allergic bronchitis)
If cough is dry without sputum or fever and is associated with other congestive symptoms, it may be due to Congestive Cardiac Failure (CCF)
If it is a repeated attack cough with wheezing but without fever, it is likely to be bronchial asthma
If it is a cough with fever, rapid breathing, and chest in-drawing, it is likely pneumonia
If it is cough with sputum that is yellowish pus-like and there is fever, it is likely acute bronchitis or pneumonia
If it is cough with blood in sputum and/or irregular fever with loss of weight and appetite, it is suspected tuberculosis
If it is cough with a large quantity of foul-smelling sputum, very foul-smelling it is likely a lung abscess or bronchiectasis
Non-Pharmacological Management
Ensure the patient is positioned in a comfortable and supportive posture
Pharmacological Management
Causative/precipitating factors, e.g., CCF, asthma, and allergies, must be established and treated accordingly. (Refer respiratory disease condition chapter 9)
Note: Refer to a high facility with expertise when a cough persists and fails to establish the cause or when associated with fever.

Approach to dyspnea (Shortness of breath)
Shortness of breath or breathlessness may result from a range of pulmonary, cardiac, and central nervous system causes. It is important to look for the underlying cause for immediate intervention.
Clinical Presentation
Increased work of breathing
Altered mental status
Diaphoresis
Additional sounds- stridors, wheezes
Differential diagnosis
Pulmonary embolism
Pulmonary oedema
Myocardial infarction
Asthma
Anaphylaxis
Airway obstruction
Investigations
Tension pneumothorax
Cardiac tamponade
Acute chest syndrome
Pneumonia
Pericarditis
Blood gases, Serum Electrolytes, Serum Creatinine and Urea, Troponins, Chest X-ray, POC ECG, Bedside Ultrasound, Lactate, Troponin, Random blood glucose, CT- PA
Non-Pharmacological Management
Obtain a thorough history and perform both primary survey (ABCs) and secondary survey, and provide necessary interventions
Obtain Vital signs
Position the patient
Give Oxygen if hypoxic or increased work of breathing
Pharmacological Management
Pharmacological Management depends on the underlying cause of difficulty in breathing. (Refer respiratory disease condition chapter 9)

Approach to Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding
Upper GI bleeding is any GI bleeding originating proximally to the ligament of Treitz.
Clinical Presentation
Hematemesis and coffee-ground emesis suggest a UGI source. On physical examination, vital signs may reveal
Hypotension
Tachycardia.
Cool, clammy skin as a sign of shock.
Abdominal examination may disclose tenderness, masses, ascites, or organomegaly.
Presence of blood and its appearance on rectal examination, whether bright red, maroon, or melanotic.
Spider angiomas, palmar erythema, jaundice, and gynecomastia, which may suggest liver disease.
Petechiae and purpura may suggest an underlying coagulopathy
Differential diagnosis
Peptic ulcer disease, upper GI malignancy, oesophageal or gastric varices, esophagitis, Mallory- Weiss tear, Boerhaave syndrome and arteriovenous malformation
Investigations
ABO Grouping and cross-matching, Complete Blood Count, Hemoglobin Level, Blood Urea Nitrogen and Creatinine, Electrolytes, (Sodium, Potassium, Calcium Chloride), PT, PTT, INR, Liver Function Tests, Lactate levels, Obtain an ECG in patients with underlying coronary artery disease and/or Bedside Ultrasound, CXR (If suspecting perforation)

Maintain ABCs, give oxygen if needed
Pharmacological Management
Give blood if severe pallor, ongoing bleeding, Hb < 5g/dl, and Hb < 7g/dl (with active bleeding)
Adults: 2 units within 1 hour and Pediatrics: 20ml/kg 1 hour (whole blood) or 10ml/kg (pRBC), If ongoing indication for blood, start transfusion in the following ratio: 1unit pRBCs (20ml/kg
Pediatric: 1unit FFP (20mls/kg in Pediatric): 1unit PLT (20ml/kg in Pediatric)

OR

Approach to Seizure and Status Epilepticus
Status epilepticus is a single seizure ≥5 minutes in length or two or more seizures without recovery of consciousness between seizures. Status epilepticus is a neurologic emergency, and treatment should be initiated in all patients with continuous seizure activity lasting more than 5 minutes.

Abrupt onset seizures
Altered mental status
Postictal drowsiness
Tongue biting
Differential diagnoses

Perform both primary and secondary assessments and provide necessary interventions

Establish IV access for administration of anticonvulsants; if unable, use the rectal route
Connect the patient to the cardiac monitor to obtain vital signs

Approach to Altered Mental Status
This is the acute alteration in brain function and may include alteration of arousal or awareness, thought content, memory or attention.
Depending on the cause but may include agitation, Restlessness, Hemiparesis, visual deficit, dysphasia
Differential diagnosis
The mnemonic AEIOU TIPS is widely preferred in the emergency department when considering a broader differential. Alcohol/acidosis, Epilepsy/Electrolytes, Insulin/Inborn Errors of Metabolism, Oxygen/Overdose, Uremia, Trauma, Infection, Psychiatric/Poisoning, Stroke/Subarachnoid Hemorrhage/Shock

Anaphylaxis
Anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening, generalized or systemic hypersensitivity reaction characterized by rapidly developing life-threatening airway (pharyngeal or laryngeal edema) and/or breathing (bronchospasm and tachypnea) and/or circulation (hypotension and tachycardia) problems usually associated with skin and mucosal changes.
Clinical Presentation
Hives
Angioedema
Wheezes
Difficult breathing
Diarrhea
Hypotension
Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis and should be suspected when:
Acute onset involving skin, mucosal tissue, with either respiratory compromise or blood pressure reduction (or syncope)
Hypotension after exposure to a known allergy for the patient (SBP <90mmHg or >30% from baseline)
Respiratory compromise (i.e., dyspnea, stridor, wheeze, hypoxemia)
Exposure to a likely allergen causes involvement of the skin, mucosal, respiratory compromization or blood pressure reduction
Investigations

Cardiac Tamponade
Cardiac tamponade is the result of compression of the myocardium by fluid, gas, pus, blood, or a combination of substances. It occurs in a physiological continuum reflecting the amount of fluid, the rate of accumulation, and the nature of the heart.
The result is increased pericardial pressure, which causes decreased ventricle compliance and decreased flow of blood into the right ventricle, which eventually leads to decreased cardiac output. Conditions that may predispose a patient to pericardial effusion and tamponade include trauma, radiation exposure, Tb pericarditis, renal failure (uremic pericarditis), autoimmune diseases, drugs that induce a lupus-like syndrome, hypothyroidism, or ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.
Clinical Presentations
Chest pain and dyspnea
Pulsus paradoxus >10 mm Hg
Beck’s triad includes low blood pressure, elevated jugular venous distention, and decreased heart sounds.
In the absence of hypotension and tension pneumothorax in a patient with PEA, consider the diagnosis of cardiac tamponade.
Investigations
Bedside ultrasound and ECHO, POC, ECG, Blood gases, Serum Electrolytes, Troponins, Pericardial fluid analysis- biochemistry, microbiology and cytology, Serum creatinine and urea, and/or Chest X-ray
Non- Pharmacological Management
Perform both primary and secondary assessments and provide appropriate interventions.
Give oxygen if hypoxic or increased work of breathing
Connect the patient to a cardiac monitor and obtain vital signs
Pericardiocentesis is the definitive management
Pharmacological Management
A: sodium chloride 0.9% (IV): Adults 1-2 litres; Pediatrics 20ml/kg to increase right-sided filling pressure
Note
The definitive treatment for cardiac tamponade is pericardiocentesis. A cardiology consultation or referral is strongly recommended. In emergency settings, pericardiocentesis may be performed by a qualified and experienced medical practitioner in the emergency department.
All patients with cardiac tamponade require inpatient management in an intensive care unit setting/HDU.

Pulmonary Edema
A life-threatening condition that occurs due to abnormal fluid build-up in the lungs, leading to impaired gaseous exchange, acute respiratory distress and may cause respiratory failure. Can be classified as cardiogenic pulmonary edema, due to increased hydrostatic pulmonary pressure (HF) and non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema, due to increased permeability (acute lung injury and allergic alveolitis).
Note: Cardiogenic and non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema have no clear-cut differences in Clinical Presentation, however identifying the specific underlying cause of pulmonary edema is significant for therapeutic and prognostic purposes.
Clinical Presentation
Shortness of breath, use of accessory muscles, diaphoresis, tachypnoea and crepitations
Investigations
Chest X-ray, Blood gases, Serum Creatinine and Urea, POC ECG, POC troponin, BNP, Serum electrolytes and/or Bedside Ultrasound
Non-Pharmacological Management
Perform both primary and secondary assessment and provide necessary interventions
Give high-flow oxygen therapy
Put the patient on a cardiac monitor (if available) and obtain vital signs

Position the patient at a 45° angle or in the sitting upright position
Perform ECG (rule out ischemia, dysrhythmia). Perform bedside ECHO (to rule out cardiac causes- contractility, pericardial effusion)
Perform chest ultrasound (comet tails and B lines)
Pharmacological Management
Control hypertension (Maintain SBP>90mmHg,
S: nitroglycerin (IV): Adults loading 100mcg/min titrate rapidly to 400mcg/min over 2 minutes
Note:
Beware of pre-load sensitive condition example inferior or right ventricular myocardial infarction, and phosphodiesterase inhibitors use.
Don’t give Nitroglycerin if SBP< 90mmHg)
Reduce intravascular volume if fluid overloaded
A: furosemide (IV/IM) 0.5-1mg/kg over 20minutes (maximum 120mg) or infusion IV 5-10mg/kg (maximum 120mg).
Note: Beware of renal insufficiency and volume-depleted patients; check the size of the IVC
Ventilation
Oxygen therapy (target saturation>95%); CPAP or BiPAP (for persistent respiratory distress, hypoxia or acidosis despite high flow oxygen therapy); Intubation and mechanical ventilation (for respiratory failure despite CPAP/BiPAP)
Goal of treatment - Relieve hypoxemia (improve oxygenation); reduce pulmonary capillary pressure and improve perfusion. Admit all patients with pulmonary edema to HDU/ICU or transfer the patient to a health facility with ICU/HDU capacity

Approach to Shock
Shock is a state of acute circulatory failure leading to decreased organ perfusion, with inadequate delivery of oxygenated blood to tissues and resultant end-organ dysfunction and it is an emergency condition. Adherence to evidence-based care of the specific causes of shock can enhance a patient’s chances of surviving.

Low blood pressure (systolic BP below 80 mmHg) is the key sign of shock
Weak and rapid pulse
Rapid and shallow breathing
Restlessness and altered mental state

Low urine output

Sepsis and Septic Shock
Septicemia (Sepsis) is defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to bacterial infection (commonly) and fungal or viral infections. Organ dysfunction can be represented by an increase in the Sequential [Sepsis-related] Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score of 2 points or more, with an in-hospital mortality greater than 10%.
Septic Shock is defined as a subset of sepsis in which particularly profound circulatory, cellular, and metabolic abnormalities are associated with a greater risk of mortality than 40%.
Clinical Presentation
Temperature of >38oC or <360C; Heart rate of >90/min; Respiratory rate of >20/min or PaCO2 <32 mm Hg
Above features plus evidence of organ dysfunction (hypotension, jaundice, oliguria, or altered state of consciousness from altered sensorium like drowsiness/lethargy
Investigations
Blood gases analysis, Bedside ultrasound- assessing the inferior vena cava and the lungs, POC ECG, Urine dipstick, Chest X-ray if suspecting pneumonia, Complete blood count, Qualitative or quantitative CRP or Procalcitonin in centers available, Serum Electrolytes, Creatinine and Urea, Liver function tests- liver enzymes, bilirubin, clotting time, Blood culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing. Primary source of infection’s clinical sample culture (e.g., urine, pus, sputum CSF etc.) and antimicrobial susceptibility testing and/or RNA/DNA PCR for viral pathogens (where indicated).
Diagnostic criteria
Sepsis: Q-SOFA in settings with limited laboratory infrastructures: two or more SOFA scores, namely: Respiratory rate
≥22/min, altered mentation, and Systolic blood pressure ≥100 mm Hg) ± bacteria or fungal proven blood culture and susceptibility testing are recommended to make a definitive diagnosis.
Other scoring criteria include SOFA, NEWS (National Early Warning Score), and MEDS (Mortality in Emergency Medicine Department Sepsis
Septic shock: Sepsis diagnostic criteria above and vasopressor therapy needed to elevate MAP ≥65 mmHg and lactate >2 mmol/L (18 mg/dL) despite adequate fluid resuscitation.

Nutritional support
Control measures focused on the primary focus of infection.

Ensure patency of the airway and give oxygen if hypoxic or increased work of breathing
Connect the patient to the cardiac monitor and obtain vital signs

Approach to Pain
Pain is an unpleasant sensation or emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage, or described in terms of such damage. Any pain of moderate or higher intensity is accompanied by anxiety and the urge to escape or terminate the feeling. Pain is subjective and unique perceptual experience with multiple dimensions that may not directly be observed by others or measured by physiological tests. Assessment is almost entirely self-reported.
Assessment of pain.
Self-report is the key to pain assessment. In non- or preverbal children, facial expression is the most valid indicator of pain; therefore, use the faces pain scale to assess severity. Pain should be assessed by:
Duration
Severity, e.g., does the patient wake up because of the pain
Site
Characteristics,	e.g.	stabbing, throbbing, crushing, cramp-like
Persistent or intermittent

Relieving or aggravating factors
Accompanying symptoms
Distribution of pain
In children, pain can be assessed by a child’s crying voice, posture, movement and colour

Anaesthesia is a state of controlled reversible loss of consciousness, usually accompanied by analgesia, muscle relaxation, amnesia and areflexia. It is usually induced for the purpose of facilitating surgery and other therapeutic or diagnostic procedures.
Anaesthesia may be achieved with either:
Local anaesthesia -topical application/spray or infiltration of local anaesthetics
Regional anaesthesia alone e.g., spinal/epidural anaesthesia, arm block
Regional anaesthesia with sedation

Patients MUST be reviewed in the pre-anesthetic outpatient clinic before any anesthetic intervention except for those admitted for emergency operations. The latter can be reviewed a few minutes before anesthesia or the night before the operation for elective inpatients.
Done by reviewing surgical, medical and anesthesia-related records, performing focused anesthesia Assessment, identify anesthesia related risks and formulate anesthesia plan.
Ultimate goals are: to optimize patient preparation, ensure safety and anticipate complications and put forward mitigation strategies

A high neuraxial block is a sensorimotor block that has reached a spinal segmental level higher than that required to achieve surgical anaesthesia (sensory level T3 and above). Local anesthetic agent spreads too high in the spinal cord, blocking cardio accelerator nerves and respiratory muscles, causing difficulty in breathing, severe hypotension and cardiac dysfunction.
Anticipate and reassure the patient.
Declare emergency and call for help. Position the head elevated to slow further spread.
Ensure the wedge is placed properly.
Use ABC approach, give Oxygen 100% by face mask or intubate (rapid sequence) with a hypnotic and muscle relaxant and ventilate if apneic.
Give rapid fluid infusion and add vasopressors- ephedrine, phenylephrine or double-diluted epinephrine (adrenaline)/baby epinephrine (adrenaline) (10mcg/ml).

Anesthesia in Diabetic Patient
Perioperative Hyperglycemia is associated with increased risk of infection, medical complications and death. The following shall be considered;
Ideally, the elective patient should have a preoperative glycated haemoglobin less than 9% or a fasting blood glucose level of 10 mmol/l or random blood glucose of 13 mmol/l.
Screen for nephropathy, cardiac disease, retinopathy and neuropathy and inform the surgical team.
If on oral hypoglycemic therapy and well controlled, and surgery is minor, omit therapy on the morning of surgery and resume therapy when eating normally.
If on insulin, adjust depending on the type of surgery and expected fasting period as follows:
Minor surgery (duration < 3hours)
Insulin: in the morning, intermediate–acting insulin, 1/2 to 2/3 of the total daily dose.
If blood glucose is above 20 mmol/l, give a small dose of short–acting insulin.
In the evening, give intermediate–acting insulin, 1/3 of the daily dose. Fluid: 5% dextrose (IV), volume according to age.
Blood glucose monitoring: every 1–2 hours, target values between 10–14 mmol/l.
Major surgery (duration > 3hours) involving general anesthesia and therefore a period of fasting.
Insulin and fluid: infusion solution containing 5% glucose and 20 mmol/l potassium chloride (maintenance volume)
Insulin infusion rate 0.05 IU/kg/hour.
Blood glucose monitoring: every 1–2 hours; values between 6–14 mmol/l, if < 5 mmol/l reduce infusion rate, continue infusion therapy intraoperatively.
Post operatively: give 5–10% dextrose (IV) 1 Litre + 20ml potassium chloride + 2/3 of total daily dose of insulin over 8hours and repeat to maintain infusion therapy until food intake is re–established.
Anesthesia in Hypertensive Patients
Monitor BP, scan monitors for HR, ECG rhythm, EtCO2, and temperature. Provided the patient is adequately oxygenated & ventilated, deepen the anesthetic.
Examine patient:
Pupils (high ICP).
Diaphoresis	&	flushing	(carcinoid, pheochromocytoma, hyperthyroidism).
Rigidity (malignant hyperthermia, serotonin syndrome).
Examine drugs & equipment:
Potential drug error
Possible TIVA or circuit disconnect (awareness)

Bladder distension.
Hot (thyroid storm, malignant hyperthermia, serotonin syndrome).
Tourniquet (pain)
Equipment error (falsely high reading)
Pharmacological Management
B: hydralazine (IV) 5-20mg (max 30mg) slow IV push every 20minutes
OR
C: labetalol (IV) 5-20mg every10min (max total 300mg)
OR
S: esmolol (IV) 0.5mg/kg over 1minute; start infusion at 50mcg/kg/min
OR
S: nitroglycerin (IV) 50-100mcg; start infusion at 10mcg/min. Treat the underlying cause, i.e., pain.
Anesthesia in Asthmatic Patients
Considerations;
Risk of perioperative respiratory complications:
Bronchospasm, mucous plugging, pneumothorax, atelectasis, pneumonia.
Possible pulmonary hypertension & RV failure.
Need for preoperative optimization:
Treatment of bronchospasm, infection, and atelectasis.
Avoidance of triggers & exacerbating factors
Avoid general anesthesia, endotracheal intubation, histamine-releasing medications, and light anesthesia.
Pharmacological Management
Continue usual inhalers pre-operatively
Stress dose steroids if recent high-dose steroid use.
For Severe Asthma Exacerbation Treatment Options, refer to the Respiratory Diseases Condition chapter.
Anesthetics
B: ketamine (bronchodilator effect)
OR
D: propofol (bronchodilator effect)
If intubation & ventilation:
Use permissive hypercapnia.
Use low respiratory rates: start at 10-12 breaths/minute but may need lower rates.
Use prolonged expiratory time (e.g. I: E ratios 1:3, 1:4, or even 1:5).
Tidal volume 6-8cc/kg.
FiO2 to achieve PaO2>60mm Hg
Anesthesia in Sickle Cell Patients
Avoid precipitants of sickle cell crisis:
Optimize perioperative pain control.
Optimization (in consultation with hematology).

Procedural risk for complications:
Low: minor surgery (e.g., inguinal hernia & extremity surgery).
Intermediate: intra-abdominal operations (e.g., cholecystectomy).
High: intracranial & intrathoracic procedures, hip surgery.
Anesthesia in Special Groups
Pediatric Anesthesia
Special anatomical, physiological and Pharmacological considerations in the pediatric group (different from adults):
Larger head relative to the body-neck flection/obstruction
Small mouth and large tongue proportion-obstruction
Large head, little hair, prone to heat loss
Breath mainly by nose, small and easy to obstruct
Larynx is more anterior (at C3/4, while adults' C6)
Short neck/Short trachea, little ETT movement-tube out
Small airways-increased airway resistance and obstruction from secretions
Narrowest part-cricoid ring in adult vocal cords. May lead to airway edema, difficult-Intubation.
Pre-anesthetic review and preparations
Prenatal history-term or preterm delivery, what is the growth milestone. Any history of respiratory tract infections and the last episode.
Airway assessment and cardiovascular examination are mandatory.
Get or estimate body weight for drug calculations.
Strict fasting guidelines with emphasis on solids up to six hours preop and pediatric patients to be first in the operating list.
Intraoperative considerations
Premedication are vital to enhance smooth separation from parents. If IV line is in place IV induction should be considered.
Otherwise, gas induction and then IV access with top up IV medications.
Strict temperature management throughout and tight calculated IV fluids.
For neonates and premature children, avoid opioid analgesics to prevent respiratory complications.
Postoperative Care:
Extubate when fully awake. For prolonged anesthesia, measure the sugar level and assess for opioid or benzodiazepine overdose
Keep the patient warm
Obstetric Anaesthesia General anaesthesia (GA)
Preparation: Prevent aspiration pneumonitis (Refer to premedication section).
Antibiotic prophylaxis: before skin incision as guided by guidelines.
In view of potential difficult airway, ALL equipment for difficult airway including supraglottic airway devices (SGAs), and video laryngoscopes when available in addition to routine airway equipment. Have small-sized ETT 6.0 and 6.5 cuffed with a stylet.
Note: Applying left lateral displacement to prevent aortocaval syndrome is mandatory
Monitoring:
Routine; Noninvasive blood pressure (NIBP), ECG, SPO2.
When available, consider Bispectral index (BIS) and neuromuscular blockage monitoring due to increased risk of awareness.
Induction agents
Hypnotics: hemodynamically stable
D: propofol (IV) 1-2mg/kg,
If hemodynamically unstable;
B: ketamine (IV) 1-1.5mg/kg;
OR
D: propofol (IV) low dose 0.5-1mg/kg, with ketamine
OR
S: etomidate (IV) 0.3-0.5mg/kg;
Analgesia: Multimodal analgesia Opioids combined with non-steroidal analgesics and or IV paracetamol.
Opioids: Same dosages as in normal general anesthesia, except they should be administered after delivery of the baby to avoid neonatal bradycardia and respiratory depression
Intubation: Perform rapid sequence intubation (RSI) with cricoid pressure using appropriate drugs and dosage (see section for RSI).
Maintenance of anaesthesia:
Volatile anaesthetics:
B: isoflurane avoiding minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) higher than 1;
AND
S: sevoflurane avoiding a minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) higher than 1.
OR
Total intravenous anaesthesia (TIVA) using propofol or Ketamine infusion with muscle relaxant, depending on availability.
Maintenance Analgesia:
Multimodal, but opioids are given after delivery of the baby Uterotonics – Administered after cord clamp:
A: oxytocin (IM) 10IU
OR
A: oxytocin (IV) 10IU slow infusion.
Note:
Other uterotonics as appropriate, depending on the risk for haemorrhage.
Recovery- Extubate when fully awake and maintaining airway reflexes.
Spinal anaesthesia (SA)
Single-shot spinal anaesthesia
B: bupivacaine heavy 0.5% (Intrathecal) alone 7.5-10mg
OR
B: bupivacaine heavy 0.5% (Intrathecal) 7.5-10mg with opioids 20-25mcg fentanyl or 100-200mcg preservative free morphine.
Combined Spinal-Epidural anaesthesia (CSE)
When surgery is anticipated to last the duration of a single shot SA and an epidural kit is available, CSE allows surgical anaesthesia and avoids conversion to GA.
Epidural anaesthesia
In selected obstetric conditions or conversion of neuraxial labour analgesia into surgical anaesthesia.
B: bupivacaine (Intrathecal) 10-15mls bolus
OR
D: ropivacaine (Intrathecal) 10-15mls bolus (with or without opioids)

Multimodal analgesia with systemic opioids, NSAIDs, and paracetamol.

Sedation
This procedural sedation and analgesia are commonly used in emergency units, radiological /diagnostic units, dentistry and for certain endoscopic and gynaecological procedures.
Pharmacological Management
Minimal Sedation/Anxiolysis (no analgesic effect is required)
D: midazolam (IV) 0.05mg/kg (In a 60 kg patient, give boluses of 1 mg every minute; may require up to 5mg)
OR
A: diazepam (IV) 0.1mg/kg (In a 60kg patient, give boluses of 2mg every minute; may require up to 10mg)
Medicines for moderate sedation & analgesia
If analgesia is required, one of the above is usually combined with an opiate. However, ketamine has analgesic activity and can be used on its own or combined with a benzodiazepine.
B: ketamine (IV) 0.5mg/kg. Repeat doses of 0.5mg/kg as required, every 5-10minutes
OR
C: morphine (IV) 0.1mg /kg in increments of 2mg every 5minutes
OR
S: fentanyl (IV) 0.25µg/kg
OR
S: dexmedetomidine (IV) 1mcg/kg bolus over 10 minutes, then 0.2-0.7µg/kg per hour infusion Alternative medicines
D: propofol (IV) 0.5mg/kg. Repeated as 0.25mg/kg boluses every 5minutes as required
OR
S: etomidate (IV) 0.1mg/kg. Repeat doses of 0.05 mg/kg (IV) every 5minutes, as required. But it is more likely to cause myoclonus
Medicines for Deep Sedation & Analgesia:
This is usually achieved with either higher doses of medications used for moderate sedation, or by combining an opiate, a benzodiazepine, and either Propofol or Etomidate. When agents are combined, lower doses may be adequate.
Supplemental Analgesia: Simple analgesics can be given before or after the procedure: A: paracetamol (IV/PO): 1g 4-6 hourly when required to a maximum of 4g per 24hours.
OR
A: diclofenac (IM) 75mg stat or 0.5mg/kg pediatric,
OR
A: ibuprofen (PO) 400mg 8hourly with meals after the procedure.

Medicines for short–term sedation (less than 24 hours)
D: midazolam (IV) 0.05–0.2mg/kg/hour.
OR
D: propofol (IV) 0.5mg/kg/hour.
Due to high fat solubility, midazolam also becomes ‘long acting’ after infusions of more than 24 hours

Medicines for longer–term sedation (72 hours or more)
C: lorazepam (IV) 0.1mg/kg/hour.
OR
D: midazolam (IV) 0.2mg/kg/hour.
Lorazepam (0.1 mg/kg/hour) is as effective (and as easy to wean) as midazolam 0.2 mg/kg/hour) but more difficult to titrate.
Supplemental analgesia
C: morphine (IV) 0.1–0.2mg/kg/hour.
OR
S: fentanyl (IV) 1 µg/kg/hour (also becomes long acting after prolonged infusion due to fat solubility)

Pain Management (Acute and Chronic Pain Management)
Pain is an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage. The relationship between pain (subjective) and actual or potential tissue damage (objective) is influenced by socio-cultural context as well as the nervous system.
Perioperative Analgesia:
Multimodal approach; IM/ IV analgesics and/or a central neuraxial or locoregional anaesthetic block may be used. The analgesic effect of these techniques may extend into the early postoperative period. However, it is best to assess pain frequently to determine additional demand of analgesia.
Non-Opioid Analgesics
D: paracetamol (IV) 15mg/kg 8hourly
OR
A: diclofenac –(IM) 75mg
OR
D: ketorolac
Weight 50kg or more: 30mg IM/IV 6hourly as needed; max dose: 120 mg/day.
Weight <50 kg: 15mg IM/IV 6hourly as needed; max dose: 60 mg/day.
Opioid analgesics
B: tramadol (IM/IV) 50-100mg 6hourly.
OR
C: morphine (IV/IM) 3–5mg as a single dose, then further boluses of 1–2mg/minute. Maximum dose of morphine 0.1–0.2mg/kg, and monitor vitals closely.

OR
B: pethidine (IV/IM) 1–2mg/kg (used for analgesia during anaesthesia, and during labour).
OR
S: fentanyl (IV) 1–2µg/kg.
OR
S: remifentanil 0.5-1mcg/kg/min or 1mcg/kg Antagonists of Opioids for opioid overdose:
B: naloxone (IV) 0.4mg–2mg, alternatively may be given IM or SC. For reversal of opioid sedation initial dose 0.1– 0.2mg (IV) at 2–3 minutes’ intervals to the desired degree of reversal.
Acute Pain Due to Gastrointestinal Colic
B: Hyoscine butyl bromide, IV/oral, 10 mg 8 hourly.
Note:
There are various medical conditions associated with severe acute pain e.g., myocardial infarction, renal colic, sickle-cell crisis and intra-articular haemorrhage due to haemophilia.
The analgesic treatment for these conditions is the same as for patients with acute postoperative pain.
Patients should be monitored for respiratory and cardiovascular depression when IV opioids are provided.
Patients already on opioids for chronic pain, who experience an acute painful event, may be opioid tolerant and require higher IV opioid boluses to control their pain.
Chronic Non-Cancer Pain: A biopsychosocial assessment is necessary for effective pain management. Look out for the etiology and perpetuating factors and manage accordingly. Note that there may be overlap between different aetiologies, and condition specific pain management is paramount.
Pharmacological Management
Paracetamol, ibuprofen and tramadol may be used alone or in combination according to the severity of the pain. Mild/moderate pain:
A: paracetamol (PO) 1 g 4-6hourly when required. Maximum daily dose: 4g in 24 hours.
OR
A: ibuprofen (PO) 400mg 8hourly with meals. May be used in combination with paracetamol or opioids. For high-risk patients or patients with peptic ulcers, add a proton pump inhibitor
C: lansoprazole (PO) 30mg once a day. Severe pain:
B: tramadol, oral, 50–100mg 4-6hourly.
OR
C: morphine syrup (PO).
Starting dose: 10-15mg (maximum 0.2 mg/kg) 4 hourly. Elderly or frail patients: 2.5–5mg (PO) (maximum 0.1 mg/kg) 4hourly. Increase dose by 50% every 24 hours if pain control is inadequate.

Critical Care
The goal is to guide the management of critically ill patients and perioperative care, emergency stabilization, and continuous ICU support. The Core Principles of Critical Care include;
Early recognition of deterioration (ABCDE).
Support failing organs: respiration, circulation, consciousness.
Prioritize oxygen, fluids, monitoring, and referral.
Table 2.4 Summary of Key Conditions and Initial Management
Condition
Key Initial Management
Sepsis/Septic Shock, hypovolemic shock
Fluids (30ml/kg), antibiotics within 1 hour, monitor BP, urine Vasopressors/Inotropes and definitive source control.
Cardiogenic Shock
Inotropes.
Haemorrhagic Shock
Oxygen, Fluids (ie RL/0.9%-NS), Tranexamic acid, Vasopressors, Blood and blood products.
Respiratory Distress/Failure
High-flow oxygen, sit the patient up, consider assisted ventilation
Status Epilepticus
Maintain and secure ABC, Anti-convulsant, check glucose & temperature.
Hypotension/Shock
IV fluids, identify cause, use vasopressors if trained
Unconscious Patient
Airway protection, GCS, glucose check, avoid aspiration
Post-op Monitoring
Observe for bleeding, hypoxia, pain, delirium, and infection
Anaphylactic Shock
Epinephrine (adrenaline) IV/IM, Steroids, Anti-histamines, plus supportive care and specific antidote if poison/toxin is known.

Fluids (ie RL/0.9%-NS), Insulin, treat any trigger, ABG and check serum electrolytes (i.e., do not start Insulin without knowing K+).
Acute kidney injury
Look for the cause, maintain minimal fluid intake, and may need urgent referral to a nephrologist (refer to a chapter for acute kidney injury)

SpO₂ < 90% despite oxygen therapy

Iron Deficiency Anaemia

CHAPTER THREE HAEMATOLOGY AND BLOOD TRANSFUSION
A lack of iron in the body (mainly due to nutritional deficiency, chronic blood loss, malabsorption and hookworm infestations and increased demand such as during pregnancy).
Risks groups
Pediatric population
Pregnant women
Patients with chronic or recurrent bleeding
Patients on chronic use of proton pump inhibitors
Gastrointestinal surgical resections.
Clinical Presentation
Fatigue, palpitation, dizziness, glossitis, koilonychias (spoon-shaped nails), and pica.
Investigations
Full blood picture (FBP)
Peripheral smear
Iron studies- serum iron levels, total iron binding capacity, serum ferritin.
Stool analysis for hookworm ova and occult blood. If stool for occult blood is positive, do an Oesophagoduodenoscopy (OGD) to confirm upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
Non-Pharmacological Management
To prevent iron deficiency;
Eat a variety of iron-rich foods like meat, eggs, legumes (dried beans, lentils, peas), spinach and dark green leafy vegetables, iron fortified breads and cereals, nuts and seeds.
To help in iron absorption from the diet
Avoid drinking tea/coffee with meals
Increase intake of Vitamin-C rich foods (e.g., citrus fruit, broccoli, cauliflower, guavas, tomatoes, bell peppers and strawberries) with meals to maintain iron in its reduced state.

Treat the underlying cause of iron deficiency anaemia. Adults
A: ferrous sulfate (PO) 200mg 24hrly for 3months. Children
A: ferrous sulphate (PO) 5mg/kg 24hrly for 3 months. Continue for 3 months after the normal hemoglobin has been achieved.
OR
B: blood transfusion (is only indicated if anaemia is life-threatening; e.g., anaemia in failure, hypoxia.)
OR
D: iron sucrose (IV) 200mg in 100ml 0.9% sodium chloride running for 15 minutes once a day, three times a week for 2 weeks.
Note
Parenteral iron is indicated in patients who cannot tolerate or are refractory to oral iron.

Megaloblastic Anemia
This is a condition whereby the bone marrow usually produces large, structurally abnormal, immature red blood cells (megaloblasts), often due to inadequate intake or malabsorption of vitamin B12 or folate.
Clinical Presentation
Pallor, depression, hair loss, pins and needles, numbness in hands or feet, tremors and palsies, mildly jaundiced (lemon yellow tint), beefy tongue, darkening of palms and ataxic gait.
Investigations
FBC-Low Hb, sometimes pancytopenia, raised mcv but maybe low or normal if coexisting with iron deficiency (combined deficiency anaemia)
Peripheral smear
Serum vitamin B12,
Serum folate level,
TSH
Reticulocyte count
Bone marrow aspiration may be indicated
Pharmacological Management
Vitamin (B12 deficiency anaemia) and other macrocytic anemias without neurological involvement
C: hydroxocobalamin (IM) initially 1mg 3times a week for 2weeks
THEN
C: hydroxocobalamin (IM) 1mg every 3months.
Review the patient’s blood counts and clinical assessment every 3months. Pernicious Anaemia (B12 deficiency) with neurological symptoms and signs
C: hydroxocobalamin (IM) initially 1mg on alternate days until no further improvement (maximum reversal or neuro- psychiatric signs and symptoms are achieved) then 1mg every 2-3months
OR
C: methylcobalamin (PO) 500µgm 8hourly for 3 months
AND
A: folic acid (PO) 5mg 24hourly for at least 3 months. This must be started simultaneously with the injection of vitamin B12
AND
A: ferrous sulphate (PO) 200mg 8hourly for at least 3months
Haemolytic Anaemia
Haemolytic anaemia results from an increase in the rate of red cell destruction in the intravascular or in the reticuloendothelial system in some pathological disorders
Clinical Presentation
Pallor, jaundice, splenomegaly, Anaemia, Reticulocytosis, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, and haemoglobinuria
Investigations
FBP
Peripheral blood smear
Reticulocyte count
Haemoglobinuria
Bilirubin (direct and indirect)
Coombs test (Direct and Indirect)
LDH
Haptoglobin
Non- Pharmacological Management
Splenectomy may be considered in those who fail to respond to Pharmacological Management.
Pharmacological Management
A: prednisolone (PO) 1-1.5mg/kg/day for 1-3 weeks until Hb > 10g/dl
AND/OR
S: cyclophosphamide (IV) 50mg/kg/day for 4days
If no response;
A: folic acid (PO) 5mg 24hourly should be given for 1to 3months.
OR
B: blood transfusion if anaemia is severe
OR
S*: High dose human immunoglobulin G (IV) 400mg/kg/day for 5days
Sickle Cell Disease (SCD) Clinical Presentation
Displays a wide spectrum of clinical manifestations with onset from 6 months of age, typically presenting with acute onset of unexplained illness, accompanied by pain and swelling of different parts of the body, fever, anaemia, jaundice, dyspnea, hepato-splenomegaly and neurological impairment with loss of vision.
Investigations
Sickling test, Point-of-care rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs),
High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC),
Hemoglobin electrophoresis, Isoelectric focusing (IEF)
Other ancillary laboratory investigations useful in the detection and monitoring of the disease include:
FBP
Peripheral Smear
Reticulocyte count,
LDH, Bilirubin Direct
Total liver and renal profile,

ECG and ECHO
Spirometry
Extended Blood grouping CXR,
Abdominal USS
Transcranial Doppler USS,
Note: Confirmatory test should be done to all patients with positive screening tests and those with negative screening test results but have Clinical Presentation suggestive of SCD.

From the age of 10 years, screen for renal disease (proteinuria by urine dipstick) and retinopathy annually Annual screening for risk of stroke by transcranial Doppler from the age of 2years to 16years.

Scheduled, long-term red cell transfusion program aims to prevent complications in SCD by maintaining the target Hb and reducing HbS level to 30%.

Excessive iron deposition in organs, including the liver, heart, pancreas, and endocrine glands, leading to fibrosis, organ dysfunction, and failure caused by Chronic Transfusions:
Each unit of transfused blood contains approximately 200–250 mg of iron and the body lacks a physiological mechanism to excrete excess iron.

SCD Emergency Conditions:
Acute chest syndrome
Life-threatening – admit the patient in a high dependency unit or ICU,
Diagnostic criteria – respiratory distress (fast breathing, SPO2<95% on air) and/or pleuritic pain, cough, fever, tachycardia, infiltrates on CXR,
Investigations – arterial blood gases, creatinine, electrolytes, ALT, FBP, malaria test, blood and urine culture and sensitivity, CRP, CXR, HPLC,
Management – Give supplemental oxygen to maintain SPO2>95%, analgesia for pain relief, fluids per hydration protocol, broad-spectrum antibiotics while awaiting culture and sensitivity results, top up blood transfusion or exchange transfusion if expertise available.
Acute anaemia
Haemoglobin < 5g/dl or recent acute drop in Hb >2g/dl below steady state.
Causes – infection, splenic sequestration, haemolytic crisis and aplastic crisis.
Investigations – do FBP, reticulocyte count, creatinine, bilirubin, ALT, LDH, malaria test, urine and blood culture and sensitivity, blood grouping and cross-matching,
Management – immediately transfuse packed red cells 10mls/kg over 4hours, repeat transfusion as needed as per transfusion protocol, treat the underlying cause, document the size of the liver and spleen.

Pancytopenia, Bone marrow hypocellularity of < 30% hematopoietic cells.

Haemophilia is an inherited, X-linked lifelong bleeding disorder that affects males almost exclusively.

Long history of Purpura, menorrhagia, epistaxis, and gingival haemorrhage.

Blood Transfusion
Currently, the following blood components are available for transfusion: packed red blood cells, Fresh Frozen Plasma, single- unit platelets (plasma-rich) and whole blood units.
Whole blood: One unit contains 450mls of blood. Indications: Open heart surgery, and in the absence of PRBCs in patients with acute blood loss and hypovolaemia.
D: Packed red blood cells (PRBCs); One unit increases haemoglobin (Hb) level by approximately 1g/dl in adult, whereas in children, a dose of 10-15mls/kg will increase the Hb by about 3g/dl.
Indications: acute blood loss, exchange transfusion, cardiac patients with Hb level <8g/dl, chronic symptomatic anaemia with Hb <5g/dl, preoperative patients with Hb level <8g/dl, pre-radiotherapy patients with Hb level <10g/dl, pre and post chemotherapy patients with Hb <9g/dl, and patients admitted to ICU with Hb <7g/dl.
D: Platelets; Dosage: 50mls per 10kg i.e., 5-6 RDP units in adults. In infants < 10kg, the dose is 5mls/kg, one adult therapeutic dose increases platelet counts by approximately 20-40 X109/L.
Indications include, Therapeutic: thrombocytopenia of platelet counts< 50X109/L with clinical evidence of bleeding. Prophylactic in patients with platelet counts of: <10 X109/L, <20X109/L with additional risk factor of bleeding, <50X109/L and planned for minor surgery, <100X109/L with multiple injuries, or microvascular bleeding, or planned for major surgery. Also, in massive transfusion to maintain a platelet count of
>50X109/L.
Contraindications: Absolutely contraindicated in heparin-induced thrombotic thrombocytopenia (HITT) and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Relatively contraindicated in idiopathic thrombocytopenia (ITP) unless a life-threatening bleeding is anticipated.
D: Fresh frozen plasma (FFP)
Dosage: 10-20ml/kg, approximately 4-6 units for adult, this will raise a minimum of 30% of plasma clotting factors.
Indications: haemophilia if factor concentrates not available, patients with significant coagulopathy eg DIC, Vitamin K deficiency and massive transfusion, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) or haemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) as top up or exchange plasma transfusion, scoline apnoea, haemorrhagic disease of the newborn.
Types of blood transfusion
Acute simple/episodic transfusion
Used in the management of symptomatic patients with anaemia or bleeding tendencies.
Chronic/top-up transfusion
Used as a prophylactic to prevent complications, e.g. In patients with sickle cell anaemia (SCA)
Exchange blood transfusion
Indications: Severe hyperbilirubinemia (per nomogram), hemolytic disease, or failed intensive phototherapy. In SCD, exchange is indicated in patients with severe disease, those undergoing a major surgery and as a preparatory procedure before Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplant.
Massive blood transfusion
Transfusion of blood volume to the patient equivalent to his/her total blood volume in less than 24 hours, or 10 units or more in 24 hours. Administer in parallel a 1:1:1 ratio of 6 Units of RBCs, 6 Units of FFP and 6 Units of Platelets. The target is to achieve 1:1:1 ratio over 6 hours. Aim the PT, PTT <1.5x control mean, fibrinogen >1 g/L, target platelet > 100x109/L if pts has CNS trauma, eye and > 50x109/L for other type of injuries.

Curative intervention that involves infusion of healthy stem cells to replace defective hematopoietic system and reconstitute the bone marrow after a high-dose chemotherapy in both hematological (Leukemia, Lymphoma, Multiple Myeloma, and Sickle Cell Disease) and other non-hematological conditions.

Monitor for drug toxicities (e.g., renal with amphotericin/amikacin, neutropenia with ganciclovir).
De-escalate therapy promptly based on cultures and clinical response.

Graft-versus-Host Disease (GVHD)
Acute GVHD: skin, liver, gut (Day 20–100)
Chronic GVHD: multi-organ autoimmune-like disease (>Day 100).
General Principles
GVHD risk highest with mismatched/unrelated donors, peripheral blood stem cells, older patients, and female donor– male recipient.
Multidisciplinary team: Transplant physician, dermatology, gastroenterology, ophthalmology, pharmacists and infectious diseases.
Early diagnosis critical — biopsy (skin/gut/liver) where feasible to exclude infection/malignancy.
Monitor for overlapping infections, drug toxicities (renal with CNIs, osteoporosis with steroids), and quality of life.
Taper immunosuppression slowly once controlled; abrupt withdrawal risks flare.
Acute GVHD (typically Day +20–100; can occur earlier/later):
Classic target organs: Skin (maculopapular rash), liver (cholestatic jaundice), gut (diarrhoea, nausea, abdominal pain).
Staging/Grading: Use modified Glucksberg or MAGIC criteria (stage 1–4 per organ; overall grade I–IV). Biopsy preferred for confirmation.

Mild (grade I, skin-only): Consider topical steroids + optimization of prophylaxis (no systemic steroids if possible). Duration: Taper steroids slowly over 4–8 weeks once complete/partial response; monitor for rebound.

Veno-Occlusive Disease / Sinusoidal Obstruction Syndrome (VOD/SOS)
Timing: Early (within 21–30 days post-HSCT)
Features: Painful hepatomegaly, ascites, rising bilirubin, weight gain, renal dysfunction.
Pharmacological Management
S: defibrotide (IV) 6.25mg/kg 6hourly for ≥21 days (only evidence-based therapy). Duration: Minimum 21 days; continue until complete resolution of symptoms/signs if longer.
Supportive: fluid balance, diuretics, avoid hepatotoxic drugs.
Monitor for bleeding (contraindicated in active haemorrhage).
Supportive care (Essential for All Cases)
Fluid balance: Strict input/output charting; restrict fluids to 1–1.5 L/m²/day if weight gain/ascites.
Diuretics: Spironolactone 100–200 mg/day + furosemide (as needed) to maintain negative fluid balance without hypotension.
Pain management: Analgesia for hepatomegaly (avoid hepatotoxic NSAIDs).
Graft Failure / Poor Graft Function
Manifestations: Persistent low blood counts (cytopenias) + mixed chimerism on chimerism test. Higher risk in SCD Reduced-intensity conditioning or history of many blood transfusions.
Treatment (stepwise)
Optimize immunosuppression – Adjust tacrolimus/cyclosporine to therapeutic levels.
Growth factors – G-CSF 5 µg/kg/day SC/IV until neutrophils recover.
Donor lymphocyte infusion (DLI) – Selected cases only (low dose to avoid GVHD).
Second transplant – Only in selected stable patients; refer to specialized centre.
Supportive care
Regular blood/platelet transfusions
Strict infection prophylaxis
Avoid marrow-toxic drugs
Hemorrhagic cystitis post-HSCT.
Timing Early (cyclophosphamide-related) or late (BK virus).
Symptoms Hematuria (blood in urine), dysuria (painful urination), clots.
Treatment (stepwise)
Aggressive hydration (IV 2–3 L/m²/day) + continuous bladder irrigation with normal saline (if clots).
Analgesia + antispasmodics e.g., D: oxybutynin (PO) 5 mg 8hourly
For BK virus (severe cases only): Antivirals (cidofovir if available) + reduce immunosuppression if feasible.
Urology input for clot retention or heavy bleeding.
Supportive care
Strict fluid balance and daily urine monitoring.
Prevent with MESNA + hydration during cyclophosphamide.
Mucositis & GI Toxicity
Timing: Early post-conditioning (peaks day +5 to +14). Treatment (stepwise)
Pain control: Paracetamol → opioids (morphine) for severe pain. Refer pain management.
Oral care protocols: Normal saline or sodium bicarbonate mouth rinses every 2–4 hours; soft brushing.
Nutrition: Enteral (NG tube) preferred; parenteral (TPN) if severe. Aim 25–30 kcal/kg/day.
Infection prophylaxis: Intensify acyclovir, antifungal, and antibacterial per Infection STG.
Supportive care
Anti-nausea medicines.
Daily mouth/gut assessment.
Cryotherapy (ice chips) during conditioning if possible.
Thrombotic Microangiopathy (TA-TMA)
Features:
Hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, renal injury, hypertension. Treatment (stepwise)
Withdraw calcineurin inhibitors immediately (stop tacrolimus/cyclosporine).
Supportive care & BP control: Aggressive hypertension management (ACEi/ARB or other agents); dialysis if needed.
Supportive care
Blood transfusions as required.
Avoid nephrotoxic drugs.
Daily monitoring of blood film, LDH, platelets, creatinine, and BP.
Organ Toxicity (Liver, Kidney, Lung)
Causes: Conditioning chemo, infections, GVHD, iron overload
Treatment
Dose adjustment/avoid nephrotoxic drugs
Manage iron overload (chelation post-engraftment if indicated) Pulmonary rehab, treat infections early
Late Effects (Months–Years)
Infertility → fertility preservation counseling pre-HSCT
Endocrine dysfunction (thyroid, growth in children) → periodic screening
Secondary malignancies (rare) → long-term surveillance
Psychosocial challenges → counseling, reintegration support
Revaccination → consider when immunosuppressants are stopped.
