Obstructive Lung Diseases
It’s a chronic airway disease which result in airway flow limitation can be either reversible or irreversible
Asthma
Asthma is chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways, characterized by variable respiratory symptoms such as wheezing, shortness of breath, chest tightness, and cough, along with variable expiratory airflow limitation.
Clinical Presentation
Asthma is likely when there are
Typical intermittent symptoms that vary over time in frequency and severity
History of atopy,
Family history of asthma,
Environmental/ occupational exposures,
Response to asthma therapy.
Investigations
Diagnosis of asthma is based on clinical assessment supported by Lung Function Test that demonstrates variable airflow obstruction in adults and children >5 years. Peak Flow Meter should be used when Spirometry is not available.
Other investigations include, CXR, FBP, ESR, S. IGE.
Note:
Diagnosing asthma in children under 5 can be challenging
The presence of frequent asthma-like symptoms (e.g., wheezing, cough, difficulty breathing) and improvement with asthma medication are key indicators.
Asthma Management
Management of Chronic Asthma
Asthma management should be an ongoing process of assessing, treating and reviewing the patient’s response.
Non-Pharmacological Management
The following factors should be addressed:
Adherence to medications
Correct inhaler technique should be demonstrated and checked regularly
Avoidance of triggers and other factors that could worsen asthma including: Exposure to Environmental Tobacco Smoke, Polluted environment (both indoors and outdoors) and Medications such as aspirin or NSAIDs, Avoid non- selective β-blockers,
Management of other medical conditions likely to affect asthma control such as cardiac disease, allergic rhinitis, obesity, Sleep Apnea and GERD.
Pharmacological Management

Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)
Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a diverse lung condition marked by persistent airflow limitation and respiratory symptoms of shortness of breath, cough, and exacerbations; resulting from structural abnormalities in the airways (Bronchitis) or in the alveoli (Emphysema). It is usually caused by significant exposure to noxious particles or gases.
Risk Factors for COPD
Indoor and outdoor air pollution
Exposure from burning wood
Exposure to biofuel
Heating in poorly vented dwellings
Occupational exposure
Coal miners
Tunnel Workers
Hard-rock miners
Concrete manufacture
Livestock farming (i.e., to pesticides)
Cigarette smoking
Use of domestic solid fuel

Childhood Asthma
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency

Shortness of breath
Cough, sometimes caused by the production of mucus
Wheezing
Slow and prolonged expiration
Chest wall hyperinflation,
Limited diaphragmatic motion on auscultation,
Distant breath sounds, and heart sounds
Coarse early inspiratory crackles.
Use of accessory muscles
Pursed-lip breathing
Signs of cor pulmonale. (Raised JVP, peripheral oedema, hepatomegaly etc.)
Cyanosis
Asterixis
Investigations
FBP (Raised hematocrit: men>52%	and women >47)
ESR /CRP/Procalcitonin

Chest radiography: Exclusion of other respiratory conditions with similar presentation as well as complications.

Sputum cytology (if the cough is persistent)
Chest CT scan: Detailed disease assessment and surgical planning when indicated.
Bronchoscopy (to exclude foreign body aspiration, tuberculosis, tumours, and other chronic diseases in patients with worsening symptoms, BAL for C/S)

Smoking cessation
Remove from hazardous environment
Prompt treatment of infective exacerbations
Controlled oxygen therapy

physiotherapy and avoid indoor and outdoor pollutants)
Nutrition support
Ventilatory support in specialized center
Lung volume reduction surgery

Pharmacological therapy has 3 major goals: Reduce symptoms, reduce frequency and severity of exacerbations and improve health status and exercise tolerance. It is guided by disease severity (GOLD stage), symptom burden, and exacerbation history.

Lung Abscess
A lung abscess is a localized collection of pus in the lung parenchyma caused by suppurative necrosis of lung tissue, resulting in cavity formation, usually with an air-fluid level.
Etiology (Causes):
Primary Lung Abscess (Most common): Aspiration of oropharyngeal contents
Risk factors:
Altered consciousness (e.g., alcohol, seizures, anesthesia), poor dentition, stroke
Anaerobic bacteria are most common (e.g., Peptostreptococcus, Bacteroides, Fusobacterium)
Secondary Lung Abscess
Post-obstructive (tumor, foreign body)
Septic emboli (e.g., endocarditis)
Immunosuppression
Bronchiectasis, necrotizing pneumonia (e.g., Staph. aureus, Klebsiella)
Direct extension from infection (e.g., empyema)
Clinical Presentation
Fever, chills, night sweats
Cough with foul-smelling, purulent sputum
Hemoptysis (may occur)
Pleuritic chest pain
Weight loss, fatigue
Clubbing (in chronic cases)

Test
Findings
Chest X-ray
Thick-walled cavity with air-fluid level
CT Chest
Better definition of cavity, rule out underlying mass or empyema
Sputum culture
Identify causative organisms (anaerobes, aerobes)
Blood cultures
Especially if febrile or septic
Bronchoscopy
If atypical features, no response to treatment, or suspicion of obstruction

Supportive Care
Chest physiotherapy, hydration, nutrition
Monitor inflammatory markers (e.g., CRP, WBC)
Drainage (If needed) Percutaneous catheter drainage if:
Large abscess
Poor response to antibiotics
Risk of rupture

Reserved for complications (e.g., massive hemoptysis, rupture, non-resolving abscess)

Sarcoidosis
Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disease of unknown cause characterized by the formation of non-caseating granulomas in affected organs, most commonly the lungs and lymphatic system.
Investigations
Chest X-ray: Stages 0–IV (Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, infiltrates, fibrosis)
High-Resolution CT (HRCT): Detailed lung parenchyma assessment
Pharmacological Management
First-line: Oral corticosteroids
A: prednisolone (PO): 0.5–1 mg/kg/day
Pulmonary Function Tests: Restrictive pattern, reduced DLCO
Serum ACE: Elevated in ~60% (nonspecific)
Calcium: Hypercalcemia or hypercalciuria
Tissue biopsy: non-caseating granulomas.
Typical dose: 20–40 mg daily: 4–6 weeks, then reassess for clinical/radiological response. Gradual taper over 6–12 months depending on response and severity.
Steroid-sparing agents:
S: methotrexate (PO) 10–25 mg weekly
OR
S: azathioprine (PO) 1–2 mg/kg/day
OR
S: hydroxychloroquine (PO) 200-400mg 24hourly (esp. for skin or hypercalcemia)
Coal Workers’ Pneumoconiosis (CWP)
A chronic occupational lung disease caused by inhalation of coal mine dust, leading to lung fibrosis. It is preventable but progressive if exposure continues.
Clinical Presentation
Often asymptomatic in early stages
Chronic cough, exertional dyspnea
Sputum production, wheeze (esp. with coexisting COPD)
Late-stage: hypoxemia, cor-pulmonale, respiratory failure
High risk for TB and COPD
Caplan's syndrome: CWP + rheumatoid arthritis
Investigations
Chest X-ray: Small nodules (simple); large masses (PMF)
HRCT: More sensitive—shows centrilobular nodules, fibrosis
PFTs:
Normal or restrictive pattern
↓ DLCO in advanced disease
Occupational history: Critical for diagnosis
Non-Pharmacological Management
No curative treatment
Prevention: Eliminate exposure (dust control, PPE)
Smoking cessation
Vaccinations: Influenza, pneumococcus
Pulmonary rehabilitation
Pharmacological Management
Symptom management
Bronchodilators (if airflow limitation): See COPD section
Oxygen therapy (if hypoxemic)
Silicosis
Silicosis is a pneumoconiosis caused by inhalation of crystalline silica dust, leading to chronic lung inflammation and progressive pulmonary fibrosis.
Clinical Presentation
Chronic cough, exertional dyspnea
Often asymptomatic early on
Can progress to respiratory failure
Crackles, cyanosis, and clubbing in advanced cases
↑ Risk of tuberculosis, lung cancer, and autoimmune diseases (e.g., scleroderma)
Complications
Progressive Massive Fibrosis (PMF)
Chronic respiratory failure
Pulmonary hypertension
Tuberculosis and atypical mycobacterial infections
Investigations
Chest X-ray:
-Small, rounded opacities (nodules) in upper lobes
-"Eggshell calcification" of hilar lymph nodes
HRCT chest
Pulmonary function tests (PFTs): Restrictive or mixed pattern; ↓ DLCO
TB screening recommended due to high risk
Non-Pharmacological Management
No cure – prevention is key
Prevention: Workplace control: wet drilling, ventilation, appropriate PPE
Health surveillance
periodic chest imaging, lung function testing
Remove from exposure
Supportive care:
Smoking cessation
Pulmonary Rehabilitation
TB prophylaxis or treatment if indicated
Lung transplant in advanced disease
Pharmacological Management
Oxygen therapy
Bronchodilators if obstruction present

Lung Cancer
Malignant neoplasm originating from lung parenchyma or bronchial epithelium. is the leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide. Main categories include Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC) and Small Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC).
Risk Factors
Active and passive (second and third hand) cigarette smoking
Occupational exposure (asbestos, silica, radon)
Biomass smoke exposure (prolonged indoor cooking using firewood or charcoal in poorly ventilated environments)
Air pollution
Family history of cancer
Chronic lung disease (COPD, pulmonary fibrosis)
HIV infection and immunosuppression
Note:
Smoking in all forms (cigarettes, cigars, pipes, shisha ) accounts for 90% of lung cancer cases and is a major preventable risk factor; smoking cessation should be strongly advised for all patients.
People living with HIV have an increased risk of lung cancer. Persistent respiratory symptoms in HIV-positive patients should prompt early imaging and specialist evaluation.
Clinical Presentation
Persistent or worsening cough
Hemoptysis
Dyspnea
Chest pain
Weight loss, anorexia
Hoarseness or wheeze
Recurrent chest infections
Clubbing
Lymphadenopathy
Pleural effusion
Features of metastasis (neurological deficits, bone pain)
Note: Symptoms and signs of lung cancer may mimic pulmonary TB, Patients with persistent or atypical features should be referred early for chest CT imaging and specialist evaluation to avoid delayed diagnosis.
Investigations
Initial Investigations
Chest X-ray
Full blood count
Liver function tests
Tumor markers: CEA
Confirmatory Tests
CT scan of chest
Bronchoscopy with biopsy
CT-guided needle biopsy
Sputum cytology
Management
Category
Management Measures
General Measures
Provide smoking cessation counselling
Administer oxygen therapy in hypoxic patients
Ensure adequate nutritional support
Provide analgesia and symptomatic management
Offer psychosocial support
Specific Treatment
Refer to Malignancies chapter 22
Palliative Management
Provide pain management, including opioids where indicated
Manage dyspnoea appropriately
Perform drainage of pleural effusion when indicated
Initiate end-of-life care planning
Referral Criteria
Suspicious chest X-ray or hemoptysis
Persistent cough >3 weeks in high-risk patient
Unexplained weight loss with respiratory symptoms
Confirmed malignancy for oncology evaluation
Prevention
Smoking cessation
Occupational safety measures

Pulmonary Vascular Diseases (PVDS) and Cor Pulmonale
Pulmonary Vascular Diseases (PVDs) encompasses a group of disorders that affect the blood vessels within the lungs. These disorders disrupt normal pulmonary blood flow, potentially leading to impaired gas exchange and right ventricular overload or failure (Cor Pulmonale).
The major types are Pulmonary embolism, Pulmonary Hypertension, Pulmonary veno-occlusive disease, Pulmonary Arterio- Venous Malformation etc.
Pulmonary Embolism
Refer cardiovascular disease conditions chapter 20
Pulmonary Hypertension
Pulmonary Hypertension is defined as a mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) ≥ 20 mmHg at rest, as measured by right heart catheterization.
Classification (WHO Groups):
Group 1 – Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH): Idiopathic, heritable, drug-induced, connective tissue disease, HIV, portal hypertension, congenital heart disease.
Group 2 – PH due to Left Heart Disease
Group 3 – PH due to lung diseases and/or Hypoxia: COPD, ILD, sleep apnea, high altitude.
Group 4 – Chronic Thromboembolic PH (CTEPH)
Group 5 – PH with Unclear Multifactorial Mechanisms: Hematologic, systemic, or metabolic disorders.
Clinical Presentation
Exertional dyspnea
Fatigue
Chest pain
Syncope or presyncope
Peripheral edema
Loud P2
Right ventricular heave
Jugular venous distension (JVD)
Hepatomegaly, ascites
Peripheral edema
Tricuspid regurgitation murmur
Investigations Initial Testing
ECG: right heart strain
Chest X-ray: enlarged pulmonary arteries
Echocardiography: RV function and estimate pulmonary pressures
Definitive Diagnosis
Right heart catheterization (gold standard): confirms elevated mPAP ≥ 20 mmHg
Additional Evaluation
V/Q scan or CTPA: to rule out CTEPH
PFTs, ABG: for lung diseases
Autoimmune panel, HIV testing, LFTs: to identify causes
Non-Pharmacological Management
Oxygen therapy as indicated
Exercise and supportive care
Pharmacological Management
Diuretics (for fluid overload)
Anticoagulation (especially in CTEPH)
Group-specific Treatments:
Group 1 (PAH):
Initial therapy:
Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (PDEi)
S: sildenafil (PO) 20 mg 8hourly
(Use the IV formulation if available for critically ill patients)
If inadequate response or intermediate risk, add Endothelin Receptor Antagonist (ERA)
S: bosentan (PO) 62.5 mg 12hourly
Early oral combination therapy (PDEi + ERA) in stage 2 or advanced disease
Calcium channel blockers (if Vaso reactive):
B: amlodipine (PO) 2.5mg - 10mg 24hourly
OR
A: nifedipine Slow Release (PO) 30mg - 120 mg 12hourly
OR
D: diltiazem 120 - 240 mg 24hourly
Group 2: Treat underlying heart failure or valvular disease
Group 3: Optimize treatment of lung disease and provide oxygen as required.
Group 4 (CTEPH):
Lifelong anticoagulation
Medical therapy including anticoagulation (could be lifelong), Pulmonary endarterectomy (surgical)
Group 5: Treat underlying disorder
Cor Pulmonale
Cor Pulmonale is right ventricular (RV) enlargement and/or failure due to pulmonary hypertension (PH) caused by diseases of the lung, chest wall, or pulmonary vasculature.
Excludes RV failure due to left heart disease or congenital heart disease.
Clinical Presentation
Progressive exertional dyspnea
Fatigue, chest discomfort
Swelling of legs
Abdominal distension
Raised JVP
Hepatomegaly
Ascites
Peripheral edema
Loud P2
RV heave
Tricuspid regurgitation murmur
Investigations
Test
Findings
ECG
Right axis deviation, RV hypertrophy
Chest X-ray
Enlarged pulmonary arteries, right heart border
Echocardiogram
RV enlargement, raised pulmonary pressures, TR
ABG
Hypoxemia ± hypercapnia
PFTs
Obstructive or restrictive pattern depending on underlying disease
BNP/NT-pro BNP
May be elevated if RV dysfunction present
Right heart catheterization
Confirms PH and RV pressure status
Non-Pharmacological Management
Optimize COPD, ILD, or other pulmonary disease treatment
Smoking cessation
Long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) if PaO₂ < 55 mmHg (or < 60 mmHg with polycythemia/cor pulmonale)
Pharmacological Management
Give Diuretics:
Furosemide, spironolactone for volume overload
Use cautiously to avoid reducing preload too much
Pulmonary Vasodilators:
Consider specific PH therapy (e.g., sildenafil, Bosentan) only if Group 1 PH or CTEPH
Others:
Non-invasive ventilation (CPAP or BiPAP) in sleep-disordered breathing
Anticoagulation if CTEPH or high risk of VTE

Pleural Effusion
Pleural effusion, is collection of fluid abnormally present in the pleural space, usually resulting from excess fluid production and/or decreased lymphatic absorption, is rarely a primary disease process but is usually secondary to other diseases.
Clinical Presentation
Progressive dyspnea
Cough
Pleuritic chest pain
Extrapulmonary symptoms that mimic features of congestive heart failure (CHF) etc.
Night sweats, fever, hemoptysis, and weight loss should suggest tuberculosis (TB)
Hemoptysis also raises the possibility of malignancy, other endotracheal or endobronchial pathology, or pulmonary infarction
Pleural friction rub
When pleural fluid >300ml
>Dullness to percussion
>Decreased tactile fremitus
>Asymmetrical chest expansion
>Displacement of the trachea and mediastinum toward the side of the effusion- observed with effusions larger than 1000 mL
>Diminished or inaudible breath sounds
Investigations
CXR
Full blood picture
Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)
Point of care bed side USS
Pleural fluid analysis:
>Gross appearance:
>Biochemistry: Glucose, PH, LDH, Protein: Use Light’s Criteria to differentiate between transudative and exudative pleural effusions
>Microbiology: Gram Stain, Gene Xpert, pleural fluid culture
Other Tests as per indication of suspected diagnosis Pleural Fluid
>ADA (High sensitivity and specificity in TB pleuritis)
>Cytology (Malignancy/autoimmune)
>Amylase (Pancreatitis)
>Triglycerides and cholesterol
>Bilirubin
Tumor markers as indicated (e.g., CA-15, CEA, CA-125etc).

Rheumatoid Factor (if indicated)
Autoimmune profile or single marker (ANA, ACE etc.)
Renal function (creatinine and BUN)
Liver function and liver enzymes (Albumin, bilirubin total, direct, PT, PTT, INR ALT, AST, GGT, ALP)
ECHO
ECG
CT-Scan Chest with contrast
Thoracoscopy
Image-guided (i.e., CT- or US-guided) pleural biopsy
Management
Serial Thoracentesis- for non-complicated pleural effusion.
Chest Tube Drainage-Hemothorax, Empyema, Complicated para-pneumonic effusion, Post-trauma, Malignant
Fibrinolytic Therapy-use of Streptokinase and Alteplase, indicated for patients with empyema and complicated loculated pleural effusions.
Thoracoscopy and video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS: For patient with fibrinopurulent pleural infections and loculated effusion.
Pleurodesis (pleural sclerosis) – Various agents can be used to sclerose the pleural space:
>Povidone-iodine 20mls of 10% mixed with 80–100 mL of 0.9% NaCl,
>Talk Slurry or Poudrage: via thoracoscope
>Doxycycline, bleomycin sulfate,
Thoracotomy, Decortication, and Open Drainage- Main salvage procedure after unsuccessful thoracoscopy.
Indication for thoracostomy/decortication
Patients with organized empyemas who cannot tolerate thoracotomy or have trapped lungs can undergo rib resection with open drainage
Chronic empyema with bronchopleural fistulas or chronic empyema that are not amenable to surgery
Critical ill and toxic patients with associated mediastinitis or bronchopleural fistulas who require mediastinal drainage or fistula closure.
For Malignant Effusions
Chest tube drainage, radiation, chemotherapy, surgical pleurectomy, pleuroperitoneal shunt, pleurodesis or decortication and indwelling pleural catheter.
Note
Emergent thoracentesis and/or chest tube placement is necessary in patients with pleural effusion causing imminent or ongoing respiratory compromise or hemodynamic instability.
Refer to specialist/specialist review: Unexplained or recurrent effusion, malignant pleural effusion, Empyema thoracic, Loculated effusion.

Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome (OSA)
Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a sleep-related breathing disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of complete (apnea) or partial (hypopnea) upper airway collapse during sleep, leading to reduced or absent airflow despite ongoing respiratory effort, often associated with oxygen desaturation and/or arousals from sleep.
Clinical Presentation
Daytime sleepiness
Restless sleep
Loud snoring
Morning headaches;
Insomnia;
Decreased sex drive;
Unexplained weight gain;
Increased	urination and/or nocturia.
Heartburn or gastro esophageal reflux disease
Trouble	concentrating; mood changes such as irritability,		anxiety	and depression; Forgetfulness; Increased heart rate and/or blood pressure;
Obesity
Large neck circumference (>43cm in male, >40.5cm in
female)
Crowded oropharynx (e.g., enlarged tonsils), nasal septum deviation
Cranio-facial abnormalities: Retrognathia / Micrognathia, Midface hypoplasia
Elevated BP
Investigations
Use STOP-BANG questionnaire and EPWORTH Sleepiness Scale for screening.
Polysomnography (PSG): Gold standard. Measures apnea–hypopnea index (AHI).
Non-Pharmacological Management
General & Lifestyle Measures
Weight loss: Most effective non-device therapy
Avoid alcohol and sedatives: Reduce airway collapsibility
Avoid supine position (positional OSA)
Smoking cessation
Positive Airway Pressure (PAP) Therapy: The mainstay of OSA treatment, moderate to severe cases: CPAP/ APAP/ BiPAP depending on tolerance and comorbidity.
Oral Appliances: Mandibular advancement devices (MADs)
Behavioral & Adjunctive Therapies: e.g., Cognitive behavioral therapy
Surgical Option: Considered when anatomic obstruction is identified and PAP is not tolerated: Refer to ENT chapter 15
UPPP (Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty): Removes/repositions tissue at soft palate
Tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy: Especially in children
Pharmacological Management
Limited role in OSA.

Respiratory Failure and ARDS
Respiratory failure is a life-threatening condition in which the respiratory system fails to maintain adequate gas exchange, resulting in hypoxemia, hypercapnia, or both.
Types of Respiratory Failure:
Type
Description
Key Feature
Type I (Hypoxemic)
Failure of oxygenation
PaO₂ < 60 mmHg (on room air)
Type II (Hypercapnic)
Failure of ventilation
PaCO₂ > 45 mmHg
Causes:
Type of Respiratory Failure
Common Causes
Type I (Hypoxemic)
Pneumonia
Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)
Pulmonary embolism
Pulmonary oedema (cardiogenic or non-cardiogenic)
Interstitial lung disease
Type II (Hypercapnic)
Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
Neuromuscular disorders (e.g., myasthenia gravis, Guillain–Barré syndrome)
Central nervous system depression (e.g., drugs, stroke)
Obesity hypoventilation syndrome
Chest wall disorders (e.g., kyphoscoliosis)
Clinical Presentation
Dyspnea, tachypnea
Cyanosis (Type I)
Headache, confusion, asterixis (Type II – due to hypercapnia)
Accessory muscle use, nasal flaring
Signs of underlying cause (e.g., wheeze, crepitations, fever)
Investigations
Arterial blood gas (ABG)
↓PaO₂ in Type I
↑PaCO₂ ± ↓PaO₂ in Type II
Chest X-ray / CT chest: Identify underlying pathology
Pulmonary function tests, if chronic cause suspected
ECG, Echocardiogram: If cardiogenic causes suspected
Labs: CBC, electrolytes, renal/liver function, infection markers
Non-Pharmacological Management
Component
Management
General Measures
Identify and treat the underlying cause
Monitor oxygenation and ventilation (SpO₂, arterial blood gases [ABG])
Provide supportive care including fluids, antipyretics, and deep vein thrombosis (DVT) prophylaxis
Oxygen Therapy
Type I Respiratory Failure (Hypoxemic):
Administer supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO₂ ≥ 92% Type II Respiratory Failure (Hypercapnic):
Use oxygen cautiously to avoid worsening hypercapnia
Target oxygen saturation according to clinical condition and ABG findings
Ventilatory Support
Non-invasive ventilation (NIV) indicated in selected patients, e.g., chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS)
Invasive mechanical ventilation for worsening hypoxia, hypercapnia, respiratory fatigue, or failure of NIV
High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) may be used in selected cases of Type I respiratory failure
Pharmacological Management
Specific Treatments
COPD exacerbation: bronchodilators, steroids, NIV
Pneumonia: antibiotics
ARDS: lung-protective ventilation, prone positioning
Neuromuscular causes: IVIG/plasmapheresis + ventilatory support
Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)
A severe inflammatory lung condition characterized by acute onset of hypoxemic respiratory failure with bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload.
Based on the Berlin Criteria:
Timing: Within 1 week of a known clinical insult or new/worsening respiratory symptoms
Chest imaging: Bilateral opacities not fully explained by effusions, collapse, or nodules
Origin of edema: Not primarily cardiac
Oxygenation (on PEEP ≥5 cm H₂O):
Severity
PaO₂/FiO₂ Ratio
Mild ARDS
200–300 mmHg
Moderate ARDS
100–200 mmHg
Severe ARDS
<100 mmHg
Common Causes:
Direct lung injury: Pneumonia (bacterial, viral including COVID-19), aspiration, inhalation injury, drowning
Indirect lung injury: Sepsis, pancreatitis, trauma, massive transfusion, drug overdose
Clinical Presentation
Acute dyspnea, tachypnea
Hypoxia refractory to oxygen therapy
Diffuse crackles on auscultation
Investigations:
ABG: Respiratory alkalosis on ABG (early), later progressing to hypoxemia and hypercapnia
Chest X-ray/CT: Bilateral infiltrates (ground-glass opacities or consolidation)
Echocardiography: To rule out cardiogenic pulmonary edema
Labs: To identify underlying cause and for monitoring (e.g., cultures, procalcitonin, inflammatory markers)
Non pharmacological
Refer to higher facility for intensive care.
Admit to ICU
Treat underlying cause (e.g., sepsis, pneumonia)
Lung-protective mechanical ventilation:
>Low tidal volume (6 mL/kg predicted body weight)
>Plateau pressure <30 cm H₂O
>Adequate PEEP to prevent alveolar collapse
Prone positioning: Especially in moderate–severe ARDS
Neuromuscular blockade: In select cases of severe ARDS
Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation (ECMO): For refractory hypoxemia despite optimal ventilation
Pharmacological Management
Conservative fluid management once hemodynamically stable
Adjunctive Therapies (selected cases):
Inhaled nitric oxide (short-term benefit)
Corticosteroids in selected cases: e.g. COVID-19 ARDS: B: Dexamethasone (IV) 6mg 24hourly.
Protease inhibitors e.g.
S: ulinastatin (IV) 200,000 to 600,000 IU/day, in 2-3 divided doses. Use restricted to ICU, under specialist supervision.
CHAPTER TEN GASTROINTESTINAL DISEASE CONDITIONS

Infections of Gastrointestinal Tract
Amoebiasis
Amoebiasis is an infection caused by the protozoa organism Entamoeba histolytica, which can cause colitis and other extra- intestinal manifestations. The infection is primarily acquired through ingestion of contaminated food and water and occasionally can be acquired through oral-anal sexual practices.
Clinical Presentation
Bloody diarrhea
Crampy abdominal pain
Fever
Weight loss
Peritonitis in severe forms
Evidence of motile trophozoites or cysts on saline wet mount from a stool specimen
Pharmacological Management
Because metronidazole and tinidazole do not kill all cysts in the bowel, a two-step approach is necessary for complete eradication:
Tissue Agents (Active Infection): Used to kill invading parasites and treat symptoms.
A: metronidazole (PO) 400–800mg 8hourly for 7-10days
OR
B: tinidazole (PO) 2g 24 hourly for 3-5days due to shorter duration
AND
C: diloxanide furoate (PO) 500 mg 8hourly for 10days
Luminal Agents (Cyst Eradication): Essential to kill cysts and prevent relapse, even if symptoms are gone.
Amoebic Liver Abscess
It is the most frequent extra-intestinal manifestation of Entamoeba histolytica infection which results from the invasion of the portal venous system from the colon leading to inflammation and subsequently abscess formation particularly involving the right lobe of the liver.
Clinical Presentation
High grade fever, 39°C
Right upper quadrant pain,
Tender and enlarged liver
Positive imaging evidence of liver abscess
Serological evidence of E. histolytica antibodies or antigens
Pharmacological Management
B: metronidazole (IV) 800mg 8hourly for 10days.
OR
B: tinidazole (PO) Adults: 2g 24 hourly for 3days
Note
Metronidazole and Tinidazole should not be given in the first trimester of pregnancy due to potential teratogenic effects.
Should not be taken with alcohol due to disulfiram-like effects
Surgery:
Consider therapeutic aspiration of amebic liver abscess in the following situations: (1) high risk of abscess rupture, as defined by cavity size greater than 5 cm; (2) left lobe liver abscess, which is associated with higher mortality and frequency of peritoneal leak or rupture into the pericardium; (3) failure to observe a clinical medical response to therapy within 5-7 days; and (4) cannot differentiate from a pyogenic liver abscess.
Giardiasis
It is the infestation of the upper small intestine caused by the flagellate protozoan Giardia lamblia (or G. intestinalis), cytopathic effects of which leads to malabsorption and diarrhea. It is more common in immune compromised individuals and is acquired through ingestion of contaminated water
Clinical Presentation
Crampy abdominal pain
Chronic diarrhoea
Steatorrhea
Weight loss
Investigations
Evidence of Giardia intestinalis trophozoites or cysts on serial 3 samples of stool examination
Serological evidence of G. Intestinalis trophozoites antigen or antibody
Evidence of G. Intestinalis in duodenal aspirates or biopsy specimen.
Pharmacological Management
A: metronidazole (PO) 400–800mg 8hourly for 5days
OR
B: tinidazole (PO) 2g 24 hourly for 3days
For refractory cases:
D: nitazoxanide (PO) 500mg 12 hourly for 3 days
Ascariasis
It is a small intestinal infestation caused by Ascaris lumbricoides which leads to malnutrition, iron deficiency anaemia, impaired growth and cognition in susceptible hosts. It is most common infestation in children, and it is acquired through ingestion of contaminated food and water.
Clinical Presentation
Chronic Diarrhea
Steatorrhea
Malnutrition
Chronic Cough (Loffler’s syndrome)
Intestinal obstruction
Obstructive jaundice
Investigations
Stool examination: evidence of ova or worms on wet mount
Pharmacological Management
A: mebendazole (PO) 500mg stat or 100mg 12hourly for 3days.
OR
A: albendazole (PO) 400mg stat
Ancylostomiasis
It is a hookworm disease caused by infestation of the small intestine with Ancylostoma duodenale or Necator americanus
leading to anaemia and malnutrition.
Clinical Presentation
Abdominal pains
Chronic diarrhea
Melena stool
Weight loss
Chronic cough (Loffler’s syndrome) PLUS
Evidence of ova or worms on wet mount stool examination
Anaemia
Pharmacological Management
A: mebendazole (PO) 500mg stat or 100mg 12hourly for 3days.
OR
A: albendazole (PO) 400mg stat
Note
If persistent, give second course after 4 weeks. Iron replacement and nutritional supplementation (protein and vitamins) should be part of the management strategy. Albendazole is contraindicated in the first trimester of pregnancy
Strongyloidiasis
Small intestinal infestation caused by Strongyloides stercoralis usually asymptomatic in immune competent adult but can lead to life-threatening infestation and disseminated strongyloidiasis in an immune-compromised host associated with high mortality rates
Clinical Presentation
Pruritic papulo–vesicular rash at the site of penetration or urticarial rash involving the perennial region extending to the buttocks, thighs and abdomen
Chronic cough
Investigations

Colicky abdominal pains
Chronic diarrhea and passage of mucus
Weight loss
Hyper-infection syndrome
Evidence of rhabditiform larva in wet mount stool examination with Serological evidence (ELISA) for anti-strongyloides antibody
Pharmacological Management
A: albendazole (PO) 400mg 12hourly for 3days (Repeat after 4 weeks if still positive stool findings)
OR
A: ivermectin (PO) 200 µg /kg 24hourly for 2days
Note: Give treatment for 10 days in case of disseminated/super infestation
Taeniasis
Is a tapeworm disease acquired from eating raw or not-well cooked food? Can be due to Taenia saginata (beef tapeworm), Taenia solium (pork tapeworm), Diphyllobothrium latum (fish tapeworm) and Hymenolepsis nana (faecal oral contamination from human and dogs) leading to chronic malnutrition (Taeniasis) or multi-organ dissemination and dysfunction (Cysticercosis)
Clinical Presentation
Taeniasis
Colicky abdominal pain
Body Weakness
Loss of or increased appetite
Constipation or diarrhea
Pruritus ani
Hyperexcitability
Investigations
Evidence of characteristic ova, proglottids or scolex in the wet mount stool examination
Cysticercosis - The cysticerci are most often located in subcutaneous and intermuscular tissues, followed by the eye and then the brain. The CNS is involved in 60-90% of patients i.e., Neurocystercosis which may manifest as:
Convulsions and/or seizures:
Intracranial hypertension: headache, nausea, vomiting, vertigo, and papilledema.
Personality	and	mental	status	changes (Neuropsychiatric changes)
Behavioral changes and learning disabilities more marked in children and immunocompromised adults. PLUS
Head CT scan OR Brain MRI
Note: Refer the patient to high centers for further investigation and expertise.
Pharmacological Management Taeniasis
A: praziquantel (PO) 5–10mg/kg stat
Cysticercosis (NCC)
A: praziquantel (PO) 50mg/kg 24hourly for 21days
OR
A: albendazole (PO) 15mg/kg 24hourly for 30days.
AND
B: dexamethasone (IV) 4mg 12hourly can be given up to 7days.
AND
A: carbamazepine (PO) initially 200 mg 12-24hourly, increased slowly to 0.8–1.2 g 24hourly in divided doses (for seizures refer to CNS chapter)
Note: Hydrocephalus should be treated with surgical shutting. Ocular manifestation cysticercosis, should be referred to eye specialist
Echinococcosis
It is a canine tape worm Echinococcus granulosus which is transmitted by dogs, sheep and horses. Human infestation is through contamination of food or water causing visceral cysts (Hydatid Cyst Disease) particularly in the liver and lungs and is usually asymptomatic in susceptible host.
Clinical Presentation
Upper abdominal discomfort and pain, poor appetite,
Upper abdominal mass swelling with enlarged liver.
Cough with features of acute hypersensitivity reaction. (for ruptured cysts)
Portal hypertension, biliary obstruction or Budd-Chiari syndrome (for complicated cases)
Investigations
Echinococcus serology
LFT, RFT, FBC
Abdominal Ultrasound
Abdominal CT scan or MRI
Pharmacological Management
A: albendazole (PO) 400mg 12hourly for 3months
OR
A: mebendazole (PO) 500mg 12hourly for 3months
Referral: For symptomatic/ complicated cases refer to higher centers with management and expertise.
PAIR (puncture, aspiration, injection, and re-aspiration) is a percutaneous treatment alternative to surgery
Surgical treatment: either radical pericystectomy or conservative deroofing
Schistosomiasis
Parasitic disease caused by blood flukes (trematodes) of the genus Schistosoma. Common species found in Tanzania are
S. haematobium responsible for urogenital schistosomiasis and S. mansoni responsible for intestinal schistosomiasis as a result of immune mediated reaction which leads to progressive inflammation and fibrosis of the urinary bladder or portal venous system respectively.
Clinical Presentation
Schistosoma mansoni
Swimmer’s itch or katayama fevers in acute infection phase.
Colicky abdominal pains
Diarrhoea and dysentery
Anemia
Hepatomegaly
Portal hypertension with bleeding esophageal varices
Decompensated liver disease
Schistosoma hematobium
Dysuria and terminal hematuria
Hematospermia
Obstructive	uropathy	(hydronephrosis, hydroureters)
Glomerulonephritis and amyloidosis
Bladder carcinoma
Chronic kidney failure
Investigations
Laboratory evidence characteristic eggs in urine, (S. Hematobium) or in stool (S. mansoni, S. japonicum) examined by kato katz thick smear procedure or PCR assays of both urine and stool samples.
Pharmacological Management
A: praziquantel (PO) 40mg/kg stat or in 2 divided doses (repeat every 6 months for continues exposure)
Typhoid and Paratyphoid
It is an acute systemic disease resulting from infection by Salmonella typhi and S. paratyphi, serovar group A and B respectively. Infection is acquired through ingestion of contaminated food and water.
Clinical Presentation
Fever, severe headache, abdominal and muscle pains (myalgia)
Delirium, obtundation, intestinal hemorrhage, bowel perforation,
Sequela neuropsychiatric complications
Investigations
Laboratory evidence of positive cultures from bone marrow aspirates; blood or stool done within 1 week of acute infection OR
Salmonella stool antigen test
Indirect fluorescent Vi antibody, ELISA for immunoglobulin M (IgM) and IgG antibodies to S. Typhi polysaccharide.
Pharmacological Management
Uncomplicated typhoid fever
A: ciprofloxacin (PO) 500mg 12 hourly for 10-14days
OR
B: azithromycin (PO) Adult 500mg 24hourly for 7days
OR
A: cefixime 400mg (PO) 24hourly for 7-14days
For complicated typhoid fever
C: ciprofloxacin (IV) 200-400 mg 12hourly daily 7days
OR
B: ceftriaxone (IV) 1-2gm 24hourly 4-7days
Note: Definitive treatment of typhoid (enteric fever) is based on susceptibility. For patients with severe or complicated disease (e.g., systemic toxicity, depressed consciousness, prolonged fever, organ system dysfunction or other features that prompt hospitalization), initial therapy with a parenteral agent is appropriate.
Shigellosis
Shigella organisms are a group of gram-negative, facultative intracellular bacteria pathogens. They are grouped into 4 species: Shigella dysenteriae, Shigella flexneri, Shigella boydii, and Shigella sonnei, also known as groups A, B, C, and D respectively. Shigellosis is spread by means of fecal- oral, by ingestion by ingestion of contaminated food or water and leads to bacillary dysentery.
Clinical Presentation
Acute abdominal cramping, high-grade fever, emesis and large-volume watery diarrhea
Tenesmus, urgency, fecal incontinence, mucoid bloody diarrhea

Treatment failure
H. pylori treatment failure is defined as the positive stool antigen test or urease breath test 5 weeks after the last dose of eradication therapy. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) should be performed after (two) treatment failures. This is associated with higher eradication rates compared with individuals without AST. Non-Pharmacological Management
Non-Pharmacological Management of functional dyspepsia (FD) focuses on dietary adjustments, lifestyle modifications, and stress reduction to alleviate symptoms like epigastric pain, burning, and early satiety. Key strategies include eating smaller, frequent meals, reducing fat and caffeine intake, avoiding trigger foods (spicy, acidic), and utilizing stress-reduction techniques like cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), yoga, or meditation.
Dietary Modifications:
Meal Frequency: Eat smaller, more frequent meals rather than three large ones to reduce the burden on the stomach.
Trigger Foods: Avoid foods that trigger symptoms, such as high-fat foods, alcohol, caffeine (coffee, tea), carbonated beverages, spicy foods, citrus fruits, and certain vegetables like broccoli or onions.
Diet Composition: Adopt a diet rich in, or similar to, the Mediterranean diet, focusing on fresh foods while reducing processed items.
Texture Modification: If necessary, ensure a portion of daily meals consists of soft or liquid foods.
Fiber Reduction: Reduce fiber-enriched foods, particularly those containing inulin.
Lifestyle Changes:
Stress Management: Implement relaxation techniques, such as yoga, meditation, or, specifically, cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), which has shown significant promise in managing symptoms.
Eating Habits: Chew food thoroughly and eat slowly.
Habit Adjustments: Smoking cessation and avoidance of NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) are recommended.
Other Therapies:
Herbal Remedies: Some herbal teas (ginger, chamomile, peppermint) or preparations like STW-5 (Iberis amara) may provide relief,
Acupuncture/Electrical Stimulation: These may be used for symptom management,
Psychotherapy:
Psychological therapies, particularly CBT, are considered effective in treating FD by addressing the gut-brain interaction,
These approaches, often used alongside reassurance from a healthcare provider, can help manage symptoms effectively,

Bleeding of Obscure Origin
Obscure GI bleeding is recurrent blood loss without an identified source of bleeding despite upper endoscopy and colonoscopy. Patients aged ≤50 years are more likely to have tumors (leiomyomas, carcinoid, adenocarcinoma, or lymphoma), Dieulafoylesion, or Crohn’s disease. Older patients are more likely to have vascular lesions, such as angiodysplasia. Angiodysplasia is the most common cause of obscure GI bleeding overall (40% of all cases). Patients may present with either melena or hematochezia or positive fecal occult blood test (FOBT). The first step is to repeat upper endoscopy and/or colonoscopy, which is diagnostic in approximately 40% of cases.

Surgery and intraoperative enteroscopy is a last diagnostic option

If unrevealing, repeat endoscopic examinations (upper endoscopy, colonoscopy, capsule endoscopy), or deep enteroscopy

Radiation Proctitis
Radiation proctopathy is defined as epithelial damage to the rectum due to radiation that is associated with minimal or no inflammation. Acute radiation proctitis occurs during or within six weeks of radiation therapy. Chronic radiation proctitis has a more delayed onset. The first symptoms often occur 9 to 14 months following radiation exposure but can occur any time post- irradiation up to 30 years after exposure.
Clinical Presentation
Symptoms of acute radiation proctitis include diarrhea, mucus discharge, urgency, tenesmus, and, uncommonly, bleeding.
Patients with chronic radiation proctitis have similar symptoms as patients with acute radiation proctitis, but bleeding is usually more severe. In addition, patients may have symptoms of obstructed defecation due to strictures with constipation, rectal pain, urgency, and, rarely, fecal incontinence due to overflow.
Concomitant injury to the genitourinary tract or small bowel may lead to fistulas, small bowel obstruction, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, urethral stenosis, and cystitis
Acute radiation proctitis should be suspected in patients with diarrhea, mucus discharge, urgency, tenesmus, or bleeding during or within six weeks of radiation therapy. Chronic radiation proctitis should be suspected in patients who develop these symptoms nine months or more after pelvic radiation exposure.

Pancreatitis
Pancreatitis is an inflammatory process in which pancreatic enzymes auto digest the pancreatic gland leading to functional and morphologic loss of the gland.
Acute Pancreatitis
It is due to sudden inflammation of the pancreas due to pancreatic enzymes auto digestion. Common risk factors which trigger the acute episode are presence of gallstones and alcohol intake.
Clinical Presentation
Severe, unremitting epigastric pain, radiating to the back
Nausea and vomiting
Signs of shock may be present
Ileus is also common
Local	complications: inflammatory		mass, obstructive jaundice, gastric
outlet obstruction
Systemic	complication: sepsis, acute respiratory distress syndrome, acute renal failure
Investigations
Raised Serum levels for lipase and amylase greater than 3 times the upper limit of normal ULN (Lipase is more specific and sensitive than amylase). And,
Radiological (ultrasound, CT, MRI) evidence of inflamed and/or necrotizing pancreatitis.
Management
Principles of management include supportive therapies.
Intravascular	volume	expansion (colloids/crystalloid)
Opiates analgesia usually required (follow WHO analgesic ladder)
Enteral feeding, (only in absence of illeus) start within 72 hours
Correction of electrolytes and metabolic deficit accordingly
Pharmacological Management
B: ceftriaxone (IV) 1g 12hourly for 7days
OR
C: ciprofloxacin (IV) 200-400mg 12hourly for 7days
AND
B: metronidazole (IV) 500mg 8hourly for 7days
OR
S: meropenem (IV) 1g 8hourly for 7days
Note
Fever can be because of pancreatitis itself; antibiotics should be avoided before 7 days. Pancreatic necrosis: Nonviable pancreatic tissue. CT-guided FNA if infection suspected. Sterile necrosis: if asymptomatic, can be managed expectantly, no role for prophylactic antibiotics. Infected necrosis: high mortality. Treat with carbapenem or metronidazole plus fluoroquinolone
If stable, defer drainage to >4 weeks. If symptomatic or unstable, percutaneous drainage and minimally invasive surgical debridement or endoscopic necrosectomy superior to open necrosectomy. ERCP + Sphincterotomy may be needed.

Recurrent attacks of pancreatitis weight loss
Diabetes

A: paracetamol (PO) 1g 8hourly daily when required
OR

A: amitriptyline (PO) 25mg nocte when required for pain control

Disorders of The Liver and Biliary Tract
Hepatitis
This is the term referring to inflammation of the liver, which may result from various causes, both infectious (i.e. viral, bacterial, fungal, and parasitic organisms) and non-infectious e.g. alcohol, drugs, autoimmune and metabolic diseases; this section focuses on viral hepatitis and its sequels.
Viral Hepatitis
It is a systemic infection predominantly affecting the liver caused hepatotropic viral agents namely Hepatitis A virus (HAV), Hepatitis B virus (HBV), Hepatitis C virus (HCV), HBV – associated delta agent or Hepatitis D virus (HDV), and Hepatitis E virus (HEV); in most cases leads to a self-limiting disease but can take a fulminant course and lead to hepatic failure or progress to chronic liver disease (HBV, HBV-HDV and HCV)
Note: For comprehensive management of viral hepatitis refer to the National Guidelines for Prevention and Management of Viral Hepatitis 2020.
Hepatitis A Virus (HAV)
HAV is the RNA virus from piconaviridae family under genus hepatovirus. It primarily infects the liver. The disease occurs sporadically or in epidemics and has an incubation period of 14- 28 days. The group most affected is aged between 5-14 years and adults are often infected by spread from children.
Clinical Presentation
Mild flu-like symptoms of anorexia, nausea and vomiting, fatigue, malaise, low-grade fever (usually < 39.5°C), myalgia, and mild headache, dark urine appears first (bilirubinuria). Pale stool soon follows; Jaundice occurs in most adults. Abdominal pain itching (pruritus), Arthralgias and skin rash, (less frequent than the above symptoms).
Investigations
Specific diagnosis involves serological detection of Hepatitis A specific immunoglobulins IgM or IgG antibodies in blood for acute and resolved infection respectively. Viral RNA detection through PCR is definitive and confirmatory specialized laboratory test. Other tests include FBP, LFT, RFT and tests for other viral hepatitis viruses (HBV±HDV, HCV, and HEV).
Management
Supportive management such as hydration, adequate feeding and avoidance of concomitant use of hepatotoxic medications including herbals is all that is required in mild infections. The disease resolves spontaneously in several weeks or months.
Hospitalization is necessary in settings of acute liver failure. Therapy is aimed at maintaining fluid replacement, balanced nutritional feeding, relief of pains and fever including specific management for liver failure.
Hepatitis B Virus (HBV)
New-onset hepatitis B infection that may or may not be icteric or symptomatic. Diagnosis is based on detection of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and IgM antibodies to hepatitis B core antigen (anti-HBc). Recovery is accompanied by clearance of HBsAg with seroconversion to anti-HBs (antibodies to hepatitis B surface antigen), usually within 3 months.
Clinical Presentation
Fever, anorexia, malaise, jaundice and abdominal pain
Enlarged and tender liver
Altered consciousness, coma (hepatic encephalopathy), and bleeding stigmata (in fulminant cases).
Investigations
Serological evidence of specific viral antigen/ core antibody tests (HBc IgM or HBc IgG); and biochemical alteration of liver transaminases (ALT, AST).
Management of Acute Viral Hepatitis B
No specific antiviral treatment is required.
Offer supportive management and counselling.
Offer a follow up plan at 4- or 6-weeks’ intervals for a clinical and laboratory re assessment for evidence of symptoms recovery and biochemical remission.
Re-test at 6 months to assess seroconversion status or progression to chronicity
Chronic Hepatitis B infection.
Defined as persistence of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) for six months or more after acute infection with HBV.
Clinical Presentation
Usually, asymptomatic
Right upper quadrant abdominal pains.
Fatigue, malaise, anorexia, low grade fever; jaundice is frequent in severe disease.
Ascites, variceal bleeding, encephalopathy, coagulopathy, and hypersplenism.
Urticaria, arthritis, vasculitis, polyneuropathy, glomerulonephritis, thyroiditis
Investigations
HBsAg, HBsAb, HBeAg, HBeAb, HBV DNA PCR
LFT, RFT, FBP, HIV,
Alfa Feto Protein (AFP)
Colour Doppler ultrasonography or duplex Doppler ultrasonography or real time ultrasonography.
Dynamic imaging: Tiphasic CT scan/contrast MRI (diagnostic for HCC/in most cases no need for liver biopsy)
Fibroscan (if available)
Management of Chronic Hepatitis B Infection Pre-Treatment Considerations – Who to Treat:
The following are the eligibility criteria for initiation of HBV treatment to a RoC (recipient of care)
Evidence of significant fibrosis or based on an APRI score of >0.5 or transient elastography value of >7 kPa* or evidence of cirrhosis (based on clinical criteria (or an APRI score of >1 or transient elastography value of >12.5 kPa). (Captures 20-25% of HBV positive)
HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL and an ALT level above the upper limit of normal (ULN). (Captures 20-35% of HBV positive)
Persistently elevated ALT above ULN on two consecutive occasions (if a ROC has an elevated ALT above ULN, a second monitoring test during a 6- to 12-month period) (captures 20% of all HBV positive)
Presence of co-infections (such as HIV, hepatitis D or hepatitis C) (captures 5-8% of HBV positive)
Family history of liver cirrhosis
Immune suppression (such as long-term steroids, solid organ or stem cell transplant)
Comorbidities (such as diabetes or metabolic dysfunction––associated steatotic liver disease) ;) or extrahepatic manifestations (such as glomerulonephritis or vasculitis), regardless of the APRI score or HBV DNA or ALT levels.
Pre-Treatment Considerations – Who not to treat:
Persistently normal ALT and,
HBV DNA <2000 IU/mL and,
Absence of coinfections, comorbidities, immune suppression, extrahepatic manifestations, family history of liver cancer or cirrhosis

Hepatitis C virus (HCV)
Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is a small enveloped RNA virus and a member of the family Flaviviridae. HCV comprises six genotypes and hundreds of subtypes with variable geographical distribution and bears significance in determining the rate of liver disease progression, development of HCC and specific therapeutic responses.
Clinical Presentation
Initial symptoms of HCV are often extrahepatic, most commonly involving the joints, muscle, and skin.
Arthralgias,
Paresthesias,
Myalgias,
Pruritus,
Sicca syndrome.
Sensory neuropath
Symptoms characteristic of complications from advanced or decompensated liver disease are related to synthetic dysfunction and portal hypertension, such as the following:
Mental status changes (hepatic encephalopathy), Ankle edema and abdominal distention (ascites), Hematemesis or melena (variceal bleeding)
Signs in patients with decompensated liver disease include the following:
Hand signs: Palmar erythema, Dupuytren contracture, asterixis, leukonychia, clubbing
Head signs: Icteric sclera, temporal muscle wasting, enlarged parotid gland, cyanosis
Fetor hepaticus, Gynecomastia, small testes
Abdominal signs: Paraumbilical hernia, ascites, caput medusae, hepatosplenomegaly, abdominal bruit, Ankle edema, Scant body hair, Skin signs: Spider nevi, petechiae, excoriations due to pruritus
Other common extrahepatic manifestations include the following:
Cryoglobulinemia, Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, Lichen planus, Keratoconjunctivitis sicca, Raynaud syndrome, Sjögren syndrome
Porphyria cutanea tarda, Necrotizing cutaneous vasculitis
Investigations
General baseline studies in patients with suspected HCV include the following:
FBP, LFT, RFT TSH, T3
Screening tests for coinfection with HIV or HBV
Screening for alcohol abuse, drug abuse, or depression
Pregnancy testing
Tests for detecting HCV infection include the following:
Hepatitis C antibody testing:(screening test for previous exposure)
Quantitative assays for HCV RNA PCR (to confirm active infection)
Other serologic testing (essential mixed cryoglobulinemia is a common finding)
Management
Use pangenotypic drugs which are efficacious, safe and cost-effective.
Who to treat
Confirmed cases of Hepatitis C irrespective of clinical stage of the liver disease
Patients with HCC who are eligible for liver transplant if feasible.
Liver transplant patients if MELD score is < 18 (pre transplant) or >18 (post-transplant)
Children >3 years of age
Who not to treat
HCC patients who are not eligible for liver transplant.
Patient with limited life expectancy due to ESLD (by MELD score or Child-Pugh), or non- hepatic related comorbidities.
Pharmacological Management
Use of fixed combination of anti HCV based therapy is recommend based on age, weight (table) and history of past treatment exposure.

Hepatitis D Virus
Hepatitis D virus (HDV) is a defective RNA virus belonging to genus of delta virus that requires the helper function of Hepatitis B (HBV) for virion assembly, release and transmission, and therefore the infection does not occur in the absence of hepatitis B virus. The routes of HDV transmission are similar for HBV the most important being sexually, percutaneous or parenteral exposure to blood or blood products.
Investigations
Serology assays for HDV immunoglobulin titres for IgM and IgG are diagnostic for acute and post exposure/chronic infections respectively. Real time PCR for HDV RNA is confirmatory.
Management
There is no specific treatment for acute or chronic HDV infection.
Note:
The more risk population includes health care workers, transfusion recipients and haemophiliacs, PWID, and immigrants of endemic areas. Nucleotide sequences of HDV obtained worldwide indicates the existence of eight genotypes, with genotype 1 being detected worldwide. HDV Antiviral nucleotide analogues for HBV have no or limited effect on HDV replication and Pegylated interferon alpha is the only drug effective against HDV now and more than one year of therapy may be necessary as most of patients relapses after discontinuation of therapy.
Hepatitis E Virus
Hepatitis E virus (HEV) belongs is an RNA virus belonging from a family Hepadna viridae under Genus Hepevirus and acute liver infection. The virus has at least 4 different types: genotypes 1, 2, 3 and 4. Genotypes 1 and 2 have been found only in humans. Genotype 3 and 4 viruses circulate in several animals (including pigs, wild boars, and deer) without causing any disease, and occasionally infect humans.
Clinical Presentation
Prodromal-phase symptoms include the following:
Myalgia, Arthralgia, Fever with mild temperature elevations
Anorexia, Nausea/vomiting, Weight loss. Dehydration, right upper quadrant pain
Icteric-phase symptoms may last days to several weeks and include the following:
Jaundice, Dark urine, Light-colored stool, Pruritus
Other features include the following
Malaise (most common), Arthritis, Pancreatitis
Aplastic anemia, Thrombocytopenia
Neurologic symptoms of polyradiculopathy, Guillain–Barré syndrome, Bell palsy, peripheral neuropathy, ataxia, and mental confusion
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis and membranous glomerulonephritis
Investigations
Serology assays for HEV immunoglobulin titres for IgM and IgG are diagnostic for acute and post exposure/chronic infections respectively. Real time PCR for HEV RNA in serum and particularly in stool is confirmatory.
Management
There is no specific treatment for cure or reversing the course of acute hepatitis E. The disease is usually self-limiting; hospitalization is generally not required except for patients with fulminant hepatitis or for symptomatic pregnant women where severity of infection is usually high and associated with high rates of fetal loss and mortality especially in third trimester.
Note
The virus is shed in the stools of infected persons and enters the human body through the intestine. It is transmitted mainly through contaminated drinking water. Usually, the infection is self-limiting and resolves within 2–6 weeks. Rarely the infection can lead to fulminant hepatitis with acute liver failure.
The virus causes sporadic cases and major epidemics of viral hepatitis and occurs in resource poor population with unhygienic conditions and through ingestion of contaminated water and food.
Autoimmune Hepatitis (AIH)
AIH: Is a chronic inflammatory liver disease caused by the immune system attacking liver cells characterized by elevated liver enzymes (AST, ALT), increased immunoglobulin G (IgG), presence of autoantibodies, and characteristic liver histology.
Diagnosis requires exclusion of other liver diseases (e.g., viral hepatitis, drug-induced liver injury, Wilson's disease, hemochromatosis)
Diagnostic Pillars
Clinical and laboratory findings
Elevated serum aminotransferases (AST, ALT) and IgG levels
Presence of autoantibodies: ANA, anti-SMA, and anti-LKM1 are commonly tested. Anti-SLA antibodies are more prognostic
Exclusion of other causes of liver disease
Liver biopsy
Crucial for diagnosis and staging the disease.
Typical findings include interface hepatitis (inflammation at the portal-parenchymal interface), often with plasma cell infiltration.
Recommended before starting immunosuppression unless risks outweigh benefits
Treatment goal - Induce and maintain biochemical remission (normalization of liver enzymes and IgG) and prevent progression to cirrhosis and liver failure.
Indications for treatment
Active AIH regardless of symptoms.
Elevated transaminases (>3xULN), elevated IgG >1.5xULN),
Moderate to severe interface hepatitis on biopsy.
Asymptomatic patients with significant inflammation
Pharmacological Management First-line therapy (standard) Corticosteroids
A: prednisolone (30 -60mg/day or 0.5-1mg/kg/day; initial higher dose, then tapered).
AND
Immunosuppressants – combine with corticosteroids to reduce steroid dose and side effects.
S: azathioprine (AZA) - 1-2 mg/kg/day,
Note: titrate to a target dose that achieves remission while minimizing side effects.
OR
S: mycophenolate Mofetil (MMF) - (PO) 1000 - 2000mg/day.
Note: Not recommended in pregnancy – teratogenic. Regularly monitor CBC and LFTs
Treatment duration and monitoring
Continue treatment for at least two years after achieving complete biochemical remission
Liver biopsy is recommended before discontinuing treatment to confirm histological remission.
Close monitoring of LFTs and IgG levels is essential during and after treatment
Non-invasive assessment of hepatic fibrosis (e.g., elastography) can be used to monitor fibrosis
changes after treatment initiation (typically after 6 months).
Special considerations and refractory cases
Acute Severe AIH/Acute Liver Failure - Prednisolone followed by liver transplantation if no improvement
Variant syndromes - consider overlap syndromes with PBC or PSC
Pregnancy: AZA can be continued; MMF is contraindicated
Refractory cases - other immunosuppressants (e.g., tacrolimus), biologics, or novel therapies targeting specific pathways may be considered
Referral to hepatologist is recommended for difficult cases
Metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease
Defined as steatotic liver disease (evidence by Imaging, blood markers or histology) in the presence of one or more cardiometabolic risk factors (Overweight /Obesity, Type II DM, HTN or Dyslipidemia) and the absence of harmful alcohol intake. The spectrum of MAFLD includes steatosis, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH, previously NASH), fibrosis, cirrhosis and MASH-related hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
Investigations
CBC, ALT, AST, GGT, Fasting blood glucose, HbA1c, Lipid profile,
FIB-4 (noninvasive fibrosis score)
Transient Elastography (Fibro scan)
Liver Biopsy – reserved for unclear or severe cases
Exclude other etiology of Liver disease such as Viral hepatitis (HBV/HCV), Alcoholic (<20 g daily for females and <30 g daily for males), Metabolic e.g., Wilson’s disease or Autoimmune Hepatitis.
Non-Pharmacological Management
A rational initial approach to treatment focuses on improving insulin sensitivity via diet, exercise and lifestyle modification, all patients should be advised to avoid alcohol.
Life style modification: Weight loss target ≥ 5% for steatosis, ≥ 7-10% for NASH & Fibrosis regression (Methods advised for weight loss are: Calorie deficit 500-1000kcal/day, Mediterranean or Low carbohydrate diet, Aerobic + resistance exercise (150-200min/week)
Pharmacological Management
For those with a BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2, particularly with other end-organ diseases such as sleep apnea, pharmacologic weight loss treatment may be considered
Pioglitazone effective in biopsy-proven NASH with Type II DM
D: pioglitazone (PO) 30mg 24hourly
Alpha Tocopherol (Vitamin E) (880 IU/day), for non-diabetics with biopsy-confirmed NASH (Caution long term risk of prostate cancer)
D: alpha Tocopherol (Vitamin E) (PO) 880 IU 24hourly
Surgical (For those with a BMI ≥ 35 kg/ m2 or diabetes, bariatric surgery, particularly gastric bypass, offers the best possibility of correcting obesity and insulin resistance and may lead to resolution of MAFLD and NASH)
Follow –up: Reassess Fibrosis (FIB-4 or Fibro Scan annually), Monitor metabolic risk eg HbA1c, BMI Or Lipid profile & Manage Comorbidities e.g. HTN, CVD
Portal Hypertension
This is high blood pressure in the hepatic portal system which includes the portal veins and its branches which drains from most of the intestines to the liver. It is indicated when the hepatic venous pressure gradient exceeds 7mmHg, while liver cirrhosis remains the most common cause which in our local setting is commonly caused by chronic viral hepatitis followed by heavy alcohol intake.
Clinical Presentation
Ascites, Splenomegaly
Esophageal varices, and hematemesis
Swollen veins of the anterior abdomen (caput medusa) and hemorrhoids
Investigations
Radiological evidence of shrunken liver, with typical features of cirrhosis.
Ascites
Ascites is the pathologic accumulation of fluid in the peritoneal cavity, and its most common cause is cirrhosis.

Refractory variceal bleeding – after failed endoscopic therapy

Biliary Tract Diseases
Cholestasis is a pathologic state of reduced bile formation or flow which can be hepatocellular (Intrahepatic), where an impairment of bile formation occurs or ductular (extra hepatic), where impedance to bile flow occurs after it is formed. Intrahepatic causes of cholestasis include viral hepatitis, alcohol, primary biliary cirrhosis, drug toxicity, Hodgkin’s lymphoma and pregnancy. Extrahepatic causes include choledocholithiasis, carcinoma, and ascariasis of the biliary tree.

Jaundice,
Dark urine,
Pale stools, and
Generalized body itching/pruritis.
Investigations
Laboratory evidence of elevated serum levels of total bilirubin, direct bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, gamma-glutamyl transferase, and transaminases. WITH
Supporting radiological evidence of dilated intra or extra hepatic biliary radicles.

Definitive treatment, identify and treat specific cause Supportive treatment:

OR
S: ursodeoxycholic acid (PO) 20–30 mg/kg/day
Note: Surgical intervention is indicated for extra hepatic cholestasis.

Cholelithiasis involves the presence of gallstones which are concretions that form in the biliary tract, usually in the gallbladder. Choledocholithiasis refers to the presence of one or more gallstones in the common bile duct (CBD). Treatment of gallstones depends on the stage of disease.

Asymptomatic in majority of patients.
Biliary pain (episodic RUQ or epigastric pain), pain radiating to scapula;
Pain precipitated by fatty foods; nausea

Full Blood count
Liver function panel
Pancreatic enzymes (Amylase, Lipase)

CT scan –superior for demonstrating stones in the distal CBD

Cholecystitis
Choledocholithiasis leading to cholangitis or gallstone pancreatitis
Mirizzi syndrome

Bleeding during pregnancy is common, especially during the first trimester. Bleeding can sometimes be a sign of something serious, therefore it is important to know the possible causes and take adequate measures.
Abortion
It is a spontaneous loss of a fetus before it is viable (has the potential to survive outside the womb). The World Health Organization (WHO) defines it as expulsion or extraction of an embryo or fetus weighing 500gm or less, approximately at or less than 24 weeks of gestation. In Tanzania abortion is defined as loss of pregnancy before 28 weeks of gestation. Clinical features will depend on the types of abortion.

Experiences offensive discharge
Severe abdominal pain

Counsel educate and provide appropriate contraceptive methods as per CPAC package
Molar Pregnancy
A molar pregnancy is a gestational trophoblastic disease which grows into a mass in the uterus that has swollen chorionic villi. These villi grow in clusters that resemble bunches of grapes. Once diagnosed it should be treated right away.
Clinical Presentation
Vaginal bleeding
Uterus that is bigger than gestational age.
Exaggerated pregnancy symptoms (Severe nausea and vomiting)
Vaginal discharge of tissue that resemble grapes
Heavy PV bleeding when the mole abort spontaneously
Management of Molar pregnancy at the dispensary and Health centers
Apply Airway, Breathing, Circulation and Dehydration principles of resuscitation
Check hemoglobin level
If the patient is actively bleeding, catheterize, Establish Iv line and Give IV RL/NS 2lts at a rapid rate
Referral: Resuscitate and refer the patient to higher level facility with a nurse escort for appropriate management
Management of molar pregnancy at the Hospital
Apply Airway,	Breathing,	Circulation	and Dehydration principles of resuscitation
If the patient is patient is actively bleeding or in shock shout for help and mobilize resources
Cheek HB, Blood grouping and Cross matching
Perform	quantitative	serum	Beta	Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (bHCG)
Check abdominal pelvic Ultrasound to confirm the diagnosis (Snowstorm appearance)
Infuse sodium lactate compound (ringer’s lactate)(IV) OR 0.9% sodium chloride (IV) as needed
Initiate blood transfusion if indicated
Perform suction curettage in operating theatre- take endometrial sample for histopathology
Perform other investigations as appropriate (chest X ray, RFT, LFT, Chemistry panel)
Follow up for Molar pregnancy after Molar Evacuation
Check weekly bHCG until when it becomes normal (5-10mIU/ml) for 3 weeks consecutively
Then check monthly bHCG and pelvic ultrasound for 12 months
Advice the patient to use effective contraception during follow up as per guideline (preferably COCs)
Missed Abortion
This happens when a Fetus less than 24weeks die in utero, but it’s not expelled out
Clinical Presentation
History of amenorrhea
Regression of the pregnancy symptoms
Uterine size smaller than dates
Mild of no PV bleeding
Management of a missed abortion at the dispensary and Health center
Referral: Refer to higher level health facility with adequate expertise and diagnostics/equipment
Management of missed abortion at the hospital Investigations
Abdominal pelvic ultrasound
Full blood count, Blood Grouping and cross matching
Clotting indices (PT, APTT, INR)
Pharmacological Management
If the GA is less than 10 weeks (Including blighted ovum/anembryonic pregnancy) C: mifepristone (PO) 200μg wait for 24 – 48 hours
THEN
A: misoprostol (BU/SL/P) 800μg stat
If the GA is 10 -12 weeks
C: mifepristone (PO) 200μg wait for 24 – 48 hours
THEN
A: misoprostol (BU/SL/PV) 800μg every 3 hours until expulsion
Alternatives for GA of 12 weeks or less perform MVA. (If cervical ripening is necessary, give A: Misoprostol (Bu/SL/PV) 400μg 1-3 hours before the procedure).
If the GA is 13-17 weeks
C: mifepristone (PO) 200μg wait for 24 – 48 hours
THEN

If the GA is 18-24 weeks
C: mifepristone (PO) 200μg wait for 24–48 hours
THEN
A: misoprostol (BU/SL/PV) 400μg 3hourly until expulsion
If the GA is 25-27 weeks
C: mifepristone (PO) 200μg wait for 24 – 48 hours
THEN
A: Misoprostol (BU/SL/PV) 200μg 3hourly until expulsion
