Ectopic Pregnancy
Ectopic pregnancy (EP) is defined as a pregnancy in which the implantation of the embryo occurs outside the uterine cavity, most frequently in one of the two fallopian tubes or, rarely, in the abdominal cavity.
Un-ruptured Ectopic Pregnancy Clinical Presentation
History of amenorrhea
PV Sport bleeding in early pregnancy
Unilateral Abdominopelvic pain. Unilateral(localized) abdominal tenderness
Management of Un-ruptured ectopic pregnancy
Referral: Patients should be referred to higher level facilities with equipment and expertise
At higher level facilities un-ruptured EP may be managed surgically or pharmacologically depending GA and available expertise
Pharmacological Management
S: methotrexate (IV) 50mg/M2 single dose (Maximum dose of 100mg in 24 hours)
OR
S: methotrexate (PO) 1mg/Kg 24 hourly (Maximum dose of 100mg) for 5 days (in case IV methotrexate is not available)
AND
S: folinic acid 0.1 mg/kg for 5 days
Perform weekly pelvic ultrasound to ensure regression of Gestation sac
Note: Laparoscopic procedure can be done in facility with expertise's and clear indications
Note: Contraindications of methotrexate include a ruptured ectopic, ectopic mass greater than 3.5 cm, fetal cardiac activity, high level hCG value (10,000 IU), breastfeeding and immunodeficiency
Ruptured Ectopic Pregnancy Clinical Presentation
History of amenorrhea
Acute generalized abdominal-pelvic pain
Hypotension
Fast and weak pulse
Abdominal distension and tenderness with rebound tenderness
Management of ruptured ectopic at the dispensary and Health Center (B-MONC facilities)
Apply ABCD principles of resuscitation
Perform abdominal pelvic ultrasound if available
Check Hb
Start sodium lactate compound (ringer’s lactate)(IV) OR 0.9% sodium chloride (IV) infuse at a rate of 500mls per hour
Referral: Ectopic pregnancy is an obstetric emergency, resuscitate and refer the patient immediately, with an escort by skilled attendant.
Management of Ectopic pregnancy at the Hospital (C-EMONC facilities) Investigations
Abdominal pelvic/Transvaginal ultrasonography
FBP or Hb level
Grouping and cross-matching
Pharmacological Management
A: sodium lactate compound (ringer’s lactate)(IV)
OR
A: sodium chloride 0.9% (IV) depending on amount of blood loss Blood transfusion if indicated depending on the blood loss
Pre operative antibiotics
B: cefazolin (I/V) 1.5gm stat,
OR
A: ampicillin (I/V) 2gm stat,
AND
B: metronidazole (I/V) 500mg stat Perform Emergency laparotomy

Antepartum Hemorrhage
It is the bleeding from the birth canal after the 28th week of gestation but before the onset of labor. The main forms are placenta previa and abruption placenta. Other rare cause may include VASA previa, heavy show and gynecological malignancies (cervical cancer)
Placenta Previa
It is an obstetric complication in which the placenta embeds itself partially or wholly in the lower segment of the uterus. It is an obstetric emergency which should be managed in a facility offering CEMONC services
Clinical Presentation
Sudden onset of bright red fresh painless bleeding after 28weeks of gestation
Non- Pharmacological Management
If partial Placenta Previa and asymptomatic – Bed rest at home and follow up every 2 weeks
If complete placenta previa then
Admit for close monitoring and observation
Perform ultrasound to localize the placenta
Perform FBP, Coagulation tests, Blood grouping and cross matching. Keep at least
2 units of blood ready in the bank for transfusion in case of acute bleeding
Consider Blood transfusion if indicated
Avoid vaginal digital examination
If ˃34weeks and no PV bleeding or contraction, expectant management
Deliver by Cesarean section preferably at 37–38 weeks of gestation
Deliver by caesarean section by C/S any time in case of onset of labor or severe PV bleeding
Partial or marginal placenta previa: Carefully perform amniotomy for vaginal delivery if the head is engaged.
Pharmacological Management
A: nifedipine (PO) 20mg 8hourly until labor symptoms subside (consider blood pressure monitoring due to risk of hypotension).
AND
D: dexamethasone (PO) 6mg 12hourly for 48 hours if pregnancy is ˂34weeks for fetal lung maturation
AND
A: magnesium sulfate as per protocol for protection of birth asphyxia and Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy complications (Refer to eclampsia section).
Placental Abruption
It is PV bleeding due to premature separation of a normally situated placenta in pregnancy after 28 weeks of gestation.
Clinical Presentation
Vaginal bleeding of dark colored blood or clots. Sometimes bleeding can be concealed
Abdominal pain is moderate to severe but may be absent in revealed AP
The uterus may be enlarged and very tender or persistent-tetanic like contractions
Fetal demise or fetal distress may be present
Management of Placenta Abruption at Dispensary and Health center.
Apply the ABCD principles of resuscitation
Insert large bore cannula IV line, start rapid infusion with RL/NS
Insert Urethral catheter
Refer: resuscitate and refer immediately to the hospital with an escort of a skilled health attendant
Management of Placenta Abruption at the hospital Investigations
Ultrasound: Fetal wellbeing, placenta localization and evidence of retro placental clot
Full blood count and cross–match
Renal function test, Liver function test and electrolytes
Fibrinogen tests if available, D-dimer, PT, PTT, INR
Note: The diagnosis of placental abruption is mainly clinical
Maternal resuscitation
Apply the ABCD principles of resuscitation
Insert two (2) large bore IV lines and give Normal Saline/Ringers Lactate. Replete crystalloids at ratio of 1 unit of blood loss: 3 unit of crystalloids
Blood Transfusion is usually necessary
Give oxygen supplementation at a flow of 6L/min
Insert a urinary catheter to monitor input/output
Obstetrical Management
If the fetus is alive and viable: emergency Caesarean section
If Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation: Give fresh frozen Plasma 1 Unit/hour, give whole blood 2–4 units
Monitor blood pressure, pulse, bleeding, hourly, full blood count, clotting profile every 2 hours
If the fetus is dead: Normal vaginal delivery is preferable if no contraindication for vaginal delivery (e.g. uterine scar)
Perform artificial rupture of membrane,
Pharmacological Management
If no spontaneous labor: induce with
A: oxytocin infusion 5IU in 500 ml sodium chloride 0.9% beginning with 10 drops/min increase the rate after every 20min until optimal contractions are achieved.
Do active management of third stage of labor and uterine massage
Emergency Caesarean section should be considered if:
Worsening of maternal condition
Failure/Non progressing vaginal delivery
Prophylactic antibiotics
A: ampicillin (IV) 2g stat.
OR
B: cefazolin 1g stat
AND
B: metronidazole (IV) 500mg stat.
OR
C: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid (FDC) (IV) 1.2g stat.
AND
B: metronidazole (IV) 500mg stat.

Obstructed Labor
Also known as labor dystocia, is when despite adequate uterine contractions the baby does not exit the pelvis during due to being physically blocked. Obstructed may commonly be caused by; big baby, narrow maternal pelvis, malpresentation and malposition.
Clinical Presentations
Prolonged labor (˃8hours of active labor)
Delayed second stage of labor (˃1hour)
Fetal distress
Severe molding (3+)
Management of obstructed labour at B-EMONC facilities
Insert IV line with and start RL/ DNS infusion 2L
Insert urethral catheter
Check Hb
Severe caput succedaneum
Maternal dehydration (neglected obstructed labour)
Bundle’s ring (sign of neglected obstructed labour)
Encourage the patient to lay in left lateral position
Management of Obstructed labour at the C-EMONC facilities
Optimize hydration by RL/NS 2lt before caesarean section
Ensure the patient is catheterized,
Perform FBP/Hb estimation
Perform emergency caesarean section.
Keep catheter for 3 or more days depending on assessment
Pharmacological Management
A: sodium lactate compound (ringer’s lactate)(IV)/sodium chloride (IV) 0.9% to ensure adequate hydration.
AND
A: ampicillin (IV) 2g within 30m before CS, continue 1g 8hourly for 3days.
OR
B: ceftriaxone (IV) 1g stat within 30min before CS, continue 1g 24hourly for 3days.
OR
C: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid (FDC) (IV) 1.2g within 30min before CS, continue 1.2gm 12 hourly for 3days.
AND
B: metronidazole (IV) 500mg within 30min before CS, continue 500mg 8hourly for 3days.
AND
A: gentamicin (IV) 80mg 12 hourly for 3-5 days

Postpartum Hemorrhage (PPH)
It is abnormal uterine bleeding following delivery through 6 weeks (42 days). It is sub classified in to Primary and Secondary PPH
Primary Postpartum Haemorrhage
It is typically loss of more than 500 ml of blood from the genital tract after vaginal delivery or more than 1000 ml after Caesarean section in the first 24 hours. OR it is any amount of blood loss after delivery that would result in hemodynamic instability.
Management of PPH at Dispensary and Health center
Insert 2 large bore cannula IV line, start rapid infusion with sodium lactate compound (ringer’s lactate)or sodium chloride
Start oxytocin (IV) 20IU in 500mls NS at a rate for 20drops per minute
Ensure no retained placental tissues
Clamp or ligate bleeding perineal tears if any.
Massage the uterus
Insert Urethral catheter
Referral: If bleeding continues, immediately refer the patient to the hospital with an escort of a skilled health attendant. Maintain IV infusion during transfer.
Management of PPH at the hospital- at a comprehensive obstruction facility
Shout for help and mobilize resources
Obtain blood samples for Hb, blood grouping and cross matching
Insert 2 large bore cannulas and start infusing compound sodium chloride or sodium chloride (IV) rapidly
Blood Transfusion depending on amount of blood loss
Non-Pharmacological Management
Perform maneuvers like balloon tamponade, TAH, Iliac artery ligation, B-Lych suture including surgical interventions depending on patient condition and available expertise.
Minimal invasive interventional radiology procedure
Uterine artery embolization for retractable hemorrhage PPH, when conventional medical and surgical measures fail, uterine artery embolization (UAE) offers a life-saving, uterus-sparing alternative. Minimally invasive alternative to hysterectomy in higher centers.
Pharmacological Management
Provide the “clinical care bundle- first response bundle for PPH”:
Start
A: oxytocin (IV) 20IU in 500mls sodium lactate compound (ringer’s lactate)or 0.9% sodium chloride (IV) titrate at 20 drops per minute
OR
A: misoprostol (PO) 1000mcg or per rectal
AND
C: tranexamic acid (IV) 1gm bolus diluted in 20cc to give over 10 minutes. Repeat after 30 minutes if bleeding is still on-going Prevention of PPH –Active management of Third Stage of Labour (AMSTL)
Ensure no remaining second twin
A: oxytocin (IM)10IU stat
AND
(In High-risk women as per guidelines)
A: misoprostol (PO) 600mcg - 1200mcg stat
OR
B: carbetocin 100mcg stat as 3rd line management after other interventions
Controlled cord traction (CCT) is recommended for vaginal births. Sustained uterine massage is not recommended as an intervention to prevent PPH in women who have received prophylactic oxytocin.
Prevention of PPH in Cesarean section
Cord traction is the recommended method for the removal of the placenta in Cesarean section
A: oxytocin (IV/IM) 10IU (is the recommended uterotonic drug for the prevention of PPH plus MOTIVE bundle as per PPH guidelines when indicated)
OR
B: carbetocin (IV/IM) 100mcg stat as 3rd line management per guideline

Prelabour Rupture of Membranes (PROM)
It is the rupture of membranes (breakage of the amniotic sac) before the onset of labor. If rupture occurs before 37weeks it is called preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (PPROM). Prolonged PROM is a case of premature rupture of membranes in which more than 24 hours have passed between the rupture and the onset of labour. Prolonged PROM for more than 18 hours is a risk of ascending infection which can lead to chorioamnionitis (infection of chorion, amnion and amniotic fluid.
Clinical Presentation
Leakage of watery fluid per vagina confirmed by performing a sterile speculum examination.
Management of PROM at the dispensary and health center
Give the following antibiotics for prophylaxis against chorioamnionitis
A: erythromycin (PO) 500mg 8hourly for 7days
AND
A: metronidazole (PO) 400mg 8hourly for 7days
Referral: Refer to the hospital for further evaluation and management
Management of PROM at the hospital Investigations
Ultrasound for fetal well-being, amount of liquor and gestation age.
Perform a sterile speculum examination to confirm leakage
Perform HVS for culture and susceptibility testing
Urinalysis, screen for other infections
Pharmacological Management
If PROM at term: Delivery within 24 hours
Assess Bishop’s Score and Induce Labour accordingly with
A: misoprostol (PO) 25mcg 8hourly (Max 3doses) if unfavorable cervix.
OR
A: oxytocin (IV) 5IU in 500ml of D5% titrate beginning with 10dpm if favorable cervix
Monitor FHR vigilantly during the process of IOL. Deliver by C/S if vaginal delivery is contraindicated, fetal distress or failed induction of labour.
For Preterm PROM:
If no sign of infection, wait for foetal maturity and give
B: dexamethasone (IM) 6mg 12hourly for 48 hours if pregnancy is ˂34weeks for fetal lung maturation
AND
A: magnesium sulfate for birth asphyxia and HIE complications protection as per protocol
AND
A: nifedipine (PO) 20mg 8hourly for tocolysis (Consider blood pressure with risk of hypotension)
Monitor for infection (FBP, CRP, Pulse, Fever) and fetal wellbeing (fetal movement, FHR, obstetric ultrasound)
Administer prophylactic antibiotics
A: ampicillin (IV) 2gm stat
THEN
A: erythromycin (PO) 500mg 8hourly for 7-10 days
OR
B: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid (FDC) (PO) 625mg 8hourly for 7-10 days
AND
A: metronidazole (PO) 400mg 8hourly 7-10 days. Deliver irrespective of gestation age in case of infection
If there are signs of infections-pyrexia, foul smelling liquor (chorioamnionitis)
B: metronidazole (I/V) 500mg 8hourly for 24 hours
THEN
A: metronidazole (PO) 400mg 8hourly for 5-7 days
AND
B: ampicillin (I/V) 1gm 8hourly for 5-7 days
OR
C: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid (FDC) (IV) 1.2g 12hourly for 5-7days
OR
D: ceftriaxone + sulbactam (FDC) (IV) 1.5g 12hourly for 5-7 days

Antenatal Care
The aim of the antenatal care is to provide a positive pregnancy experience that allows a positive transition to birth and motherhood. Basic laboratory testing during antenatal care visits are as follows:
First visit:
Investigations
Full blood count / Hemoglobin level
Blood grouping and Rhesus typing, (Indirect coombs test for Rh-Negative mothers)
Hepatitis B surface antigen screening (HBsAg)
Rapid plasma regains (RPR)/VDRL (For Positive results, TPHA is recommended)
Malaria rapid diagnostic test (MRDT) or Blood smear for malaria

Blood glucose by Oral glucose tolerance test or HbA1c or random blood sugar (RBG)
Urine analysis
Stool analysis
HIV (with partner as well)
Obstetric ultrasound (if available).
Subsequent visits:
Full blood count / Hemoglobin level
Malaria rapid diagnostic test (MRDT) or Blood smear for malaria
Urine analysis
Obstetric ultrasound depending on Clinician’s opinion/decision.
HIV (with partner as well) after 3months from last test
Anemia in Pregnancy
It is hemoglobin levels less than 11 g/dl in pregnancy. Mild anemia– hemoglobin: 8–11g/dl; Severe anemia– hemoglobin<7g/dl. Iron deficiency anemia during pregnancy has been associated with an increased risk of low birth weight, preterm delivery and perinatal mortality.
Clinical Presentation
Tiredness, weakness, palpitations and dyspnea
Exercise intolerance
Pallor of skin and mucous membranes
Dizziness, faintness, headache
Intermittent	claudication	(ache,	cramp, numbness or sense of fatigue)
Note: Some patients with anemia in pregnancy may be asymptomatic
Investigations
Full blood count and blood cross-match - red cell morphology
Red	blood	cell	electrophoresis	if haemoglobinopathies suspected
Blood smear for malaria

Stool and urine analysis
HIV test
MCA-PSV Doppler (For suspected fetal anemia)
Non-Pharmacological Management
Iron rich diet (fish, eggs, fruits and vegetables etc.)
Prevent and early treatment of malaria
Investigate and treat associated worm infestations
Pharmacological Management
Prophylaxis in Antenatal Care
A: ferrous sulfate (PO) 200mg 24hourly (60mg elemental iron and 0.4mg folic acid per day).
OR
A: multiple micronutrient supplement (MMS) (PO) 1 tab/cap 24 hourly (Target is to give 60 mg of elemental Iron per day)
If Hb is <7g/dl in 1st and second trimester give:
A: ferrous sulphate + folic acid (FDC) (PO) 1 tab 12hourly for 4 weeks.
OR
A: multiple micronutrient supplement (MMS) (PO) 1 tab/cap 24 hourly or 12hourly (Target is to give 90- 120 mg of elemental Iron per day).
If HB is ˂7g/dl in 3rd trimester or in case of signs for severe anemia (features of heart failure) Refer/admit the patient for blood transfusion at least 2 units of Packed RBCs
Continue with ferrous and folic acid, or multiple micronutrient supplementation (MMS) 1 tab/cap 12 hourly (Target is to give 90 120 mg of elemental Iron per day) as above after blood transfusion
Note: Women at high risk for neural tube defect should receive high dose of folic acid (5mg 24hourly starting 3 months before pregnancy to 12 weeks of pregnancy. After 12 weeks, normal dose of 400mcg resumes).
Hypertensive Disorders in Pregnancy
Hypertension is blood pressure (BP) 140/90 mmHg or greater, measured on two occasions at least four hours apart or elevated systolic BP >30mmHg, or diastolic BP 15mmHg from the baseline.
Chronic Hypertension
This is hypertension that is present at the booking visit or before 20 weeks or if the woman is already hypertensive before conception. Most women with chronic hypertension are asymptomatic. New onset chronic hypertension should have further evaluation to find underlying cause e.g., renal artery stenosis, chronic renal disease, Cushing syndrome etc.
Pharmacological Management
A: methyldopa (PO) 250–500mg 8hourly
AND
A: nifedipine (PO) 20mg 12hourly
For eclampsia prophylaxis, consider adding:
A: acetylsalicylic acid 75 mg 24hourly
AND
C: calcium + vitamin D 1 tab/1 cap 24hourly
Pregnancy induced hypertension (gestational hypertension)
Gestational hypertension or pregnancy-induced hypertension (PIH) is the development of new hypertension in a pregnant woman after 20 weeks of gestation without the presence of protein in the urine or other signs of preeclampsia. Usually disappears within 12 weeks postpartum.
Non-Pharmacological Management
Adequate rest at home and avoid strenuous activities
Eat a normal balanced diet and plenty of oral fluids
Schedule antenatal visits every 2 weeks up to 32 weeks and every week thereafter
Recommend to deliver in the hospital and should be delivered at 37 completed weeks of gestation
Pharmacological Management
For mild hypertension 140–159 mmHg systolic and/or 90–109 mmHg diastolic.
A: methyldopa (PO) 250–500mg 8hourly
OR
A: nifedipine (PO) 20mg 12hourly
OR
C: labetalol (PO) 100mg 12hourly a day
AND
(When indicated consider adding)
A: acetylsalicylic acid 75 mg 24 hourly
AND
C: calcium + vitamin D 1 tab/1 cap 24 hourly
Severe hypertension
Severe hypertension is Blood Pressure (BP) of 160/110 mmHg or higher. Admit the patient to hospital
A: methyldopa (PO) 500mg 8hourly
AND
B: hydralazine 10mg (slow IV) stat (over 4-5 minutes); recheck the BP after 20 minutes if DBP is more/equal to 110mmHg give another dose of hydralazine (IV slowly) 5–10mg.
AND
A: nifedipine (PO) 20mg 12hourly
OR
C: labetalol (PO)100mg 12hourly
Referral: Refer to the next level facility in case there is no improvement
Pre-eclampsia
Is diagnosed when blood pressure is ≥ 140/90 mmHg after 20 weeks of pregnancy plus proteinuria of 300 mg per 24 hours or
>2+ on urine dipstick. Or elevation of BP in pregnancy with features of end organ damage (eg pulmonary edema, renal or liver damage).
Diagnostic Criteria
Most patients are asymptomatic, but symptoms may include headaches, dizziness, blurred vision, and epigastric pain.
Blood pressure of ≥ 140/90 mmHg
Proteinuria (≥ 300mg per 24 hours)
Generalized edema may be present (not a necessary criteria)
Investigations
Urine for Proteinuria (qualitative/quantitative 24-hour urine collection)
Obstetric Ultrasound and biophysical profile
Urea, creatinine, electrolytes, liver function test and uric acid
FBP and clotting profile
Fundoscopy
Non-Pharmacological Management
Pregnancy < 37 weeks of gestation
Hospitalization and close monitoring
Bed rest
Monitoring BP, urine output, proteinuria, fetal movement and fetal heart beats (every day)
Pregnancy >37 weeks of gestation: admit and deliver accordingly.
Pre-eclampsia with Severe Features:
This is diagnosed when BP ≥ 160/110 mmHg (especially diastolic ≥110 mmHg), or BP of≥140/90mmHg with features of end organ damage e. g severe headache, epigastric pain, blurring of vision +/_vomiting, pulmonary oedema, renal or liver damage, features of hemolysis and low platelets.
Pharmacological Management
B: Hydralazine (IV) 5mg in 10ml sterile water over 4minutes’ initial dose. Followed by boluses 5–10mg as needed every 20 minutes until when the diastolic BP is less than 110mmHg)
AND
A: methyldopa (PO) 500mg 8 hourly
AND
A: nifedipine (PO) 20mg 8 hourly until BP is stabilized (Dosage should be monitored due to risk of Hypotension)
OR
(if hypertension is refractory to hydralazine)
C: labetalol (IV bolus)10–20mg stat repeat each 10–20 minutes, with doubling doses not exceeding 80mg in any single dose for maximum total cumulative dose of 300 mg.
Antenatal corticosteroids
B: dexamethasone (I.M) 6mg 12hourly for 48hours if the pregnancy is less than 34 weeks’ gestation and preterm delivery is anticipated, to enhance fetal lung maturation.
Prophylaxis for Seizures
A: magnesium sulfate (IV) 1g hourly in 250 mililitre of Compound Ringers Lactate
OR
A: magnesium sulfate (IV) 5g of 50% magnesium sulfate 4 hourly or alternate buttocks for 24 hours if GA is ≤34 weeks or until 24 hours post-delivery if GA is≥34 weeks (Refer to eclampsia section)
Obstetrical Management
If at term deliver immediately when stable, preferably vaginal delivery
HELLP syndrome
It is a life-threatening complication of pre-eclampsia characterized by Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes and Low Platelets
Diagnostic criteria Haemolysis
Abnormal peripheral smear
Total bilirubin > 1.2 mg/dL
Lactic dehydrogenase > 600 U
Elevated Liver Functions
Serum glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase > 70 U/L
Lactic dehydrogenase > 600 U/L
Low Platelets
Platelets < 1,000,000/mm3
Management of HELLP syndrome
The management is the same as for severe pre-eclampsia
Eclampsia
Eclampsia is a condition peculiar to pregnancy and post-partum periods, characterized by elevated BP and tonic-clonic convulsions which are not caused by epilepsy, severe malaria, meningitis, hypoglycemia or other causes of convulsions. Majority (50%) occur preterm. Eclampsia may occur without prior elevation of BP.
Diagnostic Criteria
Signs of severe pre-eclampsia (BP >160/110mm Hg)
Loss of consciousness
Tonic-clonic seizures, coma
Investigations
Full blood count and crossmatch
Clotting profile
Ultrasound for GA and fetal viability
Blood smear to exclude malaria
Urea and creatinine + electrolytes
Pharmacological Management

Blood sugar estimation to exclude hypoglycemia.
Liver enzymes tests
Lamber puncture may be indicated to exclude meningitis

antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) in Pregnancy
It is an autoimmune disease characterized by the presence in maternal circulation of one or more auto antibodies against membrane phospholipids. It is an acquired condition. Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is characterized by venous or arterial thrombosis and/or an adverse pregnancy outcome. APS occurs either as a primary condition or in the setting of an underlying disease, usually systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
Clinical Presentation
Recurrent pregnancy adverse outcome e.g. (miscarriages) recurrent miscarriage, intrauterine growth restriction, early severe pre-eclampsia and preterm birth.
Unexplained venous thrombosis (DVT) or arterial thrombosis (Stoke) or myocardial infarction
Thrombocytopenia (common finding but among the clinical classification criteria)
Classification with APS requires one clinical and one laboratory manifestation:
Clinical manifestations
A documented episode of arterial, venous, or small vessel thrombosis
1 or more unexplained deaths of a morphologically normal fetus ≥ 10-week GA
3 or more unexplained consecutive spontaneous abortions before the 10th weeks of GA with anatomic, hormonal or chromosomal causes excluded
Eclampsia or severe pre-eclampsia according to standard definitions, or recognized features of placental insufficiency
Laboratory:
Anti-cardiolipin IgG and/or IgM measured on 2 or more occasions, not less than 12 weeks apart;
Anti-β2 glycoprotein I IgG and/or IgM measured on 2 or more occasions, not less than 12 weeks apart
Lupus anticoagulant detected on 2 occasions not less than 12 weeks apart.

A: acetylsalicylic acid (PO) 75-100mg 24hourly beginning as soon as the pregnancy is confirmed throughout pregnancy
AND
C: unfractionated heparin (SC) 5000–10000 units 12hourly
OR
D: low molecular weight heparin (SC) 30–40mg 24hourly
Patients with Thrombosis such as stroke or pulmonary embolism need therapeutic anticoagulation. C: unfractionated heparin (SC) 5,000 bolus and subsequent 15,000–20,000 doses at 12hourly intervals
OR
D: low molecular weight heparin (SC) 1mg/kg 12hour
Note: Warfarin should be avoided in pregnancy due to the risk of teratogenicity. The aPTT needs to be checked and is best done midway between the 12hourly doses, 24hourly. A target of 1.5-2.5 times the control should be aimed

Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and acute pulmonary embolism (PE) are two manifestations of venous thromboembolism (VTE. The risk of VTE is increased in pregnancy by about five times because of a more hyper-coagulable state. VTE contributes to significant maternal morbidity and mortality. The mainstay of therapy for DVT is anticoagulation, provided there is no contraindication.

Hyperglycemia in Pregnancy
Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) is any degree of glucose intolerance first recognized in pregnancy. Diabetes in pregnancy refers to those with pre-existing diabetes, whether diagnosed or not.
Screening at first antenatal visit
Perform screening in all women at the first antenatal clinic attendance if they have:
BMI > 25 kg/m2		family history of DM
previous history of GDM		known impaired glucose tolerance/ impaired fasting glucose
previous big baby		grand multipara
poor obstetric history	glycosuria.
Women in early pregnancy with levels of HbA1c≥6.5% or blood glucose levels fasting ≥7.0 mmol/l or two hours 75g OGTT
≥11.1 mmol/l which are diagnostic of diabetes should be treated as having diabetes in pregnancy. Women with HbA1c 6.0– 6.4%, fasting glucose 5.1– 6.9 mmol/l (92-125 mg/dl) or two-hour glucose 8.6–11.0 mmol/l (153-199 mg/dl) should be assessed to determine the need for immediate home glucose monitoring and, if the diagnosis remains unclear, assessed for gestational diabetes by 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) at 24–28 weeks.
Screening later in Pregnancy
All women with risk factors (see above) should have a 75gm OGTT at 16–20 weeks
A fasting plasma glucose at 16–20 weeks is recommended in low-risk women OR where 75gm OGTT is not practically feasible.

Lifestyle management is the preferred means of managing gestational diabetes.
Diet is based on the principles of optimal nutrition and controlled weight gain. A carbohydrate-controlled meal plan that promotes adequate nutrition with appropriate weight gain, normoglycemia, and the absence of ketosis. Diet and nutrition therapy should be the first line of treatment offered together with other services.
Exercise can be helpful in lowering BG levels: the most acceptable form of exercise for most women are walking in their normal daily routine OR a planned 30mins/day brisk walking.
Glucose-lowering therapy should be considered in addition to diet + exercise where fasting or two hours glucose levels are above target, for example, where two or more values per fortnight are:
fasting or pre-prandial ≥5.5 mmol/L, or two hours postprandial ≥7 mmol/L at ≤35 weeks
fasting or pre-prandial ≥5.5 mmol/L, or two hours postprandial ≥8 mmol/L at >35 weeks
any postprandial values are >9 mmol/L.
When pharmacologic treatment of gestational diabetes is indicated, insulin and oral medications are equivalent in efficacy, and either can be an appropriate first-line therapy.
Insulin should be considered as the first-line treatment in women with GDM who are at high risk of failing on oral anti-diabetic drug therapy, including some of the following factors:
Diagnosis of diabetes <20 weeks of gestation
Need for pharmacologic therapy >30 weeks
Fasting plasma glucose levels >110 mg/dL (6.1mmol/dl)

1-hour postprandial glucose >140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/dl)
Pregnancy weight gain >12 kg

The rapid-acting insulin analogs (lispro and aspart) lower postprandial blood glucose and decrease the risk of nocturnal hypoglycemia. Patients on lispro and aspart prior to conception may continue them during pregnancy. Patients on regular insulin may be switched to lispro or aspart if 1–hour postprandial blood glucose levels are above target and/or the patient is also experiencing pre-meal or nocturnal hypoglycemia.

Induction of Labour Indications/Contraindications
The indication for induction must be documented, and discussion should include reason for induction, method of induction, and risks, including failure to achieve labour and possible increased risk of Caesarean section.
If induction of labour is unsuccessful, the indication and method of induction should be re- evaluated.
Pre-induction assessment
Health care providers should assess the cervix (using the bishop score) to determine the likelihood of success and to select the appropriate method of induction.
The bishop score should be documented.
Care providers need to consider that induction of women with an unfavorable cervix is associated with a higher failure rate and increased rate of operative deliveries.
Post-dates induction
Women should be offered induction of labour between 41+0 and 42+0 weeks as this intervention may reduce perinatal mortality and meconium aspiration syndrome without increasing the Caesarean section rate
Women who chose to delay induction >41+0 weeks should undergo twice-weekly assessment for fetal wellbeing

Trial of Labor after Cesarean (TOLAC)/Vaginal Birth after Cesarean (VBAC).
Trial of Labor after Cesarean (TOLAC) is the planned attempt to deliver vaginally in a woman with a history of one prior cesarean delivery. A successful TOLAC is referred to as Vaginal Birth after Cesarean (VBAC).
Eligibility Criteria for TOLAC
Single prior low-transverse cesarean scar, Singleton pregnancy, Cephalic presentation, Term gestation (≥37 weeks), Clinically adequate pelvis, No contraindications to vaginal birth, Efw less than 3.5kgs
Contraindications to TOLAC
Prior classical (vertical) or T-shaped uterine incision, History of uterine rupture, Prior extensive uterine surgery (e.g., myomectomy involving the endometrial cavity), Placenta previa or other contraindications to labor ≥2 previous cesarean deliveries with no prior vaginal delivery, Patient declines VBAC after counseling
Intrapartum Management of TOLAC
Pre-labor Counseling
Discuss risks and benefits of VBAC vs. elective repeat cesarean delivery (ERCD)
Highlight ~70–75% success rate of TOLAC in appropriate candidates
Uterine rupture risk: 0.5–0.9% with one prior low-transverse scar
Timing of Delivery
Await spontaneous labor up to 41 weeks in the absence of maternal/fetal complications
Mechanical induction (e.g., Foley catheter) may be considered after 41-week Misoprostol is contraindicated due to high rupture risk
Labor Monitoring
Continuous electronic fetal monitoring (EFM) is recommended
Close monitoring of uterine activity(contractions) you can use CTG if available
Early recognition of signs of uterine rupture: fetal bradycardia, loss of station, sudden abdominal pain
Labor Augmentation
Low-dose oxytocin augmentation may be used with caution if labor stalls after spontaneous onset
Avoid high-dose protocols
Preparation for Emergency Cesarean
Ensure immediate surgical and anesthesia backup
Informed consent and blood availability
Potential Complications
Uterine rupture, Scar dehiscence, Postpartum hemorrhage, Birth asphyxia or neonatal encephalopathy
Note: Risk of uterine rupture is higher with induced labor and with shorter underdeliver intervals (<18 months)
Postpartum Follow-Up
Monitor for signs of hemorrhage and uterine tenderness
Discuss outcome of delivery and implications for future pregnancies
Emphasize importance of early ANC attendance in subsequent pregnancies
Consider family planning counseling
Advise hospital delivery in future pregnancies, preferably by 36–37 weeks to avoid unmonitored labor at home
Key Evidence Summary
TOLAC should be offered in Hospitals with readiness to offer emergency cesarean delivery, with access to surgical and neonatal support. VBAC has a high success rate, especially with a previous vaginal delivery.

Advanced reproductive therapy (ART) and special cases (IUI, IVF/ICSIS)
Should be done by trained fertility specialist at a facility well equipped with embryology and andrology laboratory. ART will follow proper indication, inclusion criteria, pre-treatment diagnostic workup, lifestyle management, advice on 1st line treatment options available
Ovulation induction:

AND

Subsequent dose should be reduced or increased aiming for 2 to maximally 3 dominant follicles
Monitoring:
Usually done on day 12 to 14 of cycle but earlier (around day 10) if concern for multiple follicular development
Assess endometrial thickness (ET), follicle size and number, decide the need for serum E2, serum progesterone, and serum LH measurement
Repeat assessment as indicated until leading follicle ≥18mm and ET≥7mm
Assess mid-luteal phase progesterone unless ovulation was well established in previous cycles

Insemination: Do a single insemination 24-36 hours after LH surge

IVF and ICSI are done with treatment protocols, this guideline highlights the steps and medications used

STEPS INVOLVED IN IVF/ICSI
Controlled Ovarian Stimulation Long protocol treatment (Using GnRH –agonist) S: goserelin Acetate 3.6 mg (SC)
OR
S: leuprolide Acetate 3.75mg (IM)
Short protocol treatment (Using GnRH – antagonist) S: cetrorelix acetate 0.25 mg (SC)

S: lutropin hormone 10 IU/KG/24 hours in combination with clomiphene citrate, or letrozole as per protocol
Egg retrieval (Ultrasound–guided Ovum Pick-up) done in theater at 36 hours after the time of trigger with hCG. The WHO Safety Checklist should be observed as in any other surgical procedures.
The Embryologist should immediately examine the aspirated fluid under microscope in theater to look for oocyte before transferring to the IVF Lab
Fertilization and Embryo culture are done few hours after the egg retrieval using the culture media and incubator in a tightly controlled IVF laboratory.
The embryologist should monitor the process of fertilization, embryos development and grading them according to how the develop at each stage
The husband/partner should produce the sample on the day of the egg retrieval. The sperm sample is best produced by masturbation. It is recommended that the husband/partner should abstain from intercourse (No ejaculation) for two days before the egg retrieval in order to give a good sperm sample.
Embryo Transfer done under trans abdominal Ultrasound and the patient should be advised to have a full bladder before the procedure. The fertility specialist and Embryologist should discuss with the patient/couple on the number of embryos to be transferred at once, based on the specific patient circumstances, age of the woman and quality & number of the embryos available.
It should be noted that transferring more than one embryo carries the risks of multiple pregnancies (twins or triplets) which are serious. As globally most of ART units are moving towards single embryo transfer, it is recommended to consider transferring of single or two embryos
Luteal Phase Support achieved by supplementation of progesterone 400mg per vagina twice a day from the day of egg retrieval and continued depending on indications
Pregnancy test Serum beta-hCG should be tested 10-12 days after the embryo transfer. If the test is positive, repeat it two days later to check the rise of beta- hCG. In case of rise of beta-hCG, booking for a date of the first ultrasound scan should be done for six weeks later.
In case of negative pregnancy test, the patient/couple should be given a follow up appointment with a fertility specialist to discuss the cycle and further management

Tubal surgery for Tubal blockage under laparoscopic or open surgery approach
Myomectomy for uterine fibroids under laparoscopic or open surgery approach
Ovarian drilling is a possible surgical treatment for PCOS–related infertility under laparoscopic or open surgery approach

CHAPTER TWELVE SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED INFECTIONS
Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are generally acquired by sexual contact with a person who has an STI. The organisms (bacteria, viruses or parasites) that cause sexually transmitted diseases may pass from person to person in blood, semen, or vaginal and other bodily fluids. Reproductive tract infections (RTIs) occur in the genital tract and affect both women and men. Some RTIs, such as syphilis and gonorrhea, are sexually transmitted, but many are not. In women, overgrowth of endogenous microorganisms normally found in the vagina may cause RTIs (yeast infection, bacterial vaginosis).
Clinical Presentation
Sores or bumps on the genitals or in the oral or rectal area.
Painful or burning urination.
Discharge from the penis.
Vaginal discharge that is abnormal in colour, odour, amount or consistency.
Itching or irritation of the
vulva or vagina.

STIs/RTIs Management Approaches
Unusual vaginal bleeding.
Pain during sex.
Lower abdominal pain
Genital ulcers, sores or blisters
Swelling, lumps or ulcer in the groin area
Management of STIs/RTIs can be done in either of the following approaches:
Aetiological laboratory approach: By identification of causative agents through laboratory methods and sensitivity pattern to the medicine to used, followed by disease- specific treatment.
Aetiological clinical approach: By targeting disease treatment based on suspected causative agents diagnosed clinically. This is not appropriate at any health facility because of its demands on the clinical acumen of the service provider and the danger of incorrect diagnosis and, hence, insufficient treatment.
Syndromic approach: This identifies clinical syndromes (symptoms and signs) followed by syndrome-specific treatment that targets causative agents which cause the syndrome.
Management of STIs/RTIs using Aetiological Laboratory Approach
It identifies causative agents through laboratory methods, followed by disease-specific treatment. This is the best approach to be used at a Health Facility (HF) which has a Laboratory capable of doing the Laboratory Investigation and producing timely result(s) so as to enable the clinician to prescribe medicine (s) according to the causative agent(s) and sensitivity pattern.

Chlamydia
A common sexually transmitted infection caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, often asymptomatic but associated with significant reproductive complications if untreated.
Clinical Presentation
Often asymptomatic, especially in women.
When symptomatic, may present as:
Urethral discharge, dysuria, urethral itching (men).
Vaginal discharge, burning urination, lower abdominal pain, dyspareunia (women).
Rectal pain, discharge, or bleeding (rectal infection).
Pharyngitis (rare, oropharyngeal infection).
Investigations
Preferred: Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) from urine or swabs (urethral, cervical, rectal, or oropharyngeal sites).
If NAAT unavailable: Gram stain (limited sensitivity), culture, or ELISA where available.
In resource-limited settings, syndromic management based on symptoms is recommended.
Pharmacological Management
Non-pregnant adults and adolescents
A: doxycycline (PO) 100mg 12hourly for 7 days
OR
A: azithromycin (PO) 1g single dose
Pregnant and breastfeeding women
A: azithromycin (PO) 1g single dose
OR
A: amoxicillin (PO) 500mg 8hourly for 7 days
OR
A: erythromycin (PO) 500mg 6hourly for 7 days
Note:
Counsel patients on sexual abstinence until treatment completion and consistent condom use.
Partner notification and treatment are essential to prevent reinfection and reduce transmission.
Follow-up is recommended if symptoms persist or reinfection is suspected.
Test-of-cure is generally not required except in pregnancy, persistent symptoms, or suspected treatment failure.

Gonorrhea
A sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae, affecting the urogenital tract, rectum, pharynx, and eyes.
Clinical Presentation
Men: Urethral discharge, burning or painful urination, itchy urethra, increased frequency/urgency.
Women: Vaginal	discharge,	dysuria, intermenstrual bleeding, lower abdominal pain, dyspareunia.
Both sexes: Rectal pain/discharge (if anorectal infection), pharyngitis (if oropharyngeal infection), conjunctivitis (rare but severe).
Complications: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), epididymo-orchitis, infertility, disseminated gonococcal infection.
Investigations
Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) from urine, urethral, cervical, rectal, or pharyngeal swabs (high sensitivity and specificity).
Other options (where available):
Gram stain: Gram-negative intracellular diplococci (especially in symptomatic men).
Culture and sensitivity: Essential for antimicrobial resistance surveillance and in cases of treatment failure.
Syndromic approach:
If laboratory testing is unavailable, manage based on clinical syndrome (urethral/vaginal discharge, PID, etc.).
Pharmacological Management
First-line regimen for uncomplicated genital, anorectal, and oropharyngeal gonorrhea (adults and adolescents):
A: ceftriaxone (IM) 500 mg single dose
If >150 kg body weight, consider 1g IM single dose
AND
A: doxycycline (PO) 100 mg 12hourly for 7 days (if chlamydia not excluded)
If doxycycline contraindicated or not available,
A: azithromycin 1g PO) single dose
Alternative Regimens
A: gentamicin (IM) 240mg single dose
AND
A: azithromycin (PO) 2g single dose
OR
A: cefixime (PO) 800mg single dose

Syphilis
A chronic sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum. It progresses in stages and can involve multiple organ systems if untreated.
Clinical Presentation
Primary syphilis: Painless genital, anal, or oral ulcer (chancre) and non-tender lymphadenopathy.
Secondary syphilis: Generalized non-itchy rash (often on palms/soles), mucous patches, condylomata, fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy.
Latent syphilis: Asymptomatic; detected by serology.
Tertiary syphilis: Rare; gummatous lesions, cardiovascular or neurologic disease.
Congenital syphilis: Stillbirth, neonatal death, or multisystem disease in infants.
Neurosyphilis, ocular syphilis, otosyphilis: Can occur at any stage; present with neurological, visual, or auditory symptoms.
Investigations Serologic testing:
Non-treponemal: RPR, VDRL (for screening and monitoring).
Treponemal: TPPA, FTA-ABS, EIA (for confirmation).
Direct detection: Darkfield microscopy or NAAT from ulcer exudate/tissue (if available). CSF examination: For neurologic, ocular, or otic symptoms (cell count, protein, VDRL). HIV testing: Recommended for all patients with syphilis.
Pharmacological Management
Early Syphilis (Primary, secondary, or early latent <2 years)
A: benzathine benzylpenicillin (IM) 2.4MU single dose
Late Latent Syphilis or Syphilis of Unknown Duration
A: benzathine benzylpenicillin (IM) 2.4MU once weekly for 3 consecutive weeks (Do not exceed 14 days between doses)
Syphilis in Pregnancy
Benzathine benzylpenicillin is the only proven regimen to prevent congenital syphilis
Desensitization and penicillin treatment are recommended for allergic pregnant women.
Neurosyphilis, Ocular Syphilis, Otosyphilis
A: benzylpenicillin (IV) 18–24 million units per 24hours, administered as 3–4 million units every 4 hours or continuous infusion for 10–14 days.
For patients with penicillin allergy, the approach prioritizes confirming the allergy (e.g., via skin testing, as many reported allergies are not true IgE-mediated reactions) and considering penicillin desensitization.
When desensitization is not feasible
A: ceftriaxone 1–2 g daily (intramuscularly or intravenously) for 10–14 days can be used.

Mycoplasma genitalium
A sexually transmitted bacterium that causes non-gonococcal urethritis (NGU) and is associated with cervicitis and pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). It is notable for high antimicrobial resistance, especially to macrolides.
Clinical Presentation
Urethritis, cervicitis; often asymptomatic.
Investigations:
NAAT specific for M. genitalium (if available).
Pharmacological Management
A: doxycycline (PO) 100mg 12hourly for 7 days
THEN
A: azithromycin (PO) 1g 24hourly, then 500mg 24hourly for 3days. Resistance testing is recommended where possible.

Ectoparasites
Parasites that live on the surface of the host (skin or hair) rather than inside the body. They commonly infest humans and can cause irritation, skin disease, and transmit infections. Ectoparasites are transmitted through close contact, poor hygiene, overcrowding, or contaminated clothing/bedding.
Clinical Presentation
Intense itching, visible lice or mites, excoriations.
Investigations
Clinical diagnosis by inspection.
Pharmacological Management
D: permethrin 5% w/v cream/lotion apply topically 12 hourly for 7days
OR
D: malathion 0.5% lotion applied topically 12 hourly for 7days. Treat close contacts; wash clothing and bedding.

Trichomoniasis
A sexually transmitted infection caused by the protozoan parasite Trichomonas vaginalis. It commonly affects the urogenital tract and is often asymptomatic, especially in men.
Clinical Presentation
Frothy, yellow-green vaginal discharge, vulvar itching, dysuria.
Investigations
Wet mount microscopy, culture, NAAT.
Pharmacological Management
A: metronidazole (PO) 2g single dose
OR
A: metronidazole (PO) 400mg 12hourly for 7 days. Treat sexual partners simultaneously.

Lymphogranuloma Venereum (LGV)
A sexually transmitted infection caused by invasive strains (L1, L2, L3) of Chlamydia trachomatis. It is characterized by transient genital lesions followed by painful lymphadenopathy or proctocolitis.
Clinical Presentation
Painful inguinal buboes, genital ulcers, rectal pain and discharge.
Investigations
NAAT for C. trachomatis serovars L1-L3, PCR.
Pharmacological Management
A: doxycycline (PO) 100mg 12hourly for 21 days. Surgical drainage of buboes if necessary.

Genital Herpes (Herpes Simplex Virus type 2)
A sexually transmitted viral infection caused mainly by Herpes simplex virus type 2, though Herpes simplex virus type 1 can also cause genital disease.
Clinical Presentation
Painful vesicles and ulcers on genitalia, dysuria, systemic symptoms.
Investigations
PCR, viral culture, serology.
Pharmacological Management
B: acyclovir (PO) 400mg 8hourly daily for 7 days (initial episode). Suppressive therapy or episodic treatment for recurrences.

Anogenital Warts (Human Papillomavirus - HPV)
Anogenital warts are caused by infection with Human papillomavirus, most commonly types 6 and 11 (low-risk types). They present as benign proliferative lesions affecting the anogenital region.
Clinical Presentation
Flesh-colored, cauliflower-like growths on genital or anal skin.
Investigations
Clinical diagnosis; biopsy if uncertain.
Non-Pharmacological Management
Cryotherapy,

Management of STIs/RTIs using Syndromic Approach
This approach is recommended if the HF is not able to conduct appropriate Laboratory Investigation(s) and producing timely result(s) to enable the clinician to prescribe the medicine in accordance with causative agent(s).
Syndromic management of STIs is based on the diagnosis of defined symptoms and easily recognizable clinical signs. Each syndrome can be caused by several different causative agents.
For each syndrome, a well-defined standard treatment which has been proven to be effective against most endemic causative agents for the syndrome are used.
Syndromic approach of managing STIs/RTIs entails the service provider to follow laid down steps in a flow chart which guides him/her in making rational management decisions for treating the client. These are therefore known as treatment flow-charts. They may also be known as treatment algorithms, treatment protocols or treatment decision trees.
They guide the provider through a series of decisions and actions that need to be made. Each decision or action is enclosed in a box, with one or two routes leading out of it to another box, with another decision or action. Upon learning a patient’s symptoms and signs, the service provider turns to the flow chart for the relevant syndrome and works through the decisions and suggestions it guides to manage the client accordingly. Each flow chart is made up of a series of three steps. These are:
The clinical problem (the patients presenting symptoms and signs),
The decision that needs to be taken,
The action that needs to be carried out.

UDS refers to the presence of abnormal secretions in the distal portion of the urethra Caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae and
Chlamydia trachomatis.
Clinical Presentation

Note

Male patients complaining of urethral discharge and/or dysuria should be examined for evidence of discharge. If none is seen per inspection, the urethra should be gently milked from the ventral part of the penis towards the meatus.
Delayed or inadequate treatment may result into orchitis, epididymitis, urethral stricture and/or infertility.

VDS refers to change of colour, odour and/or amount of vaginal secretions caused by T. vaginalis, C. albicans, Bacterial Vaginosis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis.
Clinical Presentation
Abnormal vaginal discharge,

Note
A spontaneous complaint of abnormal vaginal discharge is most commonly due to a vaginal infection.
T. vaginalis, C. albicans and Bacterial Vaginosis are the commonest causes of vaginal infection while
Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis cause cervical infection.
The clinical detection of cervical infection is difficult because a large proportion of women with gonococcal or chlamydia infections are asymptomatic.
Vaginal discharge is therefore highly indicative of vaginal infection, but poorly predictive for cervical infection
Due to the high prevalence of gonorrhea and chlamydia, all women presenting with VDS should receive treatment for both vaginal and cervical infections.
Delayed or inadequate treatment of VDS may result to endometritis, salpingitis, oophoritis or ectopic pregnancy.
Gonococcal or chlamydial cervical infection may be asymptomatic

Ano-rectal Syndrome (ARS)
Defined as soreness, burning, itching or other irritation of the rectum together with redness in the area of anus. Sometimes it is accompanied by diarrhea and it may occur as a toxic side effect of oral administration of certain broad-spectrum antibiotics mainly caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, Treponema pallidum, Herpes Simplex Virus, Shigella spp., or Entamoeba histolytic.
Clinical Presentation
Purulent rectal discharge
Mucous rectal discharge
Watery rectal discharge
Soreness, burning, itching or other irritation of the rectum together with redness in the area of anus
There may also be ineffectual straining to defecate (“tenesmus”), sometimes mistakenly described as “constipation” by patients.
The anus and rectum may be intensely painful, with external and internal ulceration
Abdominal pain or cramping, abdominal swelling, distention or bloating;
Bloody stool (blood may be red, black, or tarry in texture),
Burning feeling,
Change in bowel habits, constipation, diarrhea;
Fecal incontinence (inability to control stools),
Flatulence; pain, which may be severe, in the abdomen, pelvis, or lower back
Urgent need to pass stool and watery diarrhea including multiple episodes.
A proctoscopic examination (which should be done, if feasible) will reveal rectal pus, bleeding or ulceration
Note
Proctitis may be caused by Salmonella spp., Shigella spp., or Entamoeba histolytica as a part of gastroenteritis, which may manifest as diarrhoea with fever, anorexia, and abdominal cramps.
Antibiotics that destroy normal intestinal bacteria and allow other bacteria to grow in their place may also cause proctitis.
Herpes proctitis may be mistaken for the rectal manifestation of ulcerative colitis or Crohn’s disease.
Proctitis typically causes painless bleeding or the passage of mucus (sometimes mistaken for diarrhoea) from the rectum.
All cases of proctitis in MSM should be treated for gonorrhoea and chlamydia infections.
Symptoms of diarrhoea, bloody stools, abdominal cramping, nausea, and/or bloating may indicate Giardia spp infection or amoebic dysentery.
Other non-STI causes of ARS include:
Anal fissure, Fecal impaction, Food intolerance, Gastroenteritis (bacterial and viral), Inflammatory bowel disease (includes Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis), Neurological damage, and Perirectal or perianal abscess.
Other symptoms might occur with rectal discharge include gastrointestinal symptoms which vary depending on the underlying disease, disorder or condition. These may include:
Abdominal pain or cramping, abdominal swelling, distention or bloating; bloody stool (blood may be red, black, or tarry in texture), burning feeling, change in bowel habits, constipation, diarrhea; fecal incontinence (inability to control stools), flatulence; pain, which may be severe, in the abdomen, pelvis, or lower back, urgent need to pass stool and watery diarrhea including multiple episodes.

STI/RTI flow charts
Steps in using the flow charts:
Start by asking the patient for his/her symptoms.
Find the appropriate flow chart, stated in the clinical problem box with “Patient Complaints of.”
The clinical problem box usually leads to an action box, which asks you to examine the patient and/or take the history.
Next, move to the decision box. After taking the history and examining the patient you should have the necessary information to choose Yes or No accurately.
Depending on your choice, there may be further decision boxes and action boxes.
Note
For the appropriate management of STIs/RTIs syndrome, drugs in the watch group (azithromycin, cefixime and ceftriaxone) are the standard recommended for use as a first line treatment for the most STIs/RTIs starting at the Dispensary level, therefore, should be used only for STIs/RTIs at Primary HFs)

Staphylococci and streptococci cause most bacterial skin infections, ranging from common conditions such as impetigo and cellulitis to severe multisystem disorders, including toxic shock syndrome.

Impetigo is a contagious, superficial bacterial infection that is most frequently observed in children. It can be bullous or nonbullous. The most common pathogen is Staphylococcus aureus.
Clinical Presentation:
Polycyclic flaccid vesicles or bullae with clear yellow fluid
May become pustules that enlarge and rapidly break down to form thick, adherent yellowish crusts
May be associated with mild lymphadenopathy and fever
Investigations:
Skin swab for culture and sensitivity

Regular hand washing
Avoid sharing towels or clothes
Avoid touching or scratching infected areas

Limited Disease
A: gentian violet paint (topical) 12hourly for 5days
OR
C: mupirocin ointment (topical) 12hourly for 7days
OR
C: fusidic acid cream (topical) 12hourly for 7days

Remove crusts with soap, water or saline

OR
A: erythromycin (PO): Adult 500mg; paediatric 25-50mg/kg 8hourly for 10days
OR

Folliculitis is an infection of the hair follicles commonly due to Staphylococcus aureus, and Gram-negative bacteria such as Pseudomonas, Klebsiella, Enterobacter, and Proteus species

Common areas include the scalp, face, upper trunk, buttocks, and legs
Pruritus is common

Hair should be left to grow to at least 1 mm long.

Refer to the management of impetigo

Cutaneous Drug Reactions:
It is a response to a medicinal product that is noxious and unintended. Up to 80% of Adverse drug reactions are dose-dependent and predictable, while about 20% are independent of the administered dose and unpredictable.
Classification of adverse drug reactions:
Type A: Predictable adverse reactions
Type B: Unpredictable adverse reactions
Over dosage (wrong dosage or defect in drug metabolism)
Side effects (sleepiness from antihistamines)
Indirect effects (antibiotics changing normal flora)
Drug interactions (altered metabolism of drugs; most commonly involving the cytochrome P-450 enzymes)
Allergic reaction (drug allergy or hypersensitivity; immunologic reaction to drug; requires previous exposure or cross-reaction)
Pseudo allergic reaction (non-immunologic activation of mast cells).
Idiosyncratic reaction (unexplained reaction, not related to mechanism of action, without known or suspected immunologic mechanism).
Note:80% of allergic and pseudo allergic drug reactions are caused by Beta-lactam antibiotics, aspirin, NSAIDs and sulfonamides
Non-life-threatening cutaneous adverse drug reactions may include fixed drug eruption (FDE), urticaria, exanthematous drug eruptions, and lichenoid drug eruption, while life-threatening cutaneous adverse reactions include toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP), and drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS).
Fixed Drug Eruption (FDE)
It is a cutaneous drug reaction that recurs at the same site with repeated exposure to the agent.
Clinical Presentation
Well-demarcated, round to oval, dusky red to brown/black macules that may develop into edematous plaques with or without vesiculation or blistering.
Pruritus and a burning or stinging sensation are common.
Non-Pharmacological Management
Avoidance of a triggering drug
Pharmacological Management
A: hydrocortisone (IV) 200mg 12hourly for 24hours for 2-4 weeks
OR

OR
D: clobetasol propionate cream/ointment (topical) 24hourly for 2- 4weeks
Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN)
They are rare and life-threatening mucocutaneous conditions caused by immune system activation, most commonly initiated by certain drugs and their metabolites or infections. In SJS, <10% of BSA is affected by skin detachment, 10–30% is an overlap area between SJS and TEN, and >30% is defined as TEN.
Clinical Presentation
Prodromal symptoms with fever, malaise, sore throat, and arthralgia
Early Lesions are ill-defined, erythematous, and coalescing macules
Within days, blistering and detachment of the epidermis with light pressure (positive Nikolsky sign) occur
All mucosal surfaces can be involved, including the buccal, oro/nasopharyngeal, and anogenital mucosa
Eye involvement is common
Investigations
Skin biopsy
FBP
Serum electrolyte
Serum glucose

Creatinine
Total protein
Serum albumin

Serum BUN
Skin or blood culture and sensitivity

Multi-disciplinary	approach	involving	dermatologist, ophthalmologist, gynecologist and physician
Withdrawal all suspected drugs
If SCORTEN is 0-1, admit into normal ward, if 2 or more admit to ICU
Keep warm at 28-300 C
Encourage high protein diet
Avoid debridement and consider detached epidermis as natural biological dressing
Fluid replacement with electrolyte solution 2ml/kg/%BSA in the 1st 24 hours

OR

AND

Note:
Antibiotics should only be given if there are signs of infection and should be guided culture results
Systemic therapies (corticosteroids and cyclosporine), if employed, should be used within 24 to 48 hours of symptom onset

EYE DISEASES AND REFRACTIVE ERRORS

Major Blinding Eye Diseases
Eye diseases and refractive errors are conditions affecting the eye. Diseases of most important are those leading to blindness, visual impairment (VI) or presenting with pain. Blindness is defined as a presenting visual acuity (VA) of less than 3/60 or central visual field of less than 10º in the better eye. Visual impairment is categorized by WHO onto several categories depends on VA. The definition of blindness/VI in children and infants is the same as that in adults though there are different methods for testing vision in young children until when they are at preschool age when normal visual acuity chart can be used. The common causes of blindness and visual impairment among adults are cataract, glaucoma, corneal blindness, diabetic retinopathy, uncorrected refractive errors. There are other eye diseases that do not lead into blindness or visual impairment, these are also addressed in this section. Given the asymptomatic nature of most eye diseases, it is advised that patients presenting to eye clinic with whatever complaint must have basic eye examination of both eyes which entails (VA-Plain and PH, IOP, fundoscopy and pupil exam) as a minimum.
Cataract
Cataract is clouding of the lens which prevents clear vision and if not treated can lead to visual impairment and/or blindness. Most of the time its due to ageing process (Senile Cataract) but can also result from trauma, inflammatory eye diseases or systemic conditions. Children may be born with cataract (congenital) or develop cataract in the early ages of life (developmental cataract).
Clinical Presentation
Various degrees of progressive painless vision impairment unilateral or bilateral
History of trauma with a sharp/blunt object for traumatic cataract
History of red eye for secondary cataract.
Initially glare and haloes around light
Cloudiness in the lens seen as a white mark behind the pupil and iris seen with slit lamp microscope (Leukocoria)
Conjunctiva and cornea are clear and the whole iris can be seen clearly
Obscured red reflex
For	Congenital	Cataract,	Squint	and/or nystagmus can be seen
Note:
Cataract may present in all age groups, blindness due to cataract is reversible but in children prognosis can be guarded depending on duration of the cataract.
Currently, proven treatment is only by surgical removal of the cataractous lens and IOL Implantation
IOL can range from Monofocal IOLs to premium IOLs such as Presbyopia-correcting IOL (Multifocal, EDOF and Accommodative IOLs) hence price of cataract surgery will vary depending on inserted IOL.
Early treatment in children is mandatory
White pupil in children may be a tumor in the eye, late referral may lead to permanent loss of vision, squint, loss of eye or loss of life
No Cataract surgery should be done without Biometry for precise IOL power calculations
Investigations
Visual acuity (Plain, PH and Corrected
B Scan if no fundal view
Pen torch eye exam for Cornea clarity and Pupil Exam-RAPD Check
Biometry: Keratometer, A Scan and IOL power Calculations
IOP Measurements
For elderly, Anaesthesiologists review is advised
Slit Lamp Biomicroscopy
For some patients: ECG, Echo, BP, Blood sugars is recommended
Refraction depending on the density of cataract

Glaucoma
Glaucoma is a syndrome characterized by optic nerve damage and peripheral visual field loss which may be associated with raised intraocular pressure. The main classes of glaucoma are open angle glaucoma and angle closure glaucoma.
Note:

Primary Open Angle Glaucoma (POAG) Clinical Presentation
Painless loss of peripheral vision leading to absolute glaucoma as the end stage
Affects mainly adults of 40 years of age and above
Cornea and conjunctiva are clear
Pupil in the affected eye does not react with direct light in advanced stage (RAPD +Ve)
The optic nerve is always damaged, this can be seen through fundoscopy as enlarged CDR and NRR thinning
One eye may be affected more than the other (Asymmetrical)
First degree relatives of glaucoma patients are at 3x increased risk of developing Glaucoma and at younger age.
Note
Primary Open Angle Glaucoma does not have symptoms in early stages, hence routine intraocular pressure checkup and fundus examinations should be done in all people of 40 years and above by some qualified eye care personnel on annual basis.
All suspected cases of glaucoma should be referred to qualified eye care personnel for confirmation of diagnosis, Investigations, commencement of treatment and follow up plan
Medical and/or Laser treatment (SLT, MP-TSCPC) should precede Surgical treatment
Refilling of antiglaucoma may be prescribed by a middle cadre eye worker but Biannual monitoring should be done at a centre where there is an Ophthalmologist
For advanced and complicated Glaucoma, patients should be referred to a health facility where there are Glaucoma Specialists

Ocular Trachoma
It has five grades according to WHO which are grouped into two (Active Trachoma and Cicatricial Trachoma). Active trachoma usually happened in children below age of 9 years as is an acute conjunctivitis caused by infection with Chlamydia trachomatis (bacteria). The Cicatricial trachoma (TS, TT and CO) is one of the commonest causes of corneal blindness worldwide. There is an inward turning of the eye lashes which rub against the cornea and lead to corneal opacity which is the culprit for visual impairment and/or blindness.
Clinical Presentation
Purulent whitish discharge in active disease
Photophobia in early stages or re- infection
More than 5 Follicles in the upper tarsal plate seen as round and white nodules in active disease.
In cicatricial stages, in-turned eyelashes rub on the cornea leading to corneal ulcers and eventually opacity if left untreated
Loss of vision due to corneal scarring and opacification.
Clinical Stages according to World Health Organization
Active Disease
Trachomatous Inflammation Follicular (TF) - Presence of at least 5 follicles on the upper tarsal plate
Trachomatous Inflammation Intense (TI) – There is intense inflammation, the conjunctival blood vessels cannot be seen.
Cicatricial Disease
Trachomatous Scarring (TS) – Presence of white scars in the upper tarsal plate
Trachomatous Trichiasis (TT) – Presence of some eye lashes rubbing against the cornea
Corneal Opacity (CO) – Presence of corneal opacity (scar) affecting the central cornea

Treatment options for Diabetic Macular Edema (DME)
Management of DME depends on the clinical stage of DME and treatment options available at the facility where the patient has been attended.
Primary tests are required to be performed in order to grade the DME. Macula OCT for all diabetic patients should be the baseline test to determine presence or absence of DME. Macular thickness of equal or more than 400 microns should be considered as DME. Those facilities without this tool, the clinical assessment will be the baseline test where the best corrected visual acuity will be the key point for grading which will be matched with the clinical findings. Therefore, VA of less than 6/12 should be considered as DME case. It is important to exclude other causes of visual impairment before concluding the presence of DME. Use of anti-VEGF has been found to be effective in the treatment of DME.

Retinal Detachment
Retinal detachment is a sight threatening condition with an incidence of approximately 1 in 10000. Three known forms of Retinal detachment:
Rhegmatogenous retinal detachments are often due to retinal tears associated with posterior vitreous detachment or trauma.
Tractional retinal detachments can be seen in proliferative retinopathy due to diabetic disease, sickle cell and other disease processes leading to neovascularization of the retina.
Serous/Exudative detachments are caused by a number of inflammatory, or exudative retinal disease processes such as sarcoidosis, medication toxicity, myeloma, or choroidal neoplasms.
Clinical Presentation
Sudden painless loss of vision with cuttens like complaints.
Investigations
VA,
B scan,
Fundoscopy,
OCT
At Primary level once diagnosis of RD is suspected, referral should be done immediately to tertiary center with VRS for proper management. Treatment options vary depends on type of RD.
Medical management for Serous RD. Any inflammatory disease or underlying mass should be identified and treated if possible Surgical management is indicated for rhegmatogenous and tractional detachments. Surgical options are:
Laser retinopexy is typically reserved for small, localized detachments
Pneumatic retinopexy involves the injection of an intraocular gas bubble along with retinopexy using cryotherapy or laser
Scleral buckles are silicone bands permanently placed around the outside of the globe under the extraocular rectus muscles to relieve any traction and support retinal tears
Pars plana vitrectomy with appropriate vitrectomy probe
Vitreous Hemorrhages
Vitreous Hemorrhage is a relatively common cause of acute vision loss, having an incidence of approximately 7 cases per 100,000.
The three most common causes include
Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR)
Posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) with or without retinal tear
Ocular trauma
Clinical Presentation
Sudden, painless visual loss or haze is a common presentation.
Investigations
VA,
Fundoscopy,
B scan
Management
At Primary level if VH is suspected, refer urgently for proper management at tertiary level with information to minimize strenuous activity, as an increase in blood pressure may disrupt the newly formed clot and cause new active bleeding. If history of using of anticoagulation, advise to stop.
Intravitreal injection of anti-VEGF agents may be used to cause regression of neovascularization in proliferative retinopathies such as AMD but not in DR.
Surgery
Pars plana vitrectomy is indicated for vitreous hemorrhage accompanied by retinal detachment or break seen on B-scan, non- clearing vitreous hemorrhage
Acute Retinal Vascular Occlusions
Acute retinal vascular occlusions are common causes of visual impairment. Two forms exist retinal artery occlusions (RAOs) and retinal vein occlusions (RVOs). They are both associated with increased age and cardiovascular risk factors. These are synonyms to CVA of the eye. Acute management of RAOs involves a multidisciplinary approach including neurologists with stroke expertise, while RVO treatment is provided by ophthalmologists; optimization of systemic risk factors by patients’ primary care providers is an important component of RAO and RVO management.
Clinical Presentation
Acute RAO results in acute monocular visual loss, with severity based on the size of the occluded vessel. attenuation of the retinal arteries, segmentation of the retinal arterial blood columns with sometimes visible retinal arterial emboli, and acute retinal ischemia, “cherry red spot”.
Acute RVO presents with sudden loss of vision with tomato paste fundus.
Investigations
VA,
Refraction,
IOP,
Temporal artery palpation,
B scan,
Fundoscopy,
OCT,
FFA
Systemic	work	up accordingly
At primary level, if diagnosis is suspected. Decreasing of IOP should be considered through medical therapy.
Treatment at tertiary center with VRS can either be medical or surgical depending weather its ischaemic or hemorrhagic RVO. AntiVEGF can be used.

Retinopathy of Prematurity
Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is primarily due to unmonitored supplemental oxygen. Major risk factors are Low birthweight (<1500 grams), Gestational age of <30 weeks, High, unregulated oxygen at birth and/or fluctuations in oxygenation and Poor postnatal growth
Prevention
Screenings of infants at risk with appropriate timing of exams and follow up is essential to identify infants in need of treatment as per National RoP Guideline.
Diagnosis
Following pupillary dilation using eye drops, the retina is examined with an indirect ophthalmoscope. The peripheral portions of the retina are pushed into view using scleral depression. International Classification of Retinopathy of Prematurity (ICROP3) developed a diagnostic classification of ROP. These diagnostic classifications define ROP by location (zone), severity (stage) and vascular characteristics in the posterior pole (normal, pre-plus, or plus disease).
Non-Pharmacological Management
Follow up interval and treatment will depend on classification of the disease as mentioned in the National RoP Guideline. Treatment is mainly surgical:
Cryotherapy to the avascular retina. This is mainly given to eyes with threshold RoP which is defined as defined as 5 contiguous or 8 cumulative clock hours of stage 3 ROP in zone I or zone II with plus disease
Argon and diode lasers to treat the avascular retina of threshold ROP.
Pharmacological Management
Anti-VEGF treatment for stage 3 ROP with plus disease in zone I (not zone II). Given as
S: bevacizumab intravitreal injection 0.2 mg monthly
OR
S: ranibizumab intravitreal injection 0.2 mg monthly
OR
S: aflibercept intravitreal injection 0.2mg monthly Follow up after treatment is crucial in these kids.

Low Vision and Blindness
Low vision is a permanent visual impairment that cannot be corrected by medication, surgery, or standard spectacles and interferes with daily activities. It is defined as visual acuity less than 6/18 but equal to or better than 3/60, or a visual field less than 20 degrees in the better eye with the best possible correction.
Blindness defined as a presenting visual acuity of less than 3/60 in the better eye, or a visual field of less than 10 degrees from the central fixation, even with the best possible spectacle correction.
Clinical Presentation
Inability to
Recognize people in the streets,
Read black boards,
Write at the same speed as peers
Play with friends.
Investigations
Visual acuity
Refraction
Tonometry

Mainly Rehabilitation
Assessment of the patients’ visual function
Accurate refraction and provision of spectacles if indicated

Surgical intervention is indicated e.g., if a patient has cataract
Referral: All children with low vision should be referred to high level health facility for proper assessment and management by a paediatric Eye Team

Ocular Trauma
These are eye injuries that result from blunt or sharp objects or from chemical substances injuring the eye. The management of these injuries is guided by history from the patient and ocular findings by the clinicians. Classes of ocular trauma are as follows: -
Blunt Trauma/Non-Perforating Eye Injury/Foreign Body
Establish the cause to determine the type of injury and whether there is penetration.
Clinical Presentation
Corneal abrasion/laceration with or without an imbedded foreign body.
Eye lids may also be involved.
Conjunctiva may be involved as well
Investigations
This is done after the first aid measures
Examine the injured eye with slit lamp or magnifier and pen torch
Fluorescein staining to reveal foreign body or corneal laceration
Non-Pharmacological Management
Provide first aid measures to the patients as per presentation
Fundoscopy in blunt injury or embedded foreign body
B scan in embedded foreign body
CT Scan in suspected metal foreign body
If no penetration, irrigate the eye with clean water or Ringers Lactate to reduce chemical substance in the eye
Remove foreign body if visible with a cotton bud or surgical blade if shallow after topical application of an anaesthetic drop

At the primary care:
Corneal Abrasion:
A: chloramphenicol eye ointment 1%, 8hourly to the injured eye until no fluorescein staining
AND
S: Soft Contact Lenses is indicated for pain relief and quick recovery

Traumatic Optic neuropathy
Traumatic optic neuropathy (TON) is a condition in which acute injury to the optic nerve from direct or indirect trauma results in vision loss. The most common cause of TON is indirect injury to the optic nerve, which is thought to be the result of transmitted shock from an orbital impact to the intracanalicular portion of optic nerve.
Clinical Presentation
Patients with TON may have decreased visual acuity, decreased color vision, an afferent pupillary defect, and/or visual field deficits.
Investigations
CT scan of the brain and orbits.
VA, Refraction,
IOP,
Management

EOM tests,
Pupils’ exam
Aside from observation, the two treatment options that can be considered include high-dose corticosteroids or surgical decompression.
Erythropoietin (EPO) has shown promise as a potential treatment for TON.
Note: Intervention within 48 hours or three days of injury may yield better outcomes Surgical decompression can be considered in cases of TON with evidence of optic nerve compression
Chemical Injuries/Burn
This is an Ophthalmological emergency. It occurs when chemicals such as acid or alkali (e.g., household detergents, bleaching agents), snake spit, insect bite, traditional eye medicine, cement or lime cause a damage to the eye.
Clinical Presentation
Diagnosis relies mostly with patients’ history
Patients may present with photophobia
Inability to open eyes
Excessive tearing/watery eyes
Cloudiness of cornea with blurred vision
Loss of conjunctival blood vessels
Traces of chemical substance such as cement or herbs and blisters or loss of eyelid skin in open flame injuries
Investigations
Visual acuity
Slit lamp biomicroscopy
Fluorescein staining
Non-Pharmacological Management
If a patient gives you history of being in contact with the items mentioned above, the following should be done:
Irrigate the eye with clean water or Ringer’s lactate continually for a minimum of 20–30 minutes to reduce chemical substances. Irrigate longer for severe alkali burn.
Test the patients’ vision and examine the patient’s eye
Pharmacological Management
C: tetracaine 0.5% eye drops, instill 2 drops in the affected eye. Repeat irrigation if possible. Evert the eye lids and remove the debris
AND
A: chloramphenicol 1% eye ointment, apply 6hourly to prevent infection for 3days.
OR
A: oxytetracycline eye ointment, apply 6hourly to prevent infection for 3 days.
AND
A: paracetamol (PO)1gm 4–6hourly to a maximum of 4 doses in 24hours, for 3days in adults, the dosage in children is 10– 14mg/kg 4–6hourly for 3days
Referral: Refer all cases within 12hours to eye specialist at high level health facilities for more care

This is a painful red eye condition resulting from a raw discontinuity to the corneal epithelium. It may be caused by infection (bacterial, viral e.g., Herpes simplex virus and measles, fungal, trauma (physical or chemical) and nutritional (Vitamin A deficiency). Systemic conditions can contribute to corneal ulcers as well.

Excessive tearing

Poor vision

Slit Lamp biomicroscope

Fluorescein sodium drops or a drop of local anesthetic on a fluorescein strip to assess the pattern of the ulcer and measure the size of corneal defect.

While waiting for laboratory results, give:
