Dacryocystitis
Dacryocystitis is inflammation of the lacrimal sac which typically occurs secondarily to obstruction within the nasolacrimal duct and the resultant backup and stagnation of tears within the lacrimal sac. Three clinical forms for the disease exist: Congenital- NLDO, Acute dacryocystitis usually requires systemic antibiotic therapy prior to intervention for the NLDO. Chronic dacryocystitis typically presents with fewer inflammatory signs and requires surgical therapy for the underlying cause
Clinical Presentation
In acute dacryocystitis, the symptoms may occur over several hours to several days and include
pain, erythema, and edema over the medial canthus and the area overlying the lacrimal sac at the inferomedial portion of the orbit. The redness can extend to involve the bridge of the nose. Purulent material can sometimes be expressed from the puncta and tearing may be present.
In chronic dacryocystitis,
excessive tearing and mucus reflux (mucocele) are the most common symptoms. Changes in visual acuity may be present due to altered tear film dynamics.
Investigations
The diagnosis of dacryocystitis is generally made based on the patient’s history and physical exam. Crigler maneuver, or tear duct massage, can be performed to express material for culture and gram stain. The fluorescein dye disappearance test (DDT),
Pharmacological Management
For congenital NLDO has up to a 90% chance of resolution by 1 year of age, so treatment is delayed until 2 years of age meanwhile Crigler massages is advised.
Acute dacryocystitis should be treated with oral empirical antibiotics with gram-positive coverage
A: amoxicillin (PO) 500mg 8hourly for 7 days
AND
A: ciprofloxacin (PO) 500mg 12hourly for 7 days
OR
B: azithromycin (PO) 500mg 24hourly for 5 days
If No response within 48 hours give referral for further care. Once the acute inflammation/infection is controlled, the underlying cause can then be addressed
For Chronic dacryocystitis. Patients who fail conservative treatment often undergo lacrimal probing, which is successful in 70% of cases. If the dacryocystitis still persists, additional surgical interventions may be needed, such as stenting, balloon dacryoplasty, and either external or endonasal DCR (Dacryocystorhinostomy Surgery)

Squamous Cell Carcinoma of Conjunctiva
Invasive squamous cell carcinoma of conjunctiva is the major and most common ocular malignancy of the eye in adults. The tumor typically occurs on the bulbar conjunctiva, originating at the limbus, and often spreads onto the cornea, globe, orbit and nasolacrimal system. The cancer is a slow growing tumor of middle-aged to elderly people. It is common in immunocompromised individuals
Clinical Presentation
It manifests usually as a fleshy vascularized mass at the limbus. (Temporal or nasally)
In advanced stage, it may intrude the eyeball and extend to other ocular adnexa structures
Definitive diagnosis is by histopathological assessment of excised tissue
Investigations
Visual acuity
Slit lamp Biomicroscopy
Tonometry
Fundoscopy

Histology
PITC
DM Screening
Non-Pharmacological Management
Check for HIV status of the patient as recurrences occurs most frequently in HIV positive patients
Close follow up of patients for at least the first 12 months postoperatively to look for residual or recurrent tumors
Pharmacological Management
S: 5-fluorouracil (5FU) 50mg/mL, on a sponge, for about 2.5minutes then wash off with sodium lactate compound (ringer’s lactate)solution.
OR
S: mitomycin C 0.2mg/mL, on a sponge, for about 2.5minutes then wash off with sodium lactate compound (ringer’s lactate)solution.
AND
C: dexamethasone + chloramphenicol eye drops, 0.1%–0.5 %, 6hourly, for 3–4weeks
OR
C: dexamethasone + gentamicin eye drops, 0.1–0.3%, 6hourly, for 3–4 weeks (These are post operatively until the wound is healed)
THEN
S: 5-fluorouracil (5FU) 1% eye drops, 4times daily for 2–3weeks
OR
S: cyclosporine 0.05% eye drops bid for 2-3 weeks
Note:
5-fluorouracil (5FU) is used after the excision wound has healed
5FU eye drops may cause watery eye, discomfort or eye inflammation, manage accordingly
Surgical Treatment
It depends on the tumor size, location, focality, and invasiveness
Surgical excision of the mass with clear margin of 4 mm without touching the tumor is recommended, followed with topical adjunctive cryotherapy and or chemotherapy to the residual conjunctival and scleral bed
- Double - four freeze-thaw cycles of cryotherapy to the remaining conjunctival margins, bed and limbus.
- For tumors that are adherent to the sclera, perform a superficial sclerectomy and use cryotherapy to the base.
A large or multicentric squamous conjunctival mass should be managed by a surgeon experienced in treating such lesions
Removal of the eyeball and adnexa may be indicated for advanced stage
Radiotherapy if required, for palliation after removal of the eye.
Referral:
All suspicious cases of Squamous Cell Carcinoma of Conjunctiva must be referred to eye specialist for proper evaluation and management.
Refer all patients with advanced Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the conjunctiva to Oncologist

Dry Eye Syndrome/Keratoconjunctivitis Sicca
It occurs when there is inadequate tear volume, poor quality tears or functional disorders of tear drainage.
Clinical Presentation
Feelings of dryness, grittiness, burning and foreign body sensation, usually worse during the day
Stringy discharge, redness and transient blurring of vision are also common. Exclude allergic conjunctivitis
Investigations
Visual acuity
Refraction
Fundoscopy
Schirmer tear Test

Tear break up time
Slit lamp biomicroscopy
Tear meniscus height (meniscometry)
Non-Pharmacological Management
Control symptoms and look for secondary causes for treatment such as MGDs.
Educate patients to avoid unprescribed eye medications which may worsen the dryness and control their environmental factors by e.g., blinking frequently during visual attentive tasks and the use of 20-20-20 rule avoid air conditioners directly on the face.
Use humidifier in areas with low humidity
Punctal plugins to decrease tear drainage
Tear conserving interventions such as punctal plugs or nighttime masks/goggles
Bandage Contact Lenses can be used as well
Specialty contact lenses such as scleral lenses
Pharmacological Management
C: hydroxypropyl methylcellulose 0.7%, ophthalmic drops, 1drop, 6hourly.
OR
C: carboxymethylcellulose-0.5%w/v + glycerin-0.5%w/v eye drops 12hourly for 3months
OR
S: cyclosporine 0.05%/0.09% eye drops 12hourly for 1-2months -increase tear production)
OR
S: lifitegrast 5% ophthalmic solution 12hourly 1-2 months have shown to alleviate symptoms
OR
S: autologous serum tears 12hourly for 1-2 months
Note:
Dry eye syndromes are a multifactorial disease and should be managed wholistically
Rule out risk factors and address them accordingly such as MGDs, Blepharitis
Menopause women are prone to dry eyes so advise them accordingly

Visual Problems
Visual problems may be due to refractive errors, damage to the eye or optic nerve. This may be an indication of underlying diseases such as diabetes or hypertension.
Investigations
Assess ocular alignment
Determine visual acuity accurately in both eyes by Snellen chart
If vision is diminished, (less than 6/12), perform the following: -
Pin hole test
Make a hole of about 1mm wide in a piece of dark/black paper – you can push a hole in a paper or card with a pen tip
Ask the patient to look through this hole at the Snellen chart
If vision improves, this means that the patient has a refractive error
Red Reflex Test
The patient looks past the examiners head focusing on a distant target.
	With the ophthalmoscope at 0 (zero) the examiner keeps close to his eye and then focuses the beam of light so that it falls on the pupillary area of the cornea
The examiner stands about 60cm away from the patient.
In normal individuals, the examiner should be able to see a red or pink colour (reflex) through the pupil which comes from the retina.
Significance of absent red reflex
If there is history of trauma or diabetes, the absence of a red reflex is probably due to:
Retinal detachment
A vitreous hemorrhage
Mature cataract
If there are cataracts, one usually sees:
Black shadows against the red reflex in immature cataract, or
Absence of red reflex in mature cataracts
In a >50years of age with no history of trauma, diabetes or previous eye disease, an absent red reflex is often due to cataract formation, especially with decreased visual acuity.
Note: Associated diabetes or hypertension should be adequately managed with referral, as surgery can only be considered with appropriately managed systemic disease

Onchocerciasis (River Blindness)
Onchocerciasis is a tissue parasitic infestation caused by a filarial worm, Onchocerca volvulus. The microfilariae invade lymphatic system, subcutaneous and deep tissues producing acute inflammation and chronic inflammation at a later stage
Clinical Presentation
Skin inflammation with papules
Subcutaneous nodules
Atypical skin lesions (scarred, saggy, hanging areas of skin, leopard skin)
Skin nodules under the bony prominent areas
Microfilaria in anterior chamber
Scleritis and Keratitis leading to Impaired vision as well as blindness
Investigations
Visual acuity
Rapid diagnostic test (OV-16 - Onchocerciasis IgG)
Skin snip for microscopic examination
Slit lamp eye examination.
B Scan
Pharmacological Management
Treatment is done in consultation with dermatologists and infectious disease specialists.
Apart from WHO recommended mass treatment campaign to community at risk with annual preventive chemotherapy which polarize/paralyze the worm, treatment depends on individual patient presentation.
A: ivermectin (PO) 0.15mg/kg once every 12months for 12–15years
Note:
Patients with heavy ocular infestation require retreatment every 3 to 6 months.
Treatment will only arrest progression of the clinical features but not reverse them.

EAR, NOSE AND THROAT/HEAD AND NECK DISEASES
Ear, Nose and Throat (ENT) is a specialty in medicine that deals with medical and surgical management of disorders affecting the ear, nose, throat, head and the neck. Symptoms and diseases affecting this area are common and commonly lead to patients seeking medical care.

Ear Conditions
Circumscript otitis Externa (Furunculosis)
This is a localized infection of the hair follicle on the outer one-third of the external auditory canal. It is caused by Staphylococcus aureus.
Clinical Presentation
Ear pain that is severe and disproportional to the visible lesion
Reduced hearing
Localized swelling on the external auditory canal
There may be a purulent discharge if the swelling ruptures
Non-Pharmacological Management
Aural toilet if there is otorrhea (ear suctioning under direct vision).
Aural toilet using a clean dry cotton cloth while at home.
Instruct the patient to keep the ear dry and avoiding scratching
Pharmacological Management
Antibiotics are reserved for cases with systemic symptoms (e.g., fever, cellulitis) or microbiologically confirmed resistant infections. Routine use is discouraged to prevent antimicrobial resistance

Necrotizing (Malignant) Otitis Externa
This is a life-threatening invasive infection that affects the external auditory canal leading to skull base osteomyelitis. It is common to elderly diabetic patients and other immunosuppressive conditions. Most common causative organism is Pseudomonas aeruginosa followed by Aspergillus. Controlling the underlying cause of immunosuppression is of paramount importance.

Nocturnal exquisite ear pain, discharge, fullness and hearing impairment.
May present with facial nerve paralysis or other cranial nerves palsy.
Oedema of the external auditory canal with or without presence of granulation tissues at the junction between the bony and cartilaginous parts of the inferior portion of external auditory canal
Necrosis of external auditory canal

Placement of an aural wick
Instruct the patient to keep the ear dry and avoiding scratching

Ear Keloid
This is abnormal proliferation of scar tissue that forms at the site of cutaneous injury and grows beyond the original margins of the scar. Most common causes are ear piercing, trauma or surgical incisions.
Clinical Presentation
Swelling of the involved area of the ear, most commonly ear lobe
Non-Pharmacological Management
Use of pressure therapy e.g., pressure clips
Intra-lesional steroid injection
S: triamcinolone acetonide (Intra-lesional) 40mg depending on the size of the lesion weekly for 4weeks before excision and 4weeks after excision
Surgical management
Total keloidectomy +/- Steroid injection. (should be done by expertise, involve dermatologist/plastics for best decision)

Congenital Choanal Atresia
A congenital blockage (bony, membranous, or mixed) of the posterior nasal opening, causing nasal obstruction. It may be unilateral or bilateral. Neonates are obligate nasal breathers; therefore, complete bilateral choanal atresia is a medical emergency requiring immediate oral airway support until surgical creation of a patent nasal airway. Early recognition and referral are critical in bilateral cases. Always assess for associated anomalies (e.g., CHARGE syndrome).
Clinical Presentation
Bilateral: Neonatal respiratory distress relieved by crying, difficulty feeding, cyanosis.
Unilateral: Persistent unilateral nasal obstruction or discharge.
Investigation
Thick nasal discharge on the defective nostril
Failure to pass nasogastric tube
Primary level: Failure to pass a nasogastric tube through the nostril.
Secondary level: Clinical assessment; refer.
Tertiary level: Nasal endoscopy and CT scan Paranasal sinuses (PNS) for confirmation and surgical planning.
Non-Pharmacological Management
Primary level: Maintain airway (oral airway or prone/lateral positioning), oxygen (oral) if needed, urgent referral.
Secondary level: Supportive care (suction, feeding via orogastric tube), refer to tertiary immediately.
Tertiary level: if suspected at tertiary facility, urgently follow the above approach and consult ENT on call immediately or refer.
Surgical treatment
(At a center with ENT surgeon)
Surgical correction preferably via endoscopic trans nasal approach (endoscopic stentless Cho anoplasty)
Postoperative care includes the following;
S: esomeprazole 1mg/kg once 4 weeks
AND
A: sodium chloride saline drop (irrigation) 8 hourly for 4 weeks
AND
C: oxymetazoline 0.05%/ephedrine nasal drops 8hly 5 days),
AND
D:	dexamethasone	+	ciprofloxacin	nasal	drops (0.1%+0.3%), 3 drops/nostril 12 hourly)
Monthly follow-up nasoendoscopy for 3 months
Note: Delaying unilateral choanal atresia repair until after 6 months of age may reduce the need for revision surgery as the child grows.

Nose Bleeding (Epistaxis)
Nose bleeding is a condition which is common in adults. It may be due to a local cause in the nasal cavity (e.g., trauma, tumor, foreign body, septal varices, or septal deviation); or a systemic cause (e.g., blood disorders, vascular disorders, renal failure, hepatic failure, or use of anticoagulants (warfarin, heparin). Most cases of epistaxis are minor; do not require hospitalization. Patients with significant nose bleeding do require hospitalization.
Non-Pharmacological Management
Stabilize the patient: put an open intravenous line, do blood grouping and cross matching
Put the patient in a sitting position and advise the patient to pinch the soft part of the nose gently for 5minutes
Put on a gown, glasses, head light and sterile gloves and evacuate clots. Do a thorough head and neck examination
Cauterize septal varisces (if any) using a silver nitrate pencil
Do an anterior nasal packing by introducing into the nasal cavity as far posterior as possible sterile Vaseline gauzes (or iodine-soaked gauzes if not available) or special merocele pack, using a dissecting forceps (if bayonet forceps is not available)
Put rolled dry gauze on the columella and plaster it
If the patient is still bleeding
Perform a Flexible nasoendoscopy
Do a posterior nasal packing using a Foley’s catheter introduced through the nasal cavity into the oropharynx, balloon it with normal saline up to 10–15cc while pulling it outward to impinge on the posterior nasal choana, then do anterior nasal packing as above.

Place a posterior nasal pack under general anaesthesia (GA)
Put dry gauze on the nose to prevent necrosis of the columella and fix the catheter on the nose with an umbilical clamp
Almost all of the nasal bleedings will be controlled by this way
Note: Remove the packs after 72 hours
Pharmacological Management
To prevent rhinosinusitis
Prophylactic antibiotics are not routinely recommended unless there is evidence of infection or high risk of rhinosinusitis

Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome (OSAS)
Disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of upper airway obstruction during sleep, resulting in interrupted ventilation, intermittent hypoxia, and sleep fragmentation. The obstruction typically occurs at the level of the pharynx, often due to collapse or anatomical narrowing involving ENT structures such as the adenoids, tonsils, nasal passages, soft palate, and base of tongue.
In both children and adults, ENT-related anatomical factors contribute significantly to the pathophysiology of OSAS, and their recognition is critical for effective treatment planning.
This section addresses only non-central sleep apnea. Central sleep apnea and non-Surgical treatment are discussed in the Respiratory and CNS chapters. ENT specialists play a key role in the multidisciplinary management of OSAS.
Etiology and Risk Factors
In Children
Adenoid and/or tonsillar hypertrophy (most common cause)
Nasal obstruction (e.g., allergic rhinitis, inferior turbinate hypertrophy, deviated nasal septum)
Pharyngo- Laryngomalacia
Craniofacial	anomalies	(e.g.,	midface hypoplasia, Pierre Robin sequence)
Neuromuscular disorders
Obesity (as a contributing factor)
Clinical Presentation
In Adults
Obesity (primary risk factor)
Nasal obstruction (polyps, septal deviation, turbinate hypertrophy)
Redundant soft palate and uvula
Tonsillar hypertrophy (less common)
Macroglossia or retrognathia
Alcohol or sedative use before bedtime
While symptoms vary with age, a high index of suspicion should be maintained for
Loud habitual snoring
Witnessed apneas or gasping episodes during sleep (this can be reported by bedpartner or parent/caretaker)
Daytime somnolence or hyperactivity (children)
Mouth breathing and nasal speech
Learning or behavioral difficulties (children)

Poor concentration, irritability, or morning headaches
Nocturnal enuresis in children
Decreased quality of life and sexual dysfunction (adults)
Clinical assessment
Detailed sleep history (snoring, witnessed apneas, sleep position, restlessness, daytime function)
Examination of nasal patency, tonsillar size (Brodsky scale), adenoid facies, craniofacial features
Screening tools: STOP-BANG (adults), Pediatric Sleep Questionnaire (children)
Investigations
Polysomnography (gold standard)
Pulse oximetry (overnight) as a basic alternative where polysomnography is not available
Flexible nasopharyngoscopy: to assess upper airway dynamics and obstruction

Lateral neck X-ray or soft tissue nasopharynx imaging to evaluate adenoidal size in children
Drug-Induced Sleep Endoscopy (DISE): to evaluate the site and severity of upper airway obstruction. In case where the above are inconclusive
Address modifiable risk factors (e.g., obesity, allergens, sedatives)
Multidisciplinary involvement may be required in complex or residual cases

Surgical intervention is the definitive treatment in cases of identifiable and correctable airway obstruction.

Adenoidectomy and/or tonsillectomy – first-line for OSAS with adenotonsillar hypertrophy

Cardiovascular: systemic hypertension, pulmonary hypertension, arrhythmias

Growth failure in children

Laryngitis
Inflammatory condition of the larynx can be infectious or non-infectious, acute (3–7 days) or chronic (>3 weeks). Diagnosis is often made by case history alone and treatment often targets symptoms.
Acute viral laryngitis is commonest and self-limiting, often linked to upper respiratory infections.
Bacterial laryngitis is less common but can be more severe.
Clinical Presentation may differ between children and adults.
Signs of infectious laryngitis include odynophagia, cough, fever, and respiratory distress.
Acute Laryngitis
(Please refer Respiratory chapter for more specific details)
Children are more prone to airway compromise with bacterial laryngitis—prompt recognition is critical.
In adults, reflux and occupational overuse are more common contributors to chronic or recurrent acute laryngitis.
Most cases (especially viral or traumatic) are self-limiting, requiring only supportive care.

Laryngopharyngeal reflux disease (LPR) with/without Vocal cord nodules or Laryngeal polyp)
Occurs when gastric contents reach the larynx, affecting the glottis and vocal cords.
It commonly presents with hoarseness, globus sensation, chronic throat clearing, and sometimes heartburn or regurgitation.
Unlike gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), which involves the lower esophageal sphincter, LPR is linked to dysfunction of the upper esophageal sphincter.
Proper evaluation and management require a coordinated interprofessional approach.

It is the commonest benign laryngeal tumor of the larynx caused by Human papilloma virus (HPV), occurring in both children and adults. It has a higher recurrence rate in children than in adults, among adults it may turn into a malignancy.

Hoarse voice, audible respiration (inspiratory stridor)
Progressive difficulty in breathing
Progressive inspiratory stridor
On and off cough
Perform a thorough respiratory system examination
Indirect laryngoscopy for papilloma croups on the larynx

If in distress, perform a tracheostomy first then refer

ORAL AND MAXILLOFACIAL CONDITIONS
These include diseases and disorders that affect the teeth, gums, and supporting structures of the mouth. They involve medical disorders that affect the jaw (maxilla and mandible), face, and related structures, such as sinuses, salivary glands, muscles, nerves, blood vessels and temporomandibular joint (TMJ). Before doing oral examination or any dental procedures, patients should gurgle with hydrogen peroxide 3% or povidone iodine 0.5% or chlorhexidine gluconate 0.1% to minimize infectious agent’s contamination between patient and oral health care provider.

Tooth Eruption and tooth Shedding
Eruption of Deciduous Teeth
Eruption of deciduous /primary teeth refers to the process where the first set of teeth emerge through the gingiva into the mouth. This typically begins around five months of age and continues until the child is about two and a half years old. The following conditions may associate with eruption process; eruption cysts, gingival cysts of the newborn and pre/natal teeth
Clinical Presentation
Drooling
Bulge gingiva
Gingival soreness
Mild fever; may not need treatment
Note:
Nylon teeth” is a myth/belief existing in some traditions. These are conditions associated with the eruption of deciduous/primary teeth.
Pre/ Natal teeth if they are loose may be removed by dental personnel, but if they are firm should not be removed
Shedding of Deciduous Teeth
Phenomenon where deciduous/primary teeth are replaced by permanent teeth. This process occurring between ages of 5–12 years as a normal physiological change. Deciduous teeth should be left to fall out themselves unless the teeth are carious or there is any other indication. Parents should be counseled accordingly and be instructed to assist their children to loosen the already mobile teeth.
Clinical Presentation
Mixed dentition
Loose deciduous teeth
Investigation
CBCT or OPG X-ray or/ and PA X-ray
Surgical treatment
Tooth extraction; when deciduous fail to exfoliate or permanent teeth erupt in wrong direction

A: paracetamol (PO) 1g 8hourly for 3days
AND
A: amoxicillin (PO) 250mg 8hourly for 5days (If necessary)

Malocclusions
Malocclusion is any variation in the arrangement of teeth leading to abnormal occlusion to the extent that may be functionally harmful or aesthetically objectionable.
Clinical Presentation
Class I malocclusion: Diagnosed when there is any occlusal abnormality or individual tooth malocclusion in a case with normal arch relationship in anteroposterior plane.
Class II malocclusion: Mesiobuccal cusp of upper first permanent molar occludes mesial to the buccal developmental groove of the lower first permanent molar
Class III malocclusion: The upper first permanent molar occludes distal to the buccal developmental groove of the lower first permanent molar
Skeletal malocclusions: These malocclusions are caused by defects in the underlying skeletal structure itself.
Investigation
CBCT or OPG X-ray
Non-Pharmacological Management
Preventive measures
Parents counselling on avoiding oral habits to their child
Caries control
Release of abnormal frenal attachment
Management of abnormal oral musculature and related habits
Non-surgical treatment Interceptive orthodontics
Also known as early orthodontic treatment or Phase one orthodontics, is a proactive approach aimed at addressing dental and jaw development issues in children, typically between the ages of 6 and 10 years, during the mixed dentition phase when both primary and permanent teeth are present.
Guide jaw and dental development to ensure proper alignment and function
Create space for erupting permanent teeth, reducing the risk of crowding
Correct harmful oral habits such as thumb sucking or tongue thrusting
Assessing breathing pattern of the growing child such as mouth breather in a child with adenoids, guide ENT evaluations
Address skeletal discrepancies that can affect facial aesthetics and function
Space maintainers: Preserve space for permanent teeth if baby teeth are lost prematurely
Palatal expanders: Widen the upper jaw to correct cross-bites and create space
Partial braces or aligners: Address specific alignment issues in developing teeth
Definitive Orthodontics
Often referred to as "Phase II" or comprehensive orthodontic correction, is the full-scale alignment of permanent teeth and the correction of bite relationships after early intervention (Phase I) or as a single-phase approach. Main goals include: Precise alignment of all permanent teeth, Correction of bite issues (overbite, underbite, crossbite) and achieving proper jaw harmony and long-term functional stability. This treatment should start when most permanent teeth (excluding wisdom teeth) are erupted (around ages 10–14 years).
Appliances Used; Fixed braces (metal/ceramic) or clear aligners (Invisalign)
Treatment Duration; Generally, 12–30 months, often around 18–24 months, influenced by complexity
Retention Phase: After active treatment, patients wear retainers (fixed or removable) to maintain tooth position, retainer to be worn both day and night during the first six month and another six months during the night only.
Note: Fixed orthodontic treatment is a specialized procedure which shall be performed by Orthodontist for patient of all age groups. A Pedodontist (Pediatric Dentist) Shall provide fixed orthodontic treatment only to patient below twenty (20) years of age.

Bleeding socket
Can be defined as bleeding that continues beyond 8 to 12 hours after dental/tooth extraction. Local causes of bleeding include, traumatic extraction, bleeding due to disturbing the primary blood clot by the patient through rinsing or inadequate compression on the gauze. Systemic factors include platelet problems, coagulation disorders or excessive fibrinolysis, and inherited or acquired problems (medication induced).
Clinical Presentation

Development of a large hematoma or ecchymosis within the oral soft tissues;
Primary Bleeding Socket

Patient may be dehydrated and pale if has lost significant amount of blood
Features of decreased pulse rate and volume, hypotension also if patient has lost significant amount of blood
Secondary bleeding
The socket may show features of infection or trauma
Investigations

A: amoxicillin (PO) 500mg 8hourly for 5days

AND

AND

Brawny induration
Tissues are swollen, board like, not pitted and no fluctuance
Respiratory distress
Dysphagia
Tissues may become gangrenous with a peculiar lifeless appearance on cutting
Three fascia spaces are involved bilaterally (submandibular, submental, and sublingual)
Investigations
Routine investigations
Blood Glucose (Fasting/Random)
Renal Function Tests
Complete Blood Count (CBC)
Specific investigations
OPG, CBCT, CT Scan
Chest X-ray
Pus swab for Culture and sensitivity
Non-Pharmacological Management
Incision and drainage are done (even in absence of pus) to relieve the pressure and allow irrigation
Only when the airway distress is significant and there is evidence that it is not relieved by incision and drainage then tracheostomy is needed.
Patient should be admitted for Supportive care During incision and drainage pus should be taken for culture and sensitivity. Offending tooth should be removed at the same sitting if the patient can open the mouth.

B: ceftriaxone (IV) 1g 24hourly for 5days
OR
B: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid (FDC) (PO) 625mg 12-8hourly for 5days
AND
B: metronidazole (IV) 500mg 8hourly for 5days
If allergic to penicillin use
A: erythromycin (PO) 500mg 6hourly for 5days
Once the patient can swallow, replace IV medication with oral treatment.

Dental implants
Dental implant. Is an artificial tooth root made of compatible metal usually titanium implanted in the jaw bone to replace the missing single or multiple missing teeth?

Replacement of a single missing tooth
Replacement of multiple missing teeth
Support over denture
Retention of prosthesis in severely resorbed jaw bone

In a totally edentulous patient with good bone height and width
Mandible 6 implants
Maxillary 6 implants
In severe bone loss
Maxillary 4 implants -tilted
Mandible 4 implants -tilted

Implant surgery can either be one stage or two stages surgery depending on the bone condition
In aesthetic zone consider temporization

Adequate blood supply (proper incision design and flap reflection. Using sharp gradual series of drill sizes with copious amount of irrigation by normal saline.

Management of Maxillofacial Trauma
Traumatic Dental Injuries
It may result in loosening, displacement and or loss of teeth, fracture of teeth and or bone, lacerations, and bleeding. The commonest causes are falls (in sports and play) at home or school and motor accidents. Most affected are upper incisors.
Clinical Presentation
Type
Presentation
Tooth Concussion
Is an injury to supporting tissues of tooth, without displacement
Sublaxation
Is the partial displacement, but is commonly used to describe loosening of a tooth without
displacement
Intrusion
Is the displacement of tooth into its socket often accompanied by fracture of alveolar
Bone
Luxation
Is the displacement of tooth laterally, labially or palatally
Avulsion
Is the complete loss of tooth from the socket
Soft tissue Injuries Abrasion
Where friction between an object and the surface of the soft tissue causes a wound. This wound is usually superficial, denudes the epithelium, and occasionally involves deeper layers.
Contusion/Bruising
Indicates that some amount of tissue disruption has occurred within the tissues, which resulted in subcutaneous or sub mucosal hemorrhage without a break in the soft tissue surface.
Laceration
Is a tear in the epithelial and sub epithelial tissues. They often result from blunt or penetrating injuries due to motor traffic crashes, assaults, falls, or sports injuries.
Facial Bones Injuries
Types of Facial Bone Fractures Include:
Nasal Bone Fractures.
Mandibular Fractures: includes fractures of the body, angle, symphysis, Para symphysis, condyle, and ramus.
Maxillary (Upper Jaw) Fractures: include Le Fort fractures: classified into three patterns based on fracture lines:
Le Fort I: horizontal maxillary fracture (separates maxilla from the palate)
Le Fort II: pyramidal fracture involving nasal bridge, maxilla, and orbital floor
Le Fort III: craniofacial disjunction, separating the entire midface from the skull base.
Zygomatic bone Fractures: Involves the zygomatic bone and/or its articulations with maxilla, frontal bone, temporal bone, and sphenoid.
Orbital Fractures: involves either the rims or the walls of the orbit. Common types of wall fractures: orbital floor (blowout), medial wall, lateral wall, and roof fractures.
Naso-Orbito-Ethmoid (NOE) Fractures: fractures involving the central upper face. They affect the nasal bones, medial orbital walls, and ethmoid bone, and often disrupt the medial canthal ligament and lacrimal system.
Palatal Fractures: Fractures of the hard palate, often associated with maxillary fractures.
Initial Assessment & Emergency Management
Follow ATLS principles:
Airway with cervical spine control,
Breathing,
Circulation,
Disability,
Exposure.
Facial fractures demand extra vigilance for airway compromise from bleeding, edema, or bone displacement. The airway can quickly be secured using nasal/oral airway adjuncts, intubation, or emergency tracheostomy as needed.
A thorough history from the patient is required. In emergency setting, AMPLE mnemonic is used in trauma history to quickly gather essential information about a patient's medical background during emergency assessment:
A – Allergies: Identify any known drug or food allergies (especially to antibiotics, anesthetics, or latex).
M – Medications: Current prescriptions, over-the-counter drugs, anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin, aspirin), steroids, or herbal supplements.
P – Past medical history: Includes significant illnesses (e.g., diabetes, heart disease, seizures), surgeries, previous trauma, bleeding disorders.
L – Last meal: Important for anesthesia planning (risk of aspiration); also relevant in surgical timing.
E – Events/environment related to injury: Mechanism of injury (e.g., fall, assault, MVC), use of safety gear (seatbelt, helmet), loss of consciousness, alcohol/drug use, environmental exposures (e.g., smoke inhalation).
Imaging & Diagnosis
Dental CT (CBCT) or normal CT scans are the standard radiological investigation, especially with suspected midface or complex fractures; Plain X-rays may be adequate for isolated nasal or mandibular injuries. In case of isolated mandibular fractures OPG can suffice.
Fracture Management
Closed Reduction
It is reserved for non-displaced or minimally displaced fractures (e.g., nasal, condylar, pediatric, body of the mandible). Midface bones (nasal and zygoma) closed reduction is best within 7–10 days in adults, sooner in children. For the mandibular fractures closed reduction should be carried as soon as possible.
Maxillomandibular fixation (MMF)/intermaxillary fixation (IMF): Establishes occlusion, used in closed or open techniques for mandible and midface stability. Duration typically 4–8 weeks, or shorter with rigid fixation. Use arch bars, interdental wires, or bone screws; treatment Modalities
Open Reduction and Internal Fixation (ORIF):
Indicated for displaced, unstable, comminuted, or load-bearing fractures (mandible, Le Fort, ZMC). Aim is to achieve anatomical reduction, occlusion restoration, facial contour.
Utilize titanium miniplates, reconstruction plates, 3D plates, lag screws, biodegradable implants as appropriate. Choose incision and approach based on location (intraoral for symphysis/body; extraoral like Gillies for zygoma).
Note: ORIF for fractures of the jaws and midface should be performed by a specialist Oral and Maxillofacial surgeon.
Management Principles
Nasal Fractures
Evaluate for septal hematoma; drain within 24 hours.
Closed reduction (manual or instruments) ideally within 5–7 days post-injury in adults, sooner in children.
Use external splints for 7–10 days.
Mandibular Fractures
Non displaced/minimally displaced (e.g. condylar neck): Closed treatment with MMF for 4–6 weeks.
Displaced/body/angle fractures: ORIF with rigid plating; restore occlusion via intraoperative MMF first.
Provide nutritional and oral hygiene support; instruct on MMF care.
Midface Fractures
Le Fort I–III
Indicated for displaced fractures with instability, altered occlusion, or orbital involvement.
ORIF of buttress and orbital rim; MMF for 4-6 weeks.
Zygomatico-Maxillary Complex (ZMC)
Displacement: ORIF via Gillies, intraoral, or transconjunctival approaches.
Fix plate at zygomaticomaxillary buttress and/or frontozygomatic suture.
Orbital Fractures
Symptomatic entrapment or large floor defects: ORIF with titanium mesh or porous polyethylene implants
Antibiotics & Infection Prevention and Analgesics
Give prophylactic antibiotics for open fractures or fractures communicating with oral/nasal cavities
B: amoxicillin (clavulanic acid) 625mg 12hrly for 5 days
Optimal oral hygiene (chlorhexidine rinses, brushing) and nutritional support play key roles in infection reduction.
For pain control: Start with strong analgesics (e. g Tramadol (PO), Pethidine (IV) (if admitted)) for first 24hrs to 36 hours, then moderate analgesics (paracetamol (PO) or ibuprofen (PO)) until when the patient is free from pain.
Postoperative Care & Rehabilitation
Use light pressure dressings to reduce edema; remove after 2–5 days.
Monitor overnight for bleeding, airway issues, vomiting.
Regular follow-ups: 5–7 days (sutures), every 2 weeks, and at 6–8 weeks for MMF removal if used.
Gradually reintroduce diet from liquids to soft and then normal consistencies after removal of MMF.
Site-Specific Considerations
Nasal fractures: Watch for septal hematomas—drain urgently to avoid deformity. Closed reduction within days yields favorable cosmetic results; remodeling may occur in children.
Mandibular fractures: Favor ORIF for most load-bearing body and angle fractures; reserve closed reduction for minimally displaced, pediatric, condylar neck, comminuted, or atrophic cases.
ZMC fractures: Surgery needed for displaced fractures—restore projection and orbital volume. Miniplates/screws via Gillies or similar approaches.
Le Fort and midface: ORIF with MMF to restore buttresses and occlusion.
Pediatric considerations: Prefer conservative treatment for nasal, condylar, and NOE fractures unless displaced. Surgical intervention (ORIF) indicated in displaced NOE type II–III. Growth concerns may necessitate revisional procedures later.
Comminuted fractures in atrophic or edentulous mandibles: Consider reconstruction plate with load bearing properties.
Patients with coagulation disorders: Coordinate with hematology; ensure optimized clotting profile preoperatively.
Pharmacological Management
Pain control by analgesics
A: paracetamol (PO) 1g 8hourly for 3days
OR
C: diclofenac (PO) 50mg 8hourly for 3days
OR
A: ibuprofen (PO) 400mg 8hourly for 3days
Prophylactic antibiotics are indicated in cases of suspected contamination or extensive damage
B: ampicillin + cloxacillin (FDC) (PO) 500mg 8hourly for 5days

Tumours and Tumour-Like Conditions of Oral Cavity and Facial Region
Benign Odontogenic Tumors
Each tumour presents with different cardinal features clinically, radiologically and on histopathological diagnosis.
Ameloblastoma
Clinical Presentation
Recognized between ages of 10 to 80 years80% form in the mandible and 70% develop in the posterior molar region and often involve the ramus
Painless, slow growing tumor that may be solid or cystic
Loosening of teeth, with roots resorption
Gradual facial asymmetry due to enlargement and destruction of bone
Ping pong and/or bone cracking effects
Investigations
Radiographically, the tumour presents with multilocular radiolucency, honeycomb, or soap bubble appearance.
Note: Diagnostic confirmation of this tumour is through histopathology. Complete excision e.g. e.g. marginal resection, segmental resection plus bone grafting and partial or total resection of the jaw is the treatment of choice. Hence refer the patient to the center where there is oral and maxillofacial surgeon
Calcifying odontogenic tumor Clinical Presentation
Most often found in the mandibular molar/premolar region, but 33% of cases are found in the maxilla
It is associated with an unerupted or impacted tooth in 50% of cases
Investigations
Radiographically these lesions can be radiolucent, but more characteristically are mixed lucent and opaque masses, exhibiting a snow-driven appearance
Non-Pharmacological Management
Complete excision of the tumour with border of normal bone should be curative, but curettage or incomplete excision has high recurrence rates.
Amelobastic Fibroma Clinical Presentation
Slower growing tumor than the simple ameloblastoma and does not infiltrate between bone trabeculae.
Occurs during the first two decades of life
75% of ameloblastic fibromas are found in the posterior mandible in the area of a developing tooth. It is benign and expansile, growing as a pushing front rather than invading surrounding tissues
Investigations
Radiographically this lesion appears as a uniocular or bilocular radiolucency, most often in the posterior mandible.
The radiographic appearance is identical to that of unicystic ameloblastoma, and both lesions should be differential diagnoses because they affect similar age groups and have similar clinical and radiographic appearances. Histologic examination differentiates the two.
Non-Pharmacological Management
Enucleation and curettage and extraction of associated teeth is usually adequate for small tumours. For big tumours conservative resection may be required, where necessary to be followed with reconstruction.
Adenomatoid odontogenic Tumors (AOT) Clinical Presentation.
Usually occur in the second and third decades
Usually encountered incidentally
It has a female predilection
Two thirds of the cases occur in the anterior maxilla, one third occur in the anterior mandible, and it is never found posterior to the premolars
Two thirds of the cases are associated with an impacted tooth (usually the cuspid) Present with mild swelling or in association with a clinically missing tooth
Investigations
Radiographically this lesion generally appears as a well-demarcated radiolucency. In 75% of cases, it is associated with an unerupted tooth, usually the canine. It may contain radiopaque flecks, which represent calcified material.
Non-Pharmacological Management
Enucleation is curative and recurrence is almost unknown.
Odontogenic Myxoma Clinical Presentation
Occurs mostly in the second to fourth decades of life
Clinically indistinguishable from ameloblastoma, but on aspiration while ameloblastoma yields
straw-colored or yellow fluid Odontogenic myxoma may not yield anything due to the thick mucoid clear contents of the tumour.
The radiographic appearance; typically, it has honeycomb appearance, although
It often appears quite like ameloblastoma e.g multilocular radiolucency
Investigations
OPG, CBCT, Tissue biopsy (Confirmation is through histopathology)
Non-Pharmacological Management
Wide surgical excision Similar approach to the treatment of ameloblastoma. It has a high recurrence rate if not completely removed.
Cemento-ossious lesions
These are groups of benign fibro-osseous lesions that affect the jawbones, particularly the tooth-bearing areas. These lesions involve replacement of normal bone with fibrous tissue that contains varying amounts of mineralized material (bone, cementum, or both).
Clinical Presentation
Commonly occurring in the posterior region of the mandible,
Occurs mainly in females of African origin aged between 40 and 50 years.
Three main types:
Periapical
Focal and
Florid.
Periapical type is usually seen in the anterior mandible,
Focal type is usually involving single teeth in the posterior mandible
Florid type is seen all quadrants but mainly in the posterior part of the mandible.
Generally symptomless and are incidentally diagnosed during routine radiographic examinations.
Investigations
Radiographically ranging from radioluscencies, mixed radioluscent-radioopaque, and completely radiopaque lesions.
Non-Pharmacological Management
They are only treated when they produce symptoms, interfere with other dental treatments or when infected.
When surgery is indicated, complete enucleation is necessary.
Pharmacological Management
Management is similar to chronic osteomyelitis above
Odontoma (Compound and Complex)
This is a developmental malformation made up of enamel, dentin, cementum, and pulp (odontogenic tissues) and is considered a hamartoma. It is the most common odontogenic tumours.
Clinical Presentation
Normally discovered incidentally during routine dental examinations or radiographs
Missing eruption of the permanent tooth
They can occur anywhere in the jaws but mainly in the anterior maxilla (compound) and posterior mandible (complex).
Vary in size but can grow to huge lesions
Investigation
Periapical X-ray, OPG, CBCT
Generally, the lesions appear radiopaque with compound type appears as a collection of tooth-like structures, whereas the complex type appears as a disorganized mass of dental tissues.
Management
Surgical (Enucleation)
Non-Odontogenic Benign Tumours
Pregnancy Tumours (also called pyogenic granuloma)
Clinical Presentation
Not a true tumour, but rather a rapid over growth of tissue in response to local irritation.
They most commonly appear after first trimester, grow rapidly, and typically regress after delivery.
Found on the gingiva mainly in between the teeth. Occasionally can occur on the tongue, lips and palate.
They are exophytic, lobulated, or smooth surfaced lesion with a red to purplish color and a soft, spongy texture and easily bleed
Non-Pharmacological Management
Surgical intervention is often not required. However, pregnancy tumors can be removed during the second trimester if they interfere with occlusion, are painful, bleed excessively, or are excessively large. Lesions excised during pregnancy often recur.
After delivery, pregnancy tumors typically recede spontaneously but excision may be necessary for those cases which persist.
Note: Other non- odontogenic tumors are Osteomas, Myxomas, Chondromas, Central giant cell and Fibro-osteoma.

Malignant Soft and Bone Tumours
Oral squamous cell carcinoma
Clinical Presentation
A sore in the mouth that does not heal (most common symptom).
Pain in the mouth.
Persistent lump or thickening of mucosa in the cheek.
Persistent white or red patch on the tongue, gums, tonsils, or lining of the mouth.
Difficult moving jaw or tongue.
Difficult chewing or swallowing.
Enlarged cervical lymph nodes may be present
Note: Take a tissue biopsy of the lesion and send for histopathology investigation or refer the patient as early as possible to a center where there is oral and maxillofacial surgeon and Histopathology unit.
Management
Depending on the stage of tumor, management include; wide tumour excision (stage I, II, and III) and neck dissection followed by radiotherapy or chemotherapy.
For stage IV tumor; depending with general condition of the patient, management may range from palliative chemotherapy or radiotherapy or radio-chemotherapy.
Oral Kaposi’s Sarcoma
Oral Kaposi’s Sarcoma (OKS) is a malignant angioproliferative tumour of endothelial origin involving the oral cavity. It is caused by infection with Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8).
It commonly occurs in the context of advanced HIV-related immunodepression and may represent the first manifestation of HIV infection.
Clinical Presentation
slow- to fast-growing masses
May appear as ecchymotic patches, nodular, and exophytic lesions presenting a color that can vary from dark reddish to purplish blue
Most frequently affected intra-oral sites are the hard-palatal mucosa and the gingiva
Size of the lesions varies from few millimeters to some centimeters and the growing of multiple lesions could lead to large, confluent masses involving an entire area of the oral cavity
Management.
Local surgery and highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) are considered keystones in the management of epidemic KS
Note: For detailed management of KS please refer to the malignancy on chapter twenty-two
Lymphomas
These are group of neoplasms of varying degrees of malignancy which are derived from B-cells of lymphoid tissues, the lymphocytes and histiocytes in any of their developmental stages.
While lymphoma primarily affects lymph nodes, it can also occur in non-lymph node tissue (tonsils, parotid gland, thyroid gland, tongue, paranasal sinuses, and nasal cavity), this is known as extra nodal lymphoma
Lymphoma is classified as Hodgkin lymphoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
Both types of Lymphoma have similar symptoms which may include but not limited to painless swelling of lymph nodes, fever, Night sweats, Unexplained weight loss, and fatigue
Burkitt’s lymphoma (African Jaw Lymphoma)
Burkitt lymphoma is an aggressive non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma characterized by rapid tumor growth, frequently affecting the jaw, abdomen, or central nervous system associated with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV).
Three clinical subtypes: endemic, sporadic, and immunodeficiency-related. The endemic form, common in Africa, is linked to malaria and EBV,
Clinical Presentation
Confined almost exclusively to children between 2–14years of age.
Rapidly growing tumor mass of the jaws, destroying the bone and causing teeth loosening with extension the maxillary, ethmoid and sphenoid sinuses as well as the orbit.
Visceral organ involvement may occur.
Malignant Salivary glands tumours
These are malignancies arising from major salivary glands (parotid gland, submandibular gland, sublingual gland) and minor salivary glands of the upper aerodigestive tract.
The most common malignant salivary glands tumours include mucoepidermoid carcinoma (MEC), acinic cell carcinoma (ACC), adenoid cystic carcinoma (AdCC), carcinoma ex-pleomorphic adenoma (CExPA), and adenocarcinoma.
Clinical Presentation.
Asymptomatic, firm mass with occasional pain and facial paralysis
Some presents with ulceration
Investigations
Ultrasound is the first non- invasive option for evaluating major salivary gland tumors
Computerized tomography (CT)
Management

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC)
Open tissue biopsy
Mainstay treatment of salivary gland malignancies is surgery (wide tumour excision and neck dissection) followed by adjuvant chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy.
Note: Diagnostic confirmation is through histopathology; hence, it is emphasized to do early detection and referral to all patients suspected to have head and neck malignancies. (For detailed management of malignant tumors please refer to the malignancy on chapter twenty-two)

Odontogenic and Non- Odontogenic Cysts
Odontogenic cysts
A group of jaw cysts that are formed from tissues involved in odontogenesis (tooth development).
Odontogenic cysts are closed sacs filled with fluid, and have a distinct membrane derived from rests of odontogenic epithelium.
Non-odontogenic jaw cysts
A group of cysts arising from epithelial remnants of embryonic ducts left behind after embryonal facial and jaw development; they are located deep within the tissues in the region of former epithelial ridges, epithelial walls, and primary facial fissural and cleft structures.
Some few examples of frequently encountered cysts in the orofacial region are:
Dentigerous cyst
Dentigerous cysts, also called follicular cysts, are slow-growing benign and non-inflammatory odontogenic cysts that are thought to be developmental in origin.
Clinical Presentation
Uninfected dentigerous cysts are painless and non - tender on palpation.
Larger cysts cause a marked, smooth, rounded expansion of the bone, which may be reduced to a thin layer of cortical plate.
Investigations
Radiographically, they usually present as a well-defined and unilocular radiolucency surrounding the crown of an unerupted or impacted tooth within the mandible.
Radicular (Apical) cyst
Radicular cyst is an inflammatory jaw cyst originating from epithelial remnants of the periodontal ligament because of inflammation that is generally a consequence of pulp necrosis.
The resulting cyst commonly involves the apex of the affected tooth either by dental caries or trauma.
Investigations
Take OPG or Skull X-ray, the cysts appear as rounded, radiolucent areas sharply demarcated from normal.
Apical periodontal cysts are associated with the roots of dead teeth bone by a thin, radiopaque, limiting line of compact or cortical bone.
Non Pharmacological Management
Dental cystectomy under local or general anesthesia.
Globulomaxillary cyst
The globulomaxillary cyst is a cyst that appears between a maxillary lateral incisor and the adjacent canine. It often causes the roots of adjacent teeth to diverge.
Investigations
It exhibits as an "inverted pear-shaped radiolucency" on radiographs, or X-ray films.
Non-Pharmacological Management
Dental cystectomy under local or general anesthesia.
Dermoid Cyst
Dermoid cysts are rare masses of the oral cavity derived from ectodermal elements. They are benign, slow-growing tumors that are typically asymptomatic but cause complications of inflammation or dysphagia, dystonia, and airway encroachment due to mass effects.
Clinical Presentation
Massive swelling of the floor of the mouth, which had displaced the tongue cranially.
Painless slowly growing cystic lesion in the sublingual and or submental spaces.
A dentigerous cyst may be suspected where a tooth is missing from the arch without any history of previous extraction.
Non-Pharmacological Management
Enucleation through an external approach below the mandible or intraorally though an incision in the floor of the mouth.
Ranula Cyst
A mucous extravasation cyst involving a sublingual gland and is a type of mucocele found on the floor of the mouth.
Clinical Presentation
Translucent, blue, dome-shaped, fluctuant swelling in the tissues of the floor of the mouth.
The swelling is not fixed, may not show blanching, and is non-painful unless it becomes secondarily infected.
The usual location is lateral to the midline, which may be used to help distinguish it from a midline dermoid cyst.
Non-Pharmacological Management
Excision of sublingual salivary gland which is affected.

Management of Oral Conditions during Pregnancy
The oral changes which are seen in pregnancy include gingivitis, gingival hyperplasia, pyogenic granuloma, and salivary changes.
Gastric acid secretion and the reflux of the acid into the oral cavity leads to worsening of enamel erosion, increased caries risk, increased tooth mobility and loss.
For the first trimester (1-12weeks)
During the first trimester, it is recommended that the patients be scheduled to assess their current dental health, to inform them of the changes that they should expect during their pregnancies, and to discuss on how to avoid maternal dental problems that may arise from these changes.
Recommendations
Educate the patients about the maternal oral changes which occur during pregnancy. Emphasize strict oral hygiene instructions and thereby, plaque control.
Limit dental treatment to a periodontal prophylaxis, normal filling, and emergency treatments only.
Avoid routine radiographs.
They should be used selectively and only whenever they are needed.
For the second trimester (13-24weeks)
During the second trimester, the organogenesis is complete, and the risk to the fetus is low.
The mother has also had time to adjust to her pregnancy, and the fetus has not grown to a potentially uncomfortable size that would make it difficult for the mother to remain still for long periods.
Recommendations
Maintenance of oral hygiene and plaque control.
It’s safe to perform scaling, polishing and curettage if necessary.
Active oral diseases should be controlled.
It’s safe to perform elective procedures i.e. Root canal, extraction, restorations.
Avoid routine radiographs. Use selectively and when they are needed.
For the third trimester (25-40weeks)
The fetal growth continues and the focus of the concern now, is the risk to the upcoming birth process and the safety and comfort of the pregnant woman. It is safe to perform a routine dental treatment in the early part of the 3rd trimester.
Recommendations
Maintenance of oral hygiene and plaque control.
It’s safe to perform scaling, polishing and curettage if necessary.
Active oral diseases should be controlled.
It’s safe to perform elective procedures.
The radiograph use should be minimized.
Procedures should not to be performed after mid time of the third trimester, unless it is emergency or life threatening condition
Note: Pregnancy should not be considered as an absolute reason to deny required dental care. Pregnant patients must be educated about the importance of maintaining good oral hygiene, expected changes in the oral cavity and routine dental visits.

Temporal Mandibular Disorder and Chronic Orofacial Pain
Temporomandibular disorders (TMD) are disorders of the jaw muscles, temporomandibular joints, and the nerves associated with chronic facial pain.
Temporomandibular Disorders (TMDs)
A collective term embracing several clinical problems that involve the masticatory musculature, the temporomandibular joint and associated structures, or both.
Clinical Presentation
Facial pain.
Limitation of jaw motion.
Clicking on the joint site
Muscle tenderness and stiffness.
Along with any number of associated symptoms in the head, face, and neck region.
Investigations
Plain X-ray of involved joint/ joints.
Panoramic X-ray
CBCT or CT scan
Diagnostic arthroscopy (Intervention Radiology)
Non-Pharmacological Management
Reassurance and counseling
Provide counseling to the patient on the natural history and course of temporomandibular disorders, the role of stress and parafunctional habits such as clenching and grinding of the teeth, the frequency of the problem in the population, and the self- limited nature of the disorder.
Heat application
Application of heat to the sides of the face with a heating pad, hot towel, or hot-water bottle. Vigorous treatment may be achieved with ultrasound or short-wave diathermy heat treatments, which are widely available in physiotherapy units.
Fabrication of Intraoral Occlusal Orthotic Appliances
These devices are worn on the teeth like a retainer or a removable denture and are usually made of processed, hard acrylic.
Physiotherapy
Perform manual manipulation, massage, and ultrasonography, which are helpful in reconditioning and retraining the masticatory and the other cranio-cervical muscles that are usually involved in temporomandibular disorders.
Arthrocentesis
Under Local anesthesia TMJ joint lavage is done through cutaneous needle puncture using 25 to 60ml of lactate Ringer Solution with or without intraarticular injection.

Temporomandibular Joint (TMJ) Dislocation.
TMJ dislocation occurs when the mandibular condyle moves out of its normal position in the glenoid fossa of the temporal bone, typically anterior to the articular eminence. It can be unilateral or bilateral and is often painful and distressing for the patient.
Clinical Presentation
Inability to close the mouth
Pain in the preauricular area
Difficulty speaking and swallowing
Facial asymmetry (especially in unilateral dislocations)
Mouth stuck in an open position
Palpable depression in the preauricular area
Condyle displaced anteriorly and inferiorly
Investigations
Clinical diagnosis based on history and physical examination
Plain X-rays (Panoramic or Lateral TMJ view): may help confirm dislocation
Management
Acute Anterior TMJ Dislocation:
Manual Reduction (Hippocratic technique)
Patient seated with head supported
Provider stands in front, places thumbs over the lower molars (with gauze padding) and fingers under the mandible
Downward and posterior pressure applied to guide the condyle back into place
Use sedation (e.g., midazolam, diazepam) or local anesthetic if needed to overcome muscle spasm
Post-reduction care
Apply a soft bandage (Barton bandage) to limit mouth opening
Advise soft diet for 1–2 weeks
Avoid wide mouth opening (yawning, dental procedures)
Note: for chronic TMJ dislocation, or unattended dislocation for more than two weeks, refer the patient to maxillofacial surgeon for surgical reduction.

Trigeminal Neuralgia
A sudden, usually unilateral, severe, brief, stabbing, recurrent pain in the distribution of one or more branches of the fifth cranial nerve.
Clinical Presentation
Episodes of severe, shooting, or stabbing pain that may feel like an electric shock.
Spontaneous attacks of pain triggered by things such as touching the face, chewing, speaking, or brushing teeth.
Pain in areas supplied by the trigeminal nerve, including the cheek, jaw, teeth, gums, lips, or less often the eye and forehead.
Pain affecting one side of the face at a time
Persistent Idiopathic Orofacial Pain (a Typical Facial Pain, a Typical Odontalgia)
A persistent facial pain that does not have the characteristics of the cranial neuralgias and is not attributed to another disorder.
Clinical Presentation
Poorly localized deep pain that does not follow anatomically defined patterns.
Patients may have had multiple dental treatments to try and remove the pain.
There is a female preponderance in the third to fourth decades.
Investigation
Thorough clinical history and examination
Take radiographs of the dentition preferable OPG
Non-Pharmacological Management
Irreversible or invasive procedures should not be undertaken on teeth to try and relieve the pain if the clinical picture, vitality testing or radiographic examination would not support the procedure.

Management of Cleft Lip and Palate
A cleft lip is a birth defect where the upper lip fails to form completely, creating a gap that may extend into the nose. It can occur on one side (unilateral) or both sides (bilateral) and may appear as a small notch or a wide opening.
A cleft palate occurs when the tissues that form the roof of the mouth (palate) do not fully come together during fetal development. This results in an opening that can affect the hard palate (the bony front portion) and/or the soft palate (the soft back portion) of the mouth. Cleft palates can occur with or without a cleft lip
Component of Management
Recommended Intervention
Timing/Remarks
1. Multidisciplinary Team Care
Management should be coordinated by a multidisciplinary cleft team comprising a maxillofacial/plastic surgeon, pediatrician, speech-language pathologist, orthodontist, prosthodontist, endodontist/pediatric dentist, audiologist, psychologist/social worker, nutritionist, and nurse coordinator.
Team approach from diagnosis through adulthood.
2. Prenatal Diagnosis and Counselling
Antenatal ultrasound may detect cleft lip from 18–20 weeks of gestation.
Provide genetic counselling where indicated.
Counsel parents regarding feeding, treatment plan, prognosis, and recurrence risk.
During pregnancy following diagnosis.
3. Initial Postnatal Care
Assess feeding ability, airway, associated congenital anomalies/syndromes, and hearing.
Provide feeding support using appropriate feeding techniques and specialized bottles/teats where available.
Manage airway compromise, particularly in Pierre Robin sequence.
Refer early to a specialized cleft team.
Immediately after birth.
Component of Management
Recommended Intervention
Timing/Remarks
4. Surgical Management
Cheiloplasty (Cleft Lip Repair):
Techniques: Millard rotation-advancement, Tennison-Randall, etc.
Goal: Restore normal lip anatomy, function, and symmetry.
Around 3 months of age (Rule of 10s).
Palatoplasty (Cleft Palate Repair):
Goals: Restore separation of oral and nasal cavities, enable normal speech.
Techniques: Von Langenbeck, Furlow double- opposing Z-plasty, Veau-Wardill-Kilner V-Y
Usually between 9–18 months to facilitate normal speech development.
Alveolar Bone Grafting:
Purpose: Stabilize maxillary arch, support tooth eruption.
Usually at 7–9 years before eruption of permanent canine teeth.
Secondary Procedures:
Speech surgeries (e.g., pharyngeal flap, sphincter pharyngoplasty).
Revision surgeries (lip and nose).
Orthognathic surgery (for maxillary advancement in adolescence).
Speech surgery, lip/nasal revision, fistula repair, and orthognathic surgery when indicated.
5. Dental and Orthodontic Care
Nasoalveolar moulding (NAM) before primary lip repair where expertise is available.
Preventive dental care including oral hygiene instruction and professional fluoride application.
Interceptive orthodontics for arch expansion and tooth alignment.
Comprehensive orthodontic treatment during mixed/permanent dentition.
Prosthodontic rehabilitation (obturators, crowns, implants) when indicated.
Continuous from infancy through adulthood.
6. Speech and Language Therapy
Early speech and language assessment and therapy following palate repair. Assess and manage velopharyngeal insufficiency.
Begins after palate repair and continues as required.
7. Audiology and Hearing Care
Regular hearing assessment.
Monitor for otitis media with effusion.
Insert tympanostomy (ventilation) tubes when indicated.
Manage hearing impairment according to severity.
Regular follow-up throughout childhood.
8. Psychosocial Support
Psychological assessment and counselling.
Family education and support.
Promote school and community integration and address self-esteem and body image concerns.
Throughout childhood and adolescence.
9. Long-Term Follow-Up
Regular follow-up to monitor facial growth, dental development, speech, hearing, nutrition, psychosocial wellbeing, and need for additional surgical or rehabilitative interventions.
Continue into adolescence and adulthood.
10. Public Health Measures
Promote early detection and timely referral.
Strengthen community awareness and health worker training.
Facilitate access to comprehensive cleft care through national referral systems and financial protection mechanisms.
Ongoing health system intervention.

General Management of Trauma and Injuries
Trauma may occur because of motor vehicle crashes, fights, falls, gunshots, sports, animal bites etc. and is associated with head, musculoskeletal, visceral, and neurovascular injuries. The aim of managing trauma is to prevent further injuries and life- threatening complications that may lead to increased morbidity and mortality. There is a systematic trauma protocol in place, ABCDE protocol, emphasizing on the primary survey, resuscitation, secondary survey, and finally definitive care.

Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI)
TBI is defined as an alteration in brain function, or other evidence of brain pathology, caused by an external force. TBI is a leading cause of death and permanent disability worldwide. Primary brain injury occurs at time of trauma (e.g., cortical contusions, brain lacerations, diffuse axonal injury) while secondary injury develops following the initial insult (brain edema, hypoxemia, ischemia due to elevated intracranial pressure). TBI is often associated with ophthalmic, ENT, dental and maxillofacial injuries.

Prehospital and Lower-Level Health Facilities Interventions
Take important history from patients and relatives (AMPLE)
Apply the BLS trauma protocol and perform a rapid neurological assessment
Protect the C -spine stabilizes the neck with rigid neck collar/improvised alternative devices until the x-ray c-spine is done

Give IV normal saline infusion through large gauge cannula
Avoid SBP of <90 mmHg in adults and older children
Catheterize the bladder and ensure urine output above 30ml per hour
Refer all polytrauma or isolated TBI patients with GCS<13, to center capable of providing definitive care.
Referred patients should be accompanied by a competent adult during transport.
Inform the destination hospital (by phone or letter of referring to non-emergencies) of the impending transfer.
Note: Do not give dextrose infusion for resuscitation in TBI.
Referral hospital and higher-level Facilities Interventions
Follow the ATLS ABCD trauma protocol
Send for rapid non -contrast brain CT scan all moderate and severe TBI patients
Consider CT scan in mild TBI cases with following clinical stigmata
signs of basal skull fracture (hemotympanum, racoon eyes, CSF leak, Battle's sign)
GCS of less than 15 2hrs post TBI
Persistent headache and vomiting post TBI
Post-traumatic seizures or presence of focal neurological deficits,
age 65years or older, any history of bleeding or clotting disorders, or on blood thinners/anticoagulants.
dangerous mechanism of injury or deterioration of GCS
Management of mild TBI patients
Admit and observe for 24 hours all patients with mild TBI and normal CT scan
Discharge with instructions on danger signs that may require hospital re-admission.
Seizures, severe headache, focal neurological deficits
Alteration in level of consciousness and confusion
Perform clinic al follow up assessment after 2weeks.
Individualize management of mild TBI with abnormal CT findings based on clinical judgement.
Management of Blood Pressure
Maintain SBP at 100mmHg to ensure cerebral perfusion.

Management of Moderate and Severe TBI
Multidisciplinary approach is of paramount importance in TBI management.
Admit all moderate and severe TBI patients to ICU for neurocritical care management.
Initiate a Cerebral Perfusion Pressure/Intracranial Pressure (CPP-ICP) oriented protocol.
Critical Care Management of Moderate and Severe TBI Management of Airway and Mechanical Ventilation
Consider endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation for all severe TBI patients.
Rapid sequence intubation is mostly recommended with direct laryngoscope
For intubated patients: maintain ETCO2 between 35-45mmHg, PH7.3 to 7.4, Spo2 >95%.
Maintain ventilation rates as follows: children, 20breaths/min; adolescents/adults, 10 breaths/min.
Target tidal volume of 6 -7ml/kg to maintain the ETCO2 within the above target range.
Avoid prophylactic hyperventilation except only for obvious signs of herniation.
In such cases, only mild hyperventilation is recommended with ETCO2 target range of 30- 35mmHg.
Consider early tracheostomy to reduce mechanical ventilation days in anticipated prolonged intubation patients (severe and some Moderate TBI) (within 7 to 10days)
Give IV fluid resuscitation with an initial bolus of 1L of NS and 20ml/kg.
Consider vasopressors if adequate volume resuscitation does not maintain target MAP
Note: Treatment of hypertension: In TBI, the treatment of acute hypertension is not recommended. Might be a sign of Cushing triad (High BP, Bradycardia, irregular respiration), pain or paroxysmal. sympathetic discharges, blockage of ETT or tracheostomy.
ICP Monitoring and Management
Monitor ICP using external ventricular drain (EVD) technique (gold standard of ICP monitoring) the insertion is done at OR
Consider ICP monitoring in GCS 8 or evidence of structural brain damage on initial CT scan.
Initiate ICP treatment to monitored patient whenever ICP increases to 20-25 mm Hg
Perform interval plain CT scan to monitor ICP where no invasive facilities to monitor ICP is available.
Use a “stepladder approach” with escalating treatment measures to manage ICP.
Head of bed elevation at 200 adequate analgesia sedation using short-acting agents
Prescribe hyperosmolar agents in presence of intracranial mass lesions.
C: mannitol (IV) 0.25 - 1gm/kg boluses 4-6hourly for 24-72hours.
OR
C: sodium chloride 3% (IV) at 3mls/kg infused over 4hrs, repeat electrolyte after 3hrs if still low the dose can be repeated. Don’t exceed 10Meq/ml rise in 24hrs.
Use hypertonic saline in medical management of TBI patients with hypovolemia to avoid lowering the CPP
Monitor serum sodium levels and osmolality every 6hours during hyperosmolar therapy
Stop if serum osmolality exceeds 320mOsm/L or serum Sodium level exceeds 150mEq/L
Consider barbiturate coma for patients who fail to respond to aggressive measures to control ICP
Note: The use of steroids is NOT recommended for improving outcome for reducing ICP in TBI
Neurosurgical Interventions for TBI
Refer for emergency neurosurgical evaluation all patients with epidural hematomas (EDH), subdural hematomas (SDH), cerebral contusions, or intracerebral hematomas (ICH) with significant mass effect to the brain.
Consider craniotomy and hematoma evacuation for EDH with estimated volume above 30CC and Subdural hematoma with thickness above10mm or midline shift above 5mm
A lower threshold for surgical intervention is recommended for posterior fossa mass lesions.
A formal craniotomy is necessary to perform adequate evacuation of intracranial mass lesions
Consider decompressive craniectomy to relieve ICP only when medical treatment of raised ICP has failed and benefits outweigh the risks for such a procedure.
Elevate depressed skull fractures where surgical approach is indicated:
Open depressed fractures, gross contamination to prevent infection,
Low bleeding risk, e.g., no risk of dural venous sinus lacerations.
Exoscope Cistern ostomy.
Note: Depressed skull fracture over the sagittal sinus SHOULD NOT be treated surgically because of the high risk of uncontrollable hemorrhage
Extracranial Surgical Interventions
Delay non emergent extracranial surgical interventions in TBI patients unless they are life- saving procedures.
Orthopedic operations should ideally be delayed 24 -48 hours to allow initial stabilization of ICP
Consider damage control orthopedics with initial external fixation and later definitive treatment to minimize the risk for “second hit “phenomenon

Diabetes Mellitus

CHAPTER NINETEEN
METABOLIC AND ENDOCRINE DISEASE CONDITIONS
Diabetes mellitus is a clinical syndrome characterized by persistently high blood glucose values due to deficiency or diminished effectiveness of insulin.
Classification
Diabetes mellitus can be classified as follows:
Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM) – due to autoimmune β-cell destruction
Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) – due to a progressive loss of β-cell insulin secretion frequently with underlying insulin resistance
Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) – diabetes diagnosed at any time of pregnancy that was not clearly overt diabetes prior to gestation
Specific types of diabetes – due to other causes e.g., MODY, LADA, diseases of the exocrine pancreas, endocrinopathies and drugs or chemicals.
Clinical Presentation
Main clinical features of diabetes are thirst, polydipsia, polyuria, tiredness, loss of weight, blurring of vision.
Many people have no classical symptoms and may only present late with the symptoms related to complications e.g., pruritus vulvae and balanitis due to infections, paresthesia or pain in the limbs, non-healing ulcers, and recurrent bacterial infections.
WHO diagnostic Criteria 2011
Fasting plasma glucose level ≥ 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL)
Plasma glucose≥ 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) two hours after a 75 g oral glucose load in a glucose tolerance test
Symptoms of hyperglycemia and random plasma glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL)
Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) ≥ 6.5%.
Note: HbA1c is not reliable in individuals with hemoglobinopathies (sickle cell anemia, thalassemia) other types of anemia and other conditions affecting red blood cell lifespan.
Diabetes Mellitus in Pregnancy
Women in early pregnancy with levels of HbA1c≥6.5% or blood glucose levels fasting ≥7.0 mmol/l or two hours ≥11.1 mmol/l which are diagnostic of diabetes should be treated as having pre-existing diabetes (type 1 or type2).
The diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus after 15weeks pregnancy should be based on any one of the following values:
Fasting plasma glucose = 5.1-6.9 mmol/l (92 -125 mg/dl)
1-h post 75g oral glucose load >=10.0 mmol/l (180 mg/dl) *
2-h post 75g oral glucose load 8.5 – 11.0 mmol/l (153-199 mg/dl)
At risk screening
Early diagnosis and good control reduce the risk of costly complications and reduces the deterioration of islet function in T2DM. The following people should therefore be screened with fasting blood glucose or HbA1c at least yearly when they visit health facilities:
Those aged ≥40 years
Children and adults <40 years who are overweight or obese and who have two or more additional risk factors for diabetes
Individuals with HbA1C 5.7-6.4%, FBG 5.6 to 6.9mmol/(IFG), 2hour post OGTT 75g BG 7.8 to 11mmol/l(IGT).
People on long-term steroids or immunosuppressants
Women with a history of gestational diabetes mellitus or polycystic ovary syndrome
All pregnant women at the first antenatal visit if overweight, have had gestational diabetes, babies with birth weight >4 kg, previous stillbirths or neonatal deaths. Screening should be repeated in the second trimester if negative.

Management of Diabetes during Religious Fasting
There are several types of fasting:
Normal fast (the common fast): the person abstains from all foods but can take water for a limited time. Or abstain from food and water for a specific number of hours during the day.
Total fast = total abstinence from both food and water. This should not go beyond a maximum of three days and is not recommended for those people taking insulin secretagogues or insulin.
Partial fast = abstain from selected foods and drinks, or omit a certain meal each of the fasting days.
Those with very poor glucose control should be discouraged from fasting
A total fast is not recommended for anyone with high risk. Adequate hydration is important even during the period of fasting.
For those on insulin, a partial fast is preferred to total or normal forms of fasting.
Self-blood glucose monitoring is mandatory for people with diabetes who elect to fast.
Once-a-day is adequate for patients on diet only or diet with metformin.
At least 3 times a day in patients on insulin secretagogues
More frequently if hyperglycemia is marked and the urine tested for ketones.
Consider terminating the fast if frequent hypoglycemia or intercurrent infections.
Vigorous activity should be avoided during period of fast.
Ensure ready access to a healthcare provider during the period of fast.
Management of normal fasting for people treated with oral hypoglycemic agents
Fasting is possible in this situation.
Usual dietary advice should be followed at this time.
Patients on metformin, alpha-glucosidase inhibitors and thiazolidinediones can continue taking the usual doses at the time of breaking the fast and before dawn (if they have another meal at that time).
If on a second or third generation sulphonylureas (glibenclamide, gliclazide, glipizide, glimepiride), this should be taken at the time of breaking the fast and not before dawn.
Management of normal fasting for T2DM patients on insulin
If on 24 hourly insulin before bed, this can be given as usual
If on 12 hourly short- and intermediate-acting insulin:
Before the dawn meal, give the usual evening dose of short-acting insulin without any intermediate-acting insulin.
Before the evening meal give the usual morning dose of short-acting and intermediate-acting insulin.
If on basal bolus regimen:
Usual doses of the short-acting insulin can be given before the dawn and evening meals, and usual doses of the intermediate-acting insulin can still be given at 10pm.
Regular SBGM is essential to ensure prevention of hypoglycemia
Titration of doses should occur according to SBGM results.
Neither the insulin injection nor the breaking of the skin for SBGM will break the fast.

Hyperglycemia in Pregnancy
Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) is any degree of glucose intolerance first recognized in pregnancy. Diabetes in pregnancy refers to those with pre-existing diabetes, whether diagnosed or not.
Screening at first antenatal visit
Perform screening in all women at the first antenatal clinic attendance if they have:
BMI > 30 kg/m2
Previous history of GDM
Previous big baby >4000g
Poor obstetric history
family history of DM
Older maternal age>35
Screening later in Pregnancy
Known impaired glucose tolerance (plasma glucose 7.8-11mmol/l 2hrs after 75 OGTT)
