CHAPTER TWENTY- FIVE POISONING
Poison is any substance (liquid, solid, gas), that is harmful to the body, when ingested, inhaled, injected or absorbed through the skin. There is a variability of the clinical presentation and poisonings vary by nature of poison, victims’ age group, intention, geographic region, and level of economic development. Poisons can be classified according to whether the chemical is metallic versus nonmetallic, organic versus inorganic, or acidic versus alkaline.
Common Poisons
The common poisoning in our settings are:
Household agents:
Chemicals e.g. detergents, Kerosene, Disinfectants and bleach
Pesticides e.g. Organophosphate, malathion (insecticide), nuvan top and rat poison.
Medicines e.g. Acetylsalicylic Acid, Paracetamol, Anticonvulsants (carbamazepine), Hematinic (Iron and Vitamins),
Major tranquilizers and herbal products
Foods e.g. Mushroom, infected foods
General Principles of Management of Poisoning
In managing a patient who has been exposed to toxins holistic approach should be considered.
Note
A low respiratory rate with decreased oxygen saturations may indicate hypoventilation. A normal saturation does not exclude hypercarbia or indeed hypoxia in carbon monoxide poisoning. If in any doubt, arterial blood gases should be measured. Tachypnoea can be seen with metabolic acidosis (e.g. tricyclics, methanol), anxiety, and stimulant drug overdose and as an early feature of salicylate poisoning (respiratory alkalosis).
Supplementary oxygen via facemask should be given to all patients initially, taking account of pulse oximetry (noting the limitations described above).
Many drugs exhibit cardiovascular toxicity hypotension and or cardiac arrhythmias in overdose (e.g. tricyclics, b- blockers, digoxin, lithium). ECG should be recorded, intravenous access established and initial fluid resuscitation given as appropriate
General examination may give corroborating evidence of significant ingestions or clues in unknown overdoses (SSRIs, tricyclics, phenothiazines) have serotonergic or anticholinergic effects with pupil dilatation, and extrapyramidal movements, whilst opioid type drugs will cause sedation and pin point pupils.
Temperature, blood glucose (low in b-blocker, ethanol poisoning)
Weight is important in identifying a toxic dose against the weight and may guide treatment, for example in paracetamol overdose.
Examination for injury (intentional or un-intentional self-harm) suggest appropriate methods for treatment, or the presence of other substances such as alcohol.
If clinical condition allows, an assessment of the patient’s mental state should be made.
Resuscitation and stabilization which is key to every poison refer to EMD Chapter 1
Airway, breathing and circulation should be reassessed and treated accordingly as a priority. Refer Approach to patient with Emergency conditions chapter 1.

Management of Ingested Poisons
Ingested toxins are suspected in any patient with signs and symptoms irrespective of reported dose ingested.
Clinical Presentations
General clinical features: Nausea, vomiting, drowsiness, blurred vision, and dizziness
Central Nervous System toxicity: Altered level of consciousness, convulsions, acute confusion and coma,
Renal Toxicity: Acute kidney injury/failure and papillary necrosis
Metabolic derangement: Metabolic acidosis, respiratory acidosis, hypoglycemia.
Allergic reactions: Urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis
Haematological toxicity: Aplastic anaemia, agranulocytosis
Non-Pharmacological Management
Gastric decontamination – Functional removal of an ingested toxin from the gastrointestinal tract to reduce absorption. This may include:
Gastric evacuation:
Forced emesis is not recommended and is highly discouraged.
Gastric lavage is not routinely recommended and should only be considered in life-threatening poisoning when:
>Poison was ingested within 30 minutes to 1 hour, AND
>No safer alternative decontamination method is available.
Intragastric binding:
Use of single-dose or multiple-dose activated charcoal may be considered depending on the poison ingested, timing of ingestion, and contraindications. Limitations should be assessed before use.
Enhanced gastrointestinal transit:
Whole bowel irrigation may be considered in selected cases. Routine use of cathartics is not recommended.
Contraindications to Gastric Lavage:
An unprotected airway in an unconscious patient increase aspiration risk
Ingestion of corrosives or petroleum products e.g. kerosene,
Bowel obstruction
Bowel perforation

Treatment is most effective if given as quickly as possible after the poisoning event, ideally within 1 hour.
If the patient has swallowed kerosene, petrol, or petrol-based products (note that most pesticides are in petrol-based solvents) or if the patient’s mouth and throat have been burned (for example with bleach, toilet cleaner or battery acid) do not vomit the patient but give water orally? Never use salt as an emetic as this can be fatal.

Food Poisoning
Food poisoning, also called foodborne illness, is illness caused by eating contaminated food. Infectious organisms including bacteria, viruses, and parasites or their toxins are the most common causes of food poisoning as listed in the table. Large intestine and small intestine have an intermediate incubation from about 1 to 3 days.
Large intestine
Infections of the large intestine or colon can cause bloody, mucous diarrhea associated with crampy abdominal pain.
Campylobacter spp, is the common one cause of food-borne disease
Shigella spp contaminate food and water and cause dysentery (severe diarrhea often containing mucus and blood).
Salmonella spp infections often occur because of poorly or undercooked cooked and/or poor handling of the chicken and eggs. In individuals with weakened immune systems, including the elderly, the infection can enter the bloodstream and cause potentially life- threatening infections.
Vibrio parahaemolyticus can contaminate saltwater shellfish and cause a watery diarrhea.
Small Intestine Infection
Diarrhea due to small bowel infection tends not to be bloody, but infections may affect both the small and large intestine at the same time.
E. coli (enterotoxigenic) is the most common cause of traveler's diarrhea. It lacks symptoms such as fever or bloody diarrhea.
Vibrio cholerae, often from contaminated drinking, water produces a voluminous watery diarrhea resembling rice-water.
Viruses such as Norwalk, rotavirus and adenovirus tend to have other symptoms associated with an infection including fever, chills, headache, and vomiting.
Botulism is caused by Clostridium botulinum toxin and may present with fever, vomiting, mild diarrhea, numbness, and weakness leading to paralysis.

Management of Skin Contamination
Remove all clothing and personal effects and thoroughly flush all exposed areas with copious amounts of running water running for:
5-minutes for non-irritants or mild irritants
15-20 minutes for moderate to severe irritants and chemicals that cause acute toxicity if absorbed through the skin
30 minutes for most corrosives
60 minutes for strong alkalis (e.g., sodium, potassium or calcium hydroxide)
Use non-abrasive soap and water for oily substances
Attending staff should take care to protect themselves from secondary contamination by wearing gloves and apron
Removed clothing and personal effects should be stored safely in a see-through plastic bag that can be sealed, for later cleansing or disposal.
Management of Eye Contamination Non-Pharmacological Management
Immediately irrigate the affected eye with clean running water for 15–20 minutes, ensuring that contaminated runoff does not enter the unaffected eye.
Evert the eyelids and ensure all conjunctival surfaces are adequately irrigated.
For acid or alkali exposure, irrigate t54he eye with copious amounts of water OR normal saline for at least 30 minutes, then reassess.

Continue irrigation for an additional 30 minutes if symptoms persist or ocular pH remains abnormal.
Remove contact lenses if present.
Perform thorough eye examination where possible, including:
Visual acuity assessment
Fluorescein staining to assess corneal injury
Examination for retained foreign material

Management of Inhaled Poisoning Non-Pharmacological Management
Remove the patient from the source of exposure immediately and move to fresh air.
Ensure rescuers avoid exposure to toxic fumes/gases.
Thoroughly ventilate the contaminated area.
If vomiting occurs, place the patient in the recovery position (head turned to the side) to prevent aspiration.
Initiate cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) if there are signs of cardiac arrest.
Contact National Poison Control Centre: 0800 112031 for further guidance.
Monitor for delayed respiratory complications such as: Upper airway edema, Bronchospasm, Chemical pneumonitis, delayed pulmonary edema (observe for 24–48 hours where indicated)

Do NOT perform gastric lavage routinely due to high risk of aspiration pneumonitis.

If a large ingestion occurred within 1 hour, and
Airway is protected by expert endotracheal intubation.

Bites and Stings
Most serious sting-related reactions are caused by insects of the order Hymenoptera, particularly: Bees, Wasps and Ants. Other arthropods/venomous creatures that may also cause bites or stings include: Spiders, Scorpions, Centipedes, Millipedes.

Localized pain at the bite/sting site, Swelling, Redness, Itching. Severe reactions may include: Generalized urticaria, Angioedema, Wheezing, Difficulty breathing, Hypotension, Anaphylaxis.

Clean the affected area with soap and water to remove contaminants
If a stinger is present (e.g., bee sting), remove it gently by scraping with a fingernail, card, or gauze
Avoid using tweezers because they may squeeze additional venom into the wound
Apply a cold compress/cold pack wrapped in cloth to reduce pain and swelling
Avoid scratching to prevent skin breakdown and secondary infection

CHAPTER TWENTY- SIX RHEUMATOLOGICAL DISORDERS
Rheumatological disorders, also known as rheumatic diseases, comprise a diverse group of conditions that primarily affect the joints, bones, muscles, tendons, ligaments, and connective tissues. Many are driven by autoimmune and inflammatory processes, often leading to multi-organ involvement.
These diseases are usually chronic, may cause long-term disability, and often require multidisciplinary care. Management involves immunosuppressive therapy, including corticosteroids, conventional DMARDs, and biological agents. Accurate diagnosis and thorough assessment are crucial for guiding safe and effective treatment.
Before initiating DMARDs or biologics, it is essential to conduct liver and renal function tests, a chest X-ray, and screen for tuberculosis, HIV, and hepatitis B and C to rule out latent infections and ensure the safety of treatment.

Inflammatory Arthritis
Inflammatory arthritis refers to a group of diseases characterized by inflammation of the joints, including:
Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA)
Axial Spondyloarthritis
Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)

Reactive Arthritis
Enteropathic Arthritis (associated with IBD)
RA is a chronic, systemic autoimmune disease that primarily affects synovial joints, causing symmetrical inflammation, pain, and progressive joint deformity. It often involves the hands and feet, but any synovial joint may be affected. Extra-articular manifestations (such as those affecting the skin, heart, lungs, and eyes) can also occur.
Clinical Presentation
Symmetrical joint swelling, stiffness, and pain
Morning stiffness >30 minutes
Fatigue and general malaise
Extra-articular signs (e.g., nodules, lung or eye involvement)
Small and large joint tenderness, swelling, stiffness, pain on motion, deformity, and functional limitation.
Investigations
CBC: anemia of chronic disease, thrombocytosis, or leukopenia (may occur with Felty's syndrome or DMARD toxicity).
ESR and CRP: used both for diagnosis and monitoring disease activity and treatment response. Serologic tests: RF: Positive in ~70–80% of RA cases; less specific. Anti-CCP: More specific for RA; indicates a risk of severe erosive disease and extra-articular disease.
Imaging
X-ray (hands, wrists, feet): Shows swelling, osteopenia, joint narrowing, and erosions. Chest X-ray to rule out ILD or TB
Ultrasound (US): Detects synovitis, effusion, and erosions earlier than X-ray.
CT: Used for suspected atlantoaxial subluxation, preoperative cervical spine planning, or unclear MRI findings.
MRI: More sensitive, identifying bone marrow edema and early erosions.
Diagnosis
RA is classified by ACR/EULAR 2010 criteria with a score ≥6/10 based on joints, serology, inflammation markers, and symptom duration.
Treatment consideration
Assess disease activity using the Disease Activity Score in 28 joints (DAS28), Clinical Disease Activity Index (CDAI), and Simplified Disease Activity Index (SDAI)
Monitor and adjust treatment every 3 months
Follow a treat-to-target strategy with tight control
Aim for low disease activity or remission within 6 months
Non-Pharmacological Management:
Education
Physical therapy
Occupational therapy
Lifestyle: Smoking cessation, Healthy diet & weight control, Psychosocial support.
Pharmacological Management
Disease-modifying anti-rheumatic Drugs (DMARDs)
DMARDs are the cornerstone of RA treatment. They should be started as soon as the diagnosis is made.
Conventional Synthetic DMARDs (csDMARDs)
All patients with active rheumatoid arthritis should be initiated on methotrexate as first-line therapy unless there are contraindications or intolerance
S: methotrexate (PO) Start with 10–15 mg/week; increase by 5 mg every 2–4 weeks, depending on the response, up to a maximum of 20-25mg/week.
AND
A: folic acid (PO) 5 mg weekly, taken a day before methotrexate. For severe toxicity, give daily (except on methotrexate day)
OR
S: leflunomide (PO) 10–20 mg 24hourly.
OR
S: hydroxychloroquine (PO) 200–400mg 24hourly, (usually 5 mg/kg/day, max 400 mg/day).
OR
D: sulfasalazine (PO) 500 mg twice daily initially; increase by 500 mg every week to target 2–3 g/day in divided doses maintenance dose 1–1.5 g twice daily.
If the response is inadequate, step-up combination therapy of csDMARDs is advised.
Note:
Hydroxychloroquine: Annual eye exam after 5 years or earlier if high risk.
Methotrexate: Split dose or subcutaneous if poorly tolerated.
Sulfasalazine: Avoid sulfa allergy.
Triple therapy: Combines methotrexate, sulfasalazine, and hydroxychloroquine; leflunomide may be used as an alternative to methotrexate.
Methotrexate & leflunomide: Contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Avoid leflunomide in women planning pregnancy.
Biologic DMARDs (bDMARDs)
In moderate-to-severe RA not controlled by csDMARDs, adding a bDMARD or tsDMARD is preferred.
S: rituximab (IV) 1000 mg on days 1 and 15; may repeat every 6 months or based on response.
OR
S: adalimumab (SC) 40 mg subcutaneously every other week (may increase to weekly if needed)
OR
S: tocilizumab (IV) 4mg/kg every other 4 weeks may increase to 8mg/kg (Max 800mg/dose)
Targeted Synthetic DMARDs (tsDMARDs)
JAK inhibitors are used after the failure of csDMARDs or bDMARDs.
S: tofacitinib (PO) 5 mg12hourly.
Glucocorticoids
Used for short-term (< 3 months) control and as bridging therapy.
A: prednisolone (PO) 5–15 mg/day orally (4-6 weeks). Gradually reduce over weeks to months, depending on the response
OR
D: methylprednisolone (IV/IM) 500–1000 mg daily for 1–3 days for severe flares.
OR
S: triamcinolone acetonide: deep IM 10–40 mg monthly or IA in case only 1-2 joints are affected
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs)
Used for symptom control only (do not modify disease course).

OR
C: diclofenac (PO) 50mg 8-12hourly
OR
A: piroxicam (PO) 20mg 24hourly
OR
D: meloxicam (PO) 7.5–15 mg 24hourly

OR

OR

OR
A: diclofenac gel 1% apply 6 hourly
Note: In patients at high risk of NSAID-related gastrointestinal complications, co-administration of a PPI should be considered to reduce the risk of PUD and UGB
Surgical management
is indicated when medical treatment fails to relieve pain, maintain function, or prevent deformity.
Peripheral joint care:
Joint replacement
Synovectomy
Tendon repair or transfer
Arthrodesis
Cervical Spine Involvement
Atlantoaxial subluxation should be routinely monitored in long-standing RA; surgery is indicated in cases of instability with neurological symptoms.
Basilar invagination (BI) may occur due to ligamentous and bony weakening. Surgical management includes decompression and stabilization via C1–C2 fusion or craniovertebral fusion, depending on severity.
Perioperative and Postoperative Considerations
Biologics and JAK inhibitors should be temporarily withheld perioperatively based on the risk of infection and the complexity of the procedure.
Postoperative rehabilitation is crucial for optimizing functional recovery, particularly after joint replacement or tendon procedures.
Special Considerations in RA Treatment
Subcutaneous Nodules: Use methotrexate for active disease; switch DMARD if nodules worsen
Heart Failure (HF) (NYHA III/IV): Prefer non-TNF bDMARDs or tsDMARDs over TNF inhibitors if csDMARDs fail or HF develops.
Pulmonary Disease: MTX is acceptable in mild, stable lung disease or incidental findings.
Lymphoproliferative Disorder: Rituximab is preferred if there is a history of treated lymphoproliferative disease.
Hepatitis B:
HBsAg-positive: Use rituximab with prophylactic antivirals.
Core Ab positive only: Monitor viral load and LFTs.
NAFLD: MTX is safe if LFTs are normal and no advanced fibrosis
Cardiovascular disease: Tofacitinib is contraindicated in patients with a history of myocardial infarction, stroke, or HF.
Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA)
PsA is a chronic inflammatory arthritis that is usually seen in patients with psoriasis, although it may predate skin involvement, which can be subtle. It typically presents as seronegative oligoarthritic, with features such as distal joint involvement, arthritis mutilans, or inflammation of joints, spine, entheses, nails, and skin.
Clinical Presentation
Joints: Asymmetric, DIP, spine, severe deformity (mutilans)
Dactylitis: Swollen “sausage” digits with PIP synovitis
Enthesitis: Tender tendon insertions
Skin/Nails: Psoriasis, nail pitting/onycholysis
Other: Fatigue, stiffness, joint swelling, and tenderness on exam
Investigations
ESR, CRP (sometimes normal)
RF and anti-CCP (usually negative)
HLA-B27 for those with suspected axial involvement.
X-rays: First-line; show erosions, new bone, pencil-in-cup, ankylosis, asymmetric sacroiliitis.
Ultrasound: Shows synovitis, enthesitis, tenosynovitis; Doppler detects active inflammation
MRI: gold standard test for sacroiliitis and spinal involvement
Diagnosis
PsA is diagnosed using CASPAR criteria, requiring inflammatory joint, spine, or enthesis involvement plus ≥3 points from clinical, lab, or imaging features.
Non-Pharmacological Management
Weight reduction
Skin care (avoid trauma)
Physical therapy
Stress reduction
Smoking cessation
Alcohol reduction

For mild peripheral arthritis, enthesitis, or axial symptoms without poor prognostic factors.
Relieve symptoms but don’t prevent damage.
Not for monotherapy in moderate-to-severe disease

OR

Axial Spondyloarthritis
A chronic inflammatory rheumatic disease that primarily affects the sacroiliac joints and spine, leading to pain, stiffness, and progressive fusion of the axial skeleton, resulting in reduced spinal mobility.
It is usually classified as:
Non-radiographic axSpA (nr-axSpA): No structural damage seen on X-ray. MRI may show active inflammation of the sacroiliac joints (SIJ)
Radiographic axSpA / Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS): Structural damage to SIJ visible on X-ray (per modified New York criteria). Progressive spinal fusion may occur.
Clinical Presentation
Back pain >3 months, <45 yrs onset, improves with activity, worse at rest
Night pain, buttock pain
Spinal stiffness, ↓ decreased mobility
Peripheral features: arthritis (asymmetric, lower limbs), Enthesitis (heel, Achilles), Dactylitis (sausage digits)
Uveitis (red, painful eye)
Associated diseases: Psoriasis, IBD
Fatigue, weight loss
Rare: heart (aortic regurgitation), lung (apical fibrosis)
Investigations
Laboratory Tests
HLA-B27: Positive in ~80–90% of AS cases
CRP / ESR: May be elevated in active disease
CBC: May show mild anemia of chronic disease
RF and anti-CCP: Typically, negative; helps rule out RA
Imaging
Pelvic X-ray: Sacroiliitis (unilateral or bilateral)
MRI of sacroiliac joints: Detects early inflammation (bone marrow edema)
Spine X-ray/MRI: Shows syndesmophytes or vertebral fusion in advanced disease
Eye exam: If anterior uveitis is suspected
ECG/Echocardiogram: If cardiac involvement is suspected
Diagnosis
AS is diagnosed based on the ASAS 2009 criteria, which require either the presence of sacroiliitis on imaging, accompanied by at least one clinical feature of spondyloarthritis, or HLA-B27 positivity, accompanied by at least two clinical features.
Non-Pharmacological Management
Daily spinal extension and mobility exercises
Structured physical therapy programs
Postural training to prevent kyphosis
Pharmacological Management
Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs)
Smoking cessation (smoking worsens radiographic progression)
Encourage physical activity, avoid prolonged rest or immobilization
First-line therapy: NSAIDs — effective for controlling pain and stiffness; used continuously or on-demand based on symptom severity and response
A: Ibuprofen (PO) 400–800 mg 8 hourly
OR
C: diclofenac (PO) 50 mg 8 hourly /Diclofenac gel 1% apply 6 hourly
OR
A: Piroxicam (PO) 20mg 24 hourly
OR
D: Meloxicam (PO) 7.5–15 mg 24 hourly

OR
S: Ketoprofen (PO) 75 mg 8 hourly
OR
S: Ketoprofen (PO) 50 mg every 6 hourly
OR
S: Ketoprofen gel 2.5% topical, apply to affected area 6 hourly
Biologic DMARDs (bDMARDs)
If NSAIDs are insufficient, biological DMARDs are recommended. Conventional DMARDs have no proven efficacy in axial spondyloarthritis and are not routinely recommended.
S: adalimumab (SC) 40 mg SC every two weeks
Surgical Treatment
Indicated for severe deformity, neurologic compromise, or failed medical therapy.
Corrective osteotomy: For severe kyphosis (e.g., chin-on-chest).
Spinal fusion/stabilization: For unstable fractures in the fused spine.

Decompression: For cord or nerve compression (e.g., cauda equina).
Hip replacement: For advanced hip damage; commonly needed in axSpA
Reactive Arthritis (ReA)
RA is a sterile inflammatory arthritis that occurs 1–4 weeks after an extra-articular infection, most commonly involving the gastrointestinal (e.g., Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, Campylobacter) or genitourinary tract (especially Chlamydia trachomatis).
Clinical Presentation
Arthritis: Asymmetric oligoarthritis (knees, ankles), axial spine, sacroiliitis
Enthesitis & Dactylitis: Common (heel, Achilles, sausage digits)
Genitourinary: Urethritis, cervicitis, prostatitis, circinate balanitis
Eye: Conjunctivitis, uveitis (can threaten vision)
Skin/Mucosa:	Oral	ulcers,	keratoderma blennorrhagicum, nail dystrophy
Systemic: Fatigue, fever, weight loss
Investigations
Inflammatory markers: ESR and CRP may be elevated
CBC: May show leukocytosis, anemia
Infection screen: Urine/genital PCR: Chlamydia and Stool culture: GI pathogens
HLA-B27: Positive in ~50%, linked to severe disease
Joint aspiration: Sterile inflammatory fluid (rule out sepsis)
Imaging: X-ray: May show late sacroiliitis or periostitis
MRI: Detects early sacroiliitis/enthesitis
Diagnosis
Diagnosis is supported by the exclusion of other causes of arthritis (e.g., septic arthritis, crystal arthropathy)
Non-Pharmacological Management
Rest during acute inflammation
Physical therapy to maintain joint function and mobility
Safe sexual practices (e.g., condom use to prevent STI-related recurrence)
Nutritional support, especially if enteric infection led to weight loss or malabsorption
Patient education on the self-limiting nature in most cases and possible chronicity in some cases

Enteropathic Arthritis (Associated with IBD)
Enteropathic arthritis is a seronegative spondyloarthritis associated with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). It can involve both the axial skeleton (spine and sacroiliac joints) and the peripheral joints, and may also present with enthesitis or dactylitis.
Clinical Presentation
Peripheral arthritis: Asymmetric, large joints, Type 1: <5 joints, flares with IBD, Type 2: >5 joints, not linked to IBD activity
Axial arthritis: Sacroiliitis, spondylitis,
Enthesitis (Achilles ' heel), Dactylitis (sausage digits),
Uveitis and Skin: erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum
IBD symptoms: Diarrhea, abdominal pain, bleeding, weight loss
Investigations
ESR and CRP: Often elevated in both IBD and active arthritis
Colonoscopy or gastrointestinal imaging (such as MRI/CT enterography or fluoroscopic barium studies) is used to confirm the diagnosis of IBD or to assess disease activity.
X-ray / MRI: sacroiliac joints for early axial involvement and late changes
HLA-B27: May be positive, especially in those with axial involvement
Autoantibodies: RF and anti-CCP negative (to rule out RA)
Diagnosis
There is no specific classification criterion; however, diagnosis is based on the presence of confirmed IBD (Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis), clinical features of arthritis, and the absence of RF and anti-CCP antibodies.
Non-Pharmacological Management
Physical therapy: Improves mobility and function, especially in axial involvement
Nutritional support: Address malnutrition or deficiencies associated with IBD
Management of underlying IBD: Control of intestinal inflammation often improves joint symptoms
Pharmacological Management
Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs) may ease joint symptoms but can worsen IBD. Use the lowest effective dose briefly. Prefer COX-2 inhibitors for lower GI risk.

OR
C: celecoxib (PO) 100-200mg 12 hourly
OR
S: etoricoxib (PO) 30–60 mg 24 hourly

Crystal Arthropathies
Crystal arthropathies are caused by the deposition of crystals in joints or periarticular tissues, resulting in inflammation and tissue damage. The most common types include:
Gout (Monosodium urate crystals)
Calcium Pyrophosphate Dihydrate Deposition Disease (CPPD)
Gout
A metabolic disease characterized by recurrent attacks of acute arthritis due to monosodium urate (MSU) crystal deposition, typically affecting men and postmenopausal women.
Clinical Presentation
Acute gout attack: sudden, severe joint pain and swelling, often at night
Most	commonly	affects	the	first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint (podagra)
It can also involve ankles, knees, and elbows
Investigations
Serum uric acid (note: may be normal during acute attacks)
ESR/CRP (elevated during attacks)
Renal function (before initiating urate-lowering therapy)
Monoarthritis (usually one joint at a time) is rarely polyarticular or RA-like in late stages or the elderly.
Tophaceous deposits (chronic cases)
Fever may occur in severe cases
Associated with CKD, obesity, HTN, diabetes, and CVD
Ultrasound: crystals, double contour signs
Joint X-rays (look for erosions and tophi)
Joint fluid aspiration (gold standard if feasible): needle-shaped crystals with negative birefringent
Diagnosis : The 2015 ACR/EULAR Gout Classification Criteria define gout as present when the total score is ≥8 points, based on clinical, laboratory, and imaging domains.
Non-Pharmacological Management
Modify your diet by avoiding purine-rich foods (e.g., red meat, organ meats, shellfish), limiting alcohol— especially beer and spirits—and eliminating sugary drinks.
Encourage hydration by drinking 2–3 liters of water per day.
Weight loss in overweight/obese patients
Exercise: low-impact, regular physical activity
Avoid	triggers: Acetylsalicylic acid, thiazide diuretics, excessive alcohol

Calcium Pyrophosphate Dihydrate Deposition Disease (CPPD)
Inflammatory arthritis is caused by the deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals in joint cartilage and soft tissues.
Clinical Presentation
Acute arthritis: Sudden joint pain, swelling, warmth (knees, wrists, shoulders); may mimic gout or infection.
Chronic form: Resembles OA or RA; stiffness, pain, limited motion (knees, wrists, MCPs, hips, spine)
Asymptomatic: Chondrocalcinosis on imaging
Spinal: Crowned dens syndrome (neck pain, stiffness, fever)
Associated	with:	Metabolic	disorders	(e.g., hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis)
Investigations
Synovial fluid: Rhomboid, positively birefringent crystals; inflammatory
X-ray: Chondrocalcinosis, OA-like changes
Ultrasound: Crystal deposits; no double contour
Non-Pharmacological Management
Rest the affected joint during flares
Apply ice packs to reduce swelling
CT/MRI: For spinal involvement (e.g., crowned dens)
Blood tests: ↑ESR/CRP; check calcium, phosphate, magnesium, iron, PTH for metabolic causes
Initiate physiotherapy post-flare to restore mobility
Educate patients about the chronic nature of CPPD

Apply sunscreen with a minimum SPF of 50 before going outside in the sun.

Dermatomyositis (DM) and polymyositis (PM) are inflammatory myopathies causing proximal muscle weakness. DM is marked by distinctive skin rashes (e.g., Gottron’s papules, heliotrope rash), whereas PM lacks skin involvement. Both may lead to significant functional impairment.
Gottron's papules are red or violet, flat-topped, scaly lesions that appear symmetrically over joint extensor surfaces—typically the knuckles, elbows, knees, and ankles
A heliotrope rash is a distinctive reddish-purple or lilac discoloration of the upper eyelids and periorbital region, often associated with DM, an autoimmune inflammatory myopathy.

Proximal muscle weakness: Symmetric, gradual onset

APS is an autoimmune disorder characterized by persistent antiphospholipid antibodies (aPL), leading to increased risk of thrombosis (arterial, venous, or microvascular) and pregnancy-related complications such as recurrent miscarriage, preterm birth, and preeclampsia. Fibromyalgia
Fibromyalgia is a chronic pain syndrome characterized by widespread musculoskeletal pain lasting ≥3 months, associated with fatigue, sleep disturbance, and cognitive dysfunction.
It is a disorder of central pain processing (central sensitization) rather than peripheral inflammation.
Diagnosis
The 2016 Revised ACR Fibromyalgia Diagnostic Criteria assist in diagnosing fibromyalgia. Tender point examination is no longer required; diagnosis is based on the Widespread Pain Index (WPI) and Symptom Severity Score (SSS) with symptoms present for at least 3 months.
Investigations
Laboratory testing should be limited to excluding alternative diagnoses when clinically indicated.
ESR and CRP
CK levels
Thyroid function testing
Vitamin D testing may be considered in selected patients.
Autoimmune serology should not be ordered routinely unless clinical suspicion exists.
Management
Fibromyalgia management should be multimodal and individualized, prioritizing non-pharmacological therapy first, with medications added for persistent moderate to severe symptoms.
Non pharmacological management
Patients should receive structured education about the condition.
Regular graded aerobic exercise and Strength training is strongly recommended.
Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT).

CHAPTER TWENTY- SEVEN APPROACH TO COMMON NEONATAL CONDITIONS
Common neonatal conditions are a major cause of illness and death in the first 28 days of life. Early recognition and prompt management are essential to improve survival and prevent complications.
Assessment begins with rapid identification of emergency signs including respiratory distress, apnoea, shock, convulsions, severe bleeding, hypothermia, poor feeding, and altered consciousness. Immediate management should follow the principles of airway, breathing, circulation, correction of hypoglycemia, and thermal protection.
A focused history should include maternal risk factors, antenatal and intrapartum events, gestational age, birth weight, feeding history, and any history of delayed cry or resuscitation. Physical examination should assess vital signs, respiratory status, hydration, jaundice, signs of infection, congenital abnormalities, and neurological status.
Investigations are guided by clinical findings and may include blood glucose, full blood count, C-reactive protein, blood culture, serum bilirubin, electrolytes, and relevant imaging.
Management involves supportive care (warmth, oxygen, fluids, nutrition, and glucose correction) and specific treatment for conditions such as neonatal sepsis, neonatal jaundice, respiratory distress syndrome, birth asphyxia, and neonatal seizures.
Continuous monitoring and follow-up are essential for early detection of complications and improved outcomes.

Perinatal Asphyxia
Perinatal asphyxia is failure to initiate and sustain breathing after delivery and/or APGAR score of <7 in the 5th minute.
Clinical Presentation
CNS – seizures, abnormal posture, decreased tone, impaired primitive reflexes, bulging fontanelle, irritability or loss of consciousness
CVS – shock/hypotension, myocardial dysfunction, arrhythmia
RS – respiratory distress, pulmonary haemorrhage, pulmonary oedema, apnoea
Investigations
Blood Gas Analysis (where available)
Day 1 of life - FBP and blood culture 6 hours from birth.
Day 2 of life
Check for renal function
CRP to decide on whether to stop antibiotics or not. Stop antibiotics if CRP is < 10 mg/dL.
Serum	Glucose,	Calcium,	Magnesium	and Phosphate
Perform a lumbar puncture in neonates with seizures, and CRP >20 mg/dL.
Non-Pharmacological Management
Renal – oliguria/anuria, renal failure, haematuria (acute tubular necrosis, renal vein thrombosis)
GI – paralytic ileus, bloody stools, necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC)
Hepatic – impaired coagulation of blood
Haematology – thrombocytopenia, DIC
Metabolic	–	acidosis,	hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesemia
LFTs (in those with jaundice) and cardiac enzymes (in those with hypotension/ tachycardia) may be done.
Imaging: Cranial ultrasound between days 1 and 3, at day 7 and at day 14 of life; MRI for brain injury severity, prognostication and exclude the HIE mimics.
Amplitude-integrated electroencephalography (aEEG): Assessing seizure activity, brain function and response to therapy.
Other investigations depending on the presentation and system affected
